Violent murderer Nathan Fenton’s release reignites trauma for ex who survived similar attack

New Zealand Herald November 14, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

When Nathan Fenton was granted parole after serving decades for the brutal murder of teenager Mairina Dunn, it reignited a nightmare for one of his earlier victims.

After admitting he had treated “just about every partner” with violence and disrespect, Fenton’s release has prompted one of the women to speak publicly for the first time about the trauma, guilt and fear she still carries after surviving a chillingly similar attack before Dunn was killed.

Senior journalist Anna Leask reports.

She woke up on Wednesday last week to news that made her blood run cold.

Nathan Fenton had been released from prison.

After more than 20 years behind bars – and despite a psychologist saying he fell “in a group of offenders who pose a very high risk” of reoffending – the Parole Board was satisfied he could be released safely.

Fenton, then aged 31 and a Black Power member, admitted murdering his girlfriend Mairina Dunn at a Whangārei house in August 2006.

Dunn was just 17 when Fenton arrived at her address, drunk and high on methamphetamine, and dragged her from her bed and took her to another room.

The initial beating lasted 90 minutes, during which he used a sawn-off shotgun. The attack then continued for several hours.

Dunn likely died from massive head injuries or a punctured lung.

“It was tough, I just cried for hours,” said the woman when asked about her reaction to Fenton’s release from prison.

“The murder he went inside for could have been prevented and I live with guilt daily. I would like to share my story about this man because all I want is to make people more aware of his behaviour so no one else dies.

“It was very similar … really, really similar."

The woman had been with Fenton for about five months when he attacked her.

She still feels panicked and gets very emotional when she talks about that awful day.

“We were together not long when it happened. We were at a party one night at his place and there were quite a few people there. We were walking outside and a guy smiled at me, and I smiled back,” she says.

“Well, [Fenton] didn’t like that and he attacked me … he just beat me, bad.

“I was in a fetal position outside on the ground trying to protect my face and head. He was just going hard. He picked me up by my hair and smashed me headfirst through a van window.

“People obviously left because of what was going on. But some stayed … a couple of people tried to intervene, but obviously, he is not the nicest person and [like in Dunn’s case] they just backed off and he carried on. He dragged me through the house by my hair, just ragdolling me.”

Contact senior journalist Anna Leask.

She said Fenton forced her to drive to her house to pick up her young child, who was fast asleep.

Then she was told to return to his place.

“He had his hand around my neck the whole time in the car,” she said.

“He basically held me hostage for more than 12 hours.”

The woman said Fenton subjected her to various brutal and terrifying physical assaults throughout the night.

“The only thing that kept me alive that night, the only thing that kept me sane, was my child. I kept saying I needed to go and check on her … and I just tried to survive the night, do whatever he wanted.

“In the morning I remember being in the shower and the blood was just pouring out of my head to the floor. The water was just red … I thought that if I could just get myself dressed and hold myself together, I would be okay.

“He knew I had to go to work and drop my [child] off on the way. He came with me … I promised him he could take my car for the day because he didn’t have one.

“I just tried to act like everything was normal, as if the night hadn’t even happened. I just kept him happy … I knew that if I could get [my child] safe and get to work, I would be safe.”

When the woman dropped her child at daycare, the staff took one look at her and wanted to call the police.

She asked them not to, worried about what Fenton – who was waiting in the car – might do.

“We drove to my work. He took my car and as soon as I walked into my room, they called the police,” she said.

Fenton was arrested later that day and charged with male assaults female.

She believes he had a firearm and a machete with him when he was located, making his way to her friend’s house where she was hiding from him.

Fenton was sentenced to just four months in prison.

The woman still cannot fathom why he was not charged with more serious offending. Over the years she has asked for details about the prosecution from police and the courts – most recently under the Official Information Act.

She finally has an appointment to meet with police this week to discuss the matter.

“I believe I was one of the first victims … I didn’t know about the others until I read it in the Herald – but I wasn’t surprised,” she said.

“It just makes me angry that more wasn’t done back then. He only got four months … if he had been charged with something more serious he could have still been in prison.

“I am struggling to this day … I carry a lot of guilt. I have PTSD. I am now fighting ACC for surgery for an injury from the attack … it’s just awful.

“I found out about [Dunn] when I read it in the paper … I just couldn’t believe it … I have lived with it ever since. I just feel that they did not do enough when he did what he did to me, and they should have."

Over the years, the woman has made submissions to the Parole Board to try to keep Fenton in prison.

Because his 2006 offending did not involve her, she was not able to register as a victim, which meant she did not get any formal updates from the Parole Board about upcoming hearings and she was not invited to make a submission.

However, she was able to make voluntary submissions – which meant she had to contact the board for its decisions and follow up when Fenton was due for another hearing.

She was not told – by anyone – that her attacker was being released.

He walked out of prison on October 5 and was in the community for weeks before his parole decision was made public.

“I literally had a panic attack, I just broke down,” she said.

“I luckily already had a therapist appointment booked and I had to drive to [it] and I just felt so sick and I was just crying and crying and crying.

“I was an absolute mess … even though it was (more than 20) years ago, it still feels like it was yesterday and it’s really hard.”

The woman said she understands why she could not register as a victim – but wanted to see that system changed in cases like hers.

“It’s just it’s crazy, it’s such a broken system. I was absolutely terrified when I read he was out.”

“Any woman that is on that guy’s criminal history needs to be aware.”

She had a firm warning for any woman who encountered Fenton in future.

“Run,” she said.

“Just run… because I don’t believe he can change. It’s just in the family, it’s generational and I don’t know if you can escape from that.”

When Fenton was sentenced for Dunn’s murder, the judge said his history made for “depressing reading”.

“You and your father, before you, have been long-time members of the Black Power gang. You were raised in a family environment of violence as well as drug and alcohol abuse,” he said.

“Although you claim to have blacked out and recall little of what happened on the evening in question, the summary of facts makes it clear that you were conscious of what you were doing throughout the lengthy assault on the victim.

“You have an extensive criminal history spanning some 14 years … you admitted to the probation officer, you have an obvious propensity for violence.

“Of particular concern to the probation officer was your belief that you earn the respect of others through fear and intimidation. you appear to have only limited insight into your own use of violence.”

The woman said she would never fully recover from what Fenton did to her.

“It’s just a living nightmare, to be honest.

“I just wish I could close my eyes and it all goes away, but it’s always just there – and [his release] has just been like repeating history all over again.

“It’s horrible … and it just feels like there wasn’t much justice done for me.”

She would like to see changes to the Victim Notification Register that would allow people in her position to find out when their attackers were being released from prison. She appreciates Fenton’s most recent offending was not against her but it was eerily similar and she still lives in fear of him so it would have helped her to know he was going to be back in the community.

Chief Victims Advisor Ruth Money said the issue was “absolutely on my radar”.

“Sadly this is not an uncommon occurrence, and it is because of the current legislative settings.

“I do think that there is a pragmatic approach where victims and victim survivors can and should be able to have their say and be notified when the offender is someone as serious as this.

“And I think it makes for better decision-making – it makes the process safer for everybody and at the end of the day, that’s what the public wants and should expect.

“These previous victim survivors have got a lot of intel and the more information that goes into the system to make a safe decision, the better.”

Money said in the cases of offenders as violent and frequent as Fenton, all victims “need more rights”.

“And the system needs their input – the system should be welcoming their feedback.

“But, with the current legislation, our victims’ rights clash against the offender’s privacy rights

“My position is obviously that the victim survivors’ rights, and safety to the community should privilege the offender’s privacy rights in decisions like this. But there is always a tension between how much information you can get as a victim survivor.”

In future, Money hoped to see a system governed by legislation that allowed for anyone to submit to the Parole Board about an offender “should they have relevant and compelling information”.

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

Bay of Plenty rugby league players get Manly pathway through Rotorua academy

New Zealand Herald November 14, 2026

Whetu Pewhairangi, 16, signed a rugby league contract with Manly Warringah Sea Eagles at a celebration at his school, Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Koutu.

Playing in the NRL could be a dream come true for more Bay of Plenty players after the announcement of a Rotorua-based league partnership.

The Manly Warringah Sea Eagles have struck a two-year deal with Bay of Plenty District Rugby League to nurture local talent and progress high achievers to the Australian junior league system.

The two organisations have joined forces to establish the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles – Bay of Plenty Rugby League Academy in Rotorua.

It comes one month after Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Koutu student Whetu Pewhairangi, 16, signed a two-year deal with Manly until 2029 to play in the Australian junior representative system.

In a statement, Manly said the strategic two-year partnership gave the Sea Eagles an important foothold in the Bay of Plenty, which it described as one of New Zealand’s strong rugby league regions.

It also allowed Manly to “identify, nurture and develop” elite young talent with the potential to progress into Manly’s junior teams.

The statement said it allowed players to develop within their local communities, with access to the coaching expertise, high-performance programmes and professional standards of an NRL club.

Initially targeting male players aged 14-17, the academy will also deliver development programmes for female players aged 16-19, while providing development opportunities for local coaches.

The programme would feature structured development camps, individual player development plans, position-specific coaching, coach education and guidance across nutrition, recovery, wellbeing, leadership and education.

Selected players would also have opportunities to visit Sydney, experience Manly’s development activities and gain exposure to the club’s junior pathways and high-performance environment.

Sea Eagles recruitment and elite pathways head Craig Walker said the initiative complemented the club’s existing pathways programme.

“This is a really important step for our club as we continue to invest in our pathways and build a sustainable pipeline of talented young players,” Walker said.

“The bulk of our efforts will continue to be in developing local players, but expanding our reach into other catchment areas will be beneficial long term.”

He said New Zealand had an “incredible” rugby league culture and a history of producing outstanding players.

“Rather than simply looking to recruit that talent once players arrive in Australia, we want to build relationships, invest in their development, and identify those players at an earlier age.”

Bay of Plenty District Rugby League chairman Anaru Pewhairangi – Whetu’s father – welcomed the partnership.

“We are incredibly grateful to the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles for believing in our district and sharing our vision for the future of rugby league.

“This is a world-class opportunity for our rangatahi, and I’m excited about what we can achieve together for our players, whānau and the wider Bay of Plenty community.”

Pewhairangi understands more than most what it means to players to further their NRL dreams, with his son signing with Manly last month.

The occasion was marked with a celebration at Whetu’s kura, Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Te Koutu.

“As Whetu’s parents, my wife Shelley and I are really proud of him and what this opportunity with Manly means for him.”

Pewhairangi said league was a team sport and the milestone was a reflection of not only Whetu’s hard work and commitment, but also of his teammates, coaches, and everyone who had supported him.

“We know Whetu is proud to be joining Manly and hopes his journey can show other young people from Rotorua and smaller communities that where you come from does not define how far you can go.”

Pewhairangi said with hard work, belief, the right support and a commitment to your goals, opportunities like this were possible – even more so now thanks to the partnership.

George Uata from Rotorua, whose son Kobe has dreams of making it to the NRL, was rapt to hear the news about the partnership.

“Kobe has loved the game of league from when he first played at the age of 5, he’s played both league and union throughout his life but has always told me league is his passion.”

Uata said league had given his son “so many blessings”, including representing his grandmother’s and grandfather’s sides, both Tongan and Māori, at national level.

He looked forward to the new pathways the partnership could open up for Kobe and other budding players like him.

“Having a major NRL club teaming up with the Bay of Plenty District Rugby League is going to help a lot of our kids showcase their talents and will boost the opportunities for them in our little regions.”

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 30 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

How two former accountants transformed a Central Otago sheep and beef farm

New Zealand Herald November 14, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

How many accountants wake up one day and say, “I think we should buy a farm and become farmers”? Kem Ormond chats to Amanda Currie, who, along with her husband Adrian, did just that.

So, two accountants with not a scrap of farming knowledge decided to take the plunge and become farmers.

It’s the sort of story that reads more like a novel than a farming case study.

The driving force behind the change was Amanda Currie, while her husband Adrian was alongside her for the ride.

Tinwald Farm is a 750ha sheep and beef farm based between Cromwell and Wānaka.

The Curries’ story is an interesting one.

Amanda doesn’t mind talking openly about their journey, which entailed making a huge decision to shift a farming system that just didn’t work, and the changes that had to be made that ultimately helped move the business from significant losses to profitability.

Over the past eight years, the Otago farming business made changes that cut around $200,000 from its annual cost base.

But the journey hasn’t been straightforward, and it is the years of trial, error, measurement and learning behind those results that make this story particularly interesting.

Amanda and Adrian Currie bought Tinwald Farm in 2012.

By 2018, after dealing with cattle disease and another year of significant losses, Amanda said they reached a point where they had to ask themselves: do we sell, or do we find a completely different way to run this business? They chose the latter.

With farm manager Jason Sutherland, who was not averse to change, they began their journey.

What followed wasn’t an overnight success story.

In fact, Amanda is refreshingly open about the fact that they initially had little idea what they were doing.

They stopped using synthetic fertiliser, experimented with diverse seed mixes and biological inputs and, at times, watched production plummet.

They said goodbye to their agricultural advisers and jumped in knee-deep.

Over the following years they became far more systematic, educating themselves about soil biology, changing grazing management and continually running their own paddock trials to understand what worked and, equally importantly, what didn’t.

Amanda said that a critical part of that evolution was recognising the limitations of observation alone.

“It can be quite easy to see what you expect to see.”

Covid arrived in 2020, and lockdown gave Amanda time to source info on soil from various websites; she then decided to do some courses to get a better understanding of soil.

This led Tinwald to begin working with Āta and Ecological Outcome Verification (EOV) in 2022.

Āta founder Dr Hugh Jellie has visited the farm over the past five years, usually every April.

He assesses the same 11 sites on the farm to evaluate the landscape, wind erosion, water erosion, and landscape regeneration.

The results guide the on-farm decision-making.

EOV puts a neutral lens over the farm, independently measuring what is actually changing in the landscape rather than prescribing or auditing a particular set of farming practices.

Āta then helps the team interpret those results through the principles of regenerative agriculture, identifying what appears to be working, where the limiting factors might be and how that evidence can inform their next decisions.

For Amanda, the independence of that advice has been particularly important.

It isn’t linked to selling them fertiliser, seed, chemicals, or another farm input.

Instead, the starting point is what the evidence from their own land is telling them.

Today, the economics of Tinwald look vastly different.

Annual operating costs have fallen from about $800,000 to $600,000.

They no longer carry what Amanda estimates would now be a $200,000-$300,000+ annual synthetic fertiliser bill, have eliminated winter cropping and its associated costs, use less machinery and diesel, and say the business is now genuinely profitable.

At the same time, they’re starting to see indicators of greater resilience across the farm, including animals reaching target weights earlier, improved reproductive performance and measurable changes in soil biology.

One recent experiment involved applying urea to half of two 5-ha paddocks; Amanda said they saw no difference in pasture response between the treated and untreated halves.

“We no longer drench our cattle or ewes as we work on the basis that healthy animals are resistant to diseases,” she said.

“We have imported dung beetles, four different types from four colonies, and they are doing a fantastic job keeping paddocks clear of dung.”

It’s not a story of everything working.

Amanda and the team are continually testing different approaches, and some have failed.

Their experience has instead become a cycle of change, measure, learn and adjust, using independent evidence alongside what they’re observing on the farm to determine what genuinely is effective.

Amanda’s advice to other farmers is similarly pragmatic.

“Don’t flick a switch and change the whole farm,” she said.

“Take one paddock, identify the limiting factor, change something, measure it, and see what happens.”

There’s another interesting commercial evolution underway too.

Tinwald has begun testing the nutritional profile of its beef, is selling some directly to consumers and exploring local retail opportunities, rather than simply sending its best product into the export system.

Tinwald offers a look at the economics and realities of regenerative farming: what has worked, what hasn’t, what happens to profitability when high fixed costs are removed, and the role independent measurement and advice can play in helping farmers make decisions without having a product to sell them.

Relaxation at Tinwald comes from overseeing the small Pinot Noir vineyard they have established on the farm to enjoying the company of their nine beautiful Clydesdales.

These magnificent horses are very much part of the property’s charm and a pleasant break from regular farm work.

RNZ’s budget crisis threatens its core purpose. But there’s an obvious solution

New Zealand Herald November 14, 2026

“News and information you can trust,” says the voiceover before each RNZ news bulletin. Unfortunately, it seems the same couldn’t be said for the state broadcaster’s internal accounting.

RNZ’s 2025-26 annual report, released on November 9, revealed an $11.8 million deficit – well in excess of the projected $470,000 loss in its earlier statement of performance expectations.

The accounting discrepancy (now subject to an independent review) is a huge embarrassment for the RNZ board and executive team. The consequences for RNZ’s ability to fulfil its public service remit are potentially dire.

Management and board were apparently unaware of the problem until the sudden resignation of the chief financial officer in early October.

A subsequent external audit of the accounts found multiple accounting errors relating to land sales, the Auckland office relocation, operational expenses, and personnel and redundancy costs.

A $5m loan facility was also found to have been set up without ministerial approval, in breach of the Crown Entities Act.

These anomalies raise serious questions about the integrity of RNZ’s financial governance, including the role of the board and its audit and risk committee. But the backdrop to the budget blowout is, if anything, of even greater concern.

As RNZ’s statement acknowledged, the errors were not picked up in time to take corrective action during the financial year, meaning “RNZ did not reduce its cost base as it needed to in response to a 7% reduction in baseline funding”.

That refers to the Government’s 2025 budget, which cut RNZ’s annual funding by $4.6m a year, to $62.3m – a reduction of $18.4m over four years. The 2026 budget further reduced RNZ’s budget by $1.4m.

In response, RNZ had already planned to cut 20 to 30 positions by mid-2027 (18 of which had already been agreed through a voluntary process).

But the unexpected $11.8m shortfall is now projected to mean the loss of 58 positions by next March – about 16% of the workforce – with at least a 5% cut to operating expenditure.

RNZ maintains it has adequate reserves to sustain it through a period of transition. But it projects a further $7.8m deficit in the 2026-27 financial year, after which it will return to a sustainable footing.

As board chairman Brent Impey has indicated, the crisis is not an existential threat to RNZ: the $11.8m deficit mainly comprises one-off losses, including office relocation expenses and wrongly-accounted land sales.

But if the board’s plan is to balance the books by the 2027-28 financial year, the concern is surely the impact this has on RNZ’s role as a public service media operation.

In contrast to its financial management, RNZ’s actual performance has been very positive.

In line with its letter of expectations from shareholding ministers, it has increased its online and linear audiences, reaching 83% of New Zealanders aged 18-plus each month. The 2026 JMAD Trust in News report ranked RNZ the most trusted New Zealand news source.

RNZ also played a civil defence role in 26 emergencies. It shared news content with dozens of other news media (within New Zealand and in the Pacific), and supported the expansion of the Local Democracy Reporting scheme to 22 regional reporters.

According to a survey quoted in its annual report, 79% of New Zealanders agreed it is important for the country to have a public media organisation.

In this light, it’s also important the apparent failure of financial governance not be conflated with wider criticism of RNZ as an essential civic institution.

But the latest budget shock has undoubtedly played into the hands of government politicians whose open hostility towards RNZ is well known.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters (at the time also Deputy Prime Minister) directly threatened the organisation’s funding. Meanwhile, Act’s David Seymour (a shareholding minister of RNZ) criticised presenter appointments, alleged political bias and suggested cuts to RNZ’s budget. He also called for an overhaul of the board and management.

Tempting as it may be for RNZ’s ideological critics to point to recent financial failings as vindication of their concerns, it does not logically follow that RNZ’s performance as a public media operation is in question.

On the contrary, what does merit review is the previous coalition Government’s decision to repeatedly cut RNZ’s budget at the same time as demanding constant improvements in its programming performance.

Whatever the complexion of the new Government, a bailout would likely be a politically untenable response to a crisis ostensibly of RNZ’s own making.

But that is not necessary anyway. As Impey has noted, the sale of a transmitter site in Auckland is due to bring in $51m in the next financial year. The only question is how much of this revenue RNZ will be permitted to retain by Treasury.

Even a quarter of that sum would be sufficient to offset the $11.8m deficit. If that were permitted, there would be no need for additional redundancies and operational cost-cutting. RNZ could continue to deliver the services for which it is justifiably funded.

There is therefore an obvious solution and a straightforward political decision to be made. But it will require the support of RNZ’s incoming shareholding ministers.

Regardless of which parties comprise the next Government, they have a responsibility to ensure RNZ’s civic, democratic and cultural functions are not undermined.

Peter Thompson, Associate Professor in Media and Communication, Te Herenga Waka — Victoria University of Wellington

Keeping children off social media is “not a silver bullet” for online hate, says Tauranga law lecturer Dr Rachel Tan.

Tan’s PhD research argues restricting social media access will do little to change harmful content and algorithms platforms use to keep people engaged.

She wants New Zealand to consider a statutory duty of care that makes social media companies responsible for harm their services create.

Netsafe, New Zealand’s online safety organisation, supports stronger protections for young people but says age restrictions alone will not prevent online harm and platforms must take greater responsibility.

National proposed an Under-16 social media ban in August that requires platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent children from creating accounts and report on managing risks.

Labour supports a ban alongside stronger obligations for platforms.

The Greens, Act and New Zealand First raised concerns about privacy, enforcement and whether age restrictions address the role social media companies play in online harm.

Tan told the Bay of Plenty Times about an incident at an Australian petrol station where a stranger threw a paper bag at her and yelled: “Go back to where you came from”.

Tan said experiences like these contributed to her interest in online hate speech and how social media could give hateful views another way to spread.

The Tauranga-based law lecturer recently graduated with her PhD examining online hate speech and how New Zealand could better regulate social media companies.

Her research argues age restrictions may limit young people’s access to social media but do little to address the harmful content and algorithms operating behind the platforms.

“If the goal is to make the online environment safer, then we need to look beyond access alone.”

Tan said the proposed under-16 ban could be part of a broader approach but should not distract from the responsibility of the companies running the platforms.

“It’s not a silver bullet, honestly.

“We cannot actually place the entire burden on online safety alone on individual users while overlooking responsibilities of platforms.”

Her research was influenced by the 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks and the role social media platforms played in spreading extremist content.

Tan said online hate was not confined to a screen, allowing people with similar views to connect, reinforce their beliefs and carry those attitudes into the real world.

She said social media could also embolden users to express views they might never voice face-to-face.

A key concern was the role algorithms played in directing users towards increasingly similar content, keeping them engaged longer.

Tan argued that responsibility should not rest solely with individual users, but also with the platforms designed to amplify and distribute content.

She said social media companies should face stronger legal obligations to identify and reduce the risks their services create.

Tan wants New Zealand to consider introducing a statutory duty of care requiring social media companies to take greater responsibility for the harm their services could cause.

That could include greater transparency, risk reporting and changes to platform design rather than relying solely on removing harmful posts.

Researching the subject had changed her view of social media, which she once saw as a way for people to connect.

Tan said she now preferred to use social media to look at “cute things like kitty cats and bunny rabbits”.

Victoria University of Wellington senior lecturer in information management Dr Alex Beattie told The Front Page in October that effective change would require a combination of Government regulation and community-led efforts to help parents support each other.

He said social media was deeply embedded in young people’s lives and parents were understandably concerned about its influence.

Beattie pointed to grassroots movements, where parents agreed to delay giving their children smartphones and social media accounts, which could help ease social pressure.

Netsafe welcomed the move to strengthen online protections for young people but cautioned that age restrictions were not a complete solution to online harm.

In a statement issued when the ban was proposed, the online safety organisation said young people needed the knowledge, skills and support to navigate online environments safely, while social media platforms needed to take greater responsibility for preventing and responding to harm.

It said the proposed legislation required careful scrutiny and should not be rushed, with questions remaining about how the rules would work in practice and who would oversee and enforce them.

The organisation said the focus should remain on what would genuinely reduce online harm rather than whether someone was above or below a certain age.

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post.

When is it acceptable to put up the Christmas tree? – Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald November 14, 2026

How early is too early to put up your Christmas tree? Photo / 123rf

It’s that time of year again.

Decorations are appearing in the shops, Christmas music is starting to sneak on to the radio, and households across New Zealand are preparing for one of the great annual domestic arguments.

When is it acceptable to put up the Christmas tree?

There are two distinct camps when it comes to putting up the Christmas tree. They’re as divided as Kiwis over whether feijoas are delicious or little green anti-taste grenades.

On one side are the Christmas enthusiasts.

These are the people who would happily put their tree up in July, start playing Mariah Carey in August and genuinely believe forcing the family dog to wear reindeer antlers isn’t a violation of the SPCA’s Geneva Convention on animal humiliation.

For them, Christmas isn’t a day. It’s a season, and preferably one that lasts six months.

On the other side are the Christmas Grinches.

These people believe December 24 is quite early enough and even then; they’d prefer to wait until the evening.

They regard Christmas decorations as unnecessary clutter, Christmas music as a form of psychological warfare, and the whole business of putting up a tree as something that could probably be avoided if everyone just agreed to meet at the pub.

But somewhere between these two extremes, there must be a sensible answer.

And because I believe in approaching important domestic disagreements with the same scientific rigour normally reserved for CSI Miami, I’ve decided to investigate.

First, we need to establish some ground rules. And the most important is that we’re talking about a real Christmas tree.

I appreciate that artificial trees have their advantages.

You can put one up in September, take it down in February, and apart from the occasional missing branch, it’ll look exactly the same.

But that’s cheating.

If we’re going to establish the correct date for putting up a Christmas tree, we need to judge it by the genuine article.

Something green, fragrant and capable of shedding enough needles to keep the robot vacuum cleaner busy.

So, how long does a real Christmas tree actually last?

According to the experts, a freshly cut Christmas tree, properly cared for, should last around three to four weeks indoors.

That’s encouraging, although the key words “properly cared for” immediately raise some concerns.

Apparently, you’re supposed to make a fresh cut at the bottom of the trunk, stand it in water, check that water regularly and keep the tree away from excessive heat and direct sunlight.

So basically, you’re adopting a rather large and demanding houseplant.

And we’ve all been there.

Standing in the garden centre, convinced that this peace lily will be a piece of the family for years to come.

This time will be different. We’ll follow every instruction on that little plastic label.

Keep the soil moist but not wet, provide bright but indirect sunlight, feed regularly during the growing season, maintain moderate humidity and occasionally wipe the dust from its leaves.

Then we get it home.

The soil goes from moist to something resembling the Sahara Desert; the bright indirect sunlight becomes a dark corner of the lounge; feeding is forgotten, humidity is whatever the weather happens to be doing; and the only time we wipe the leaves is when we’re checking to see if the poor thing is still alive.

And somehow, we’re genuinely surprised when it dies.

So, given our rather questionable track record with house plants, what makes us think we’ll be any better at looking after a Christmas tree?

Yet every December, we convince ourselves that this time will be different.

Of course, there is another option.

You could adopt the “goldfish approach”.

Anyone who grew up with a goldfish will understand the concept.

When the original fish unexpectedly departed this world, Mum or Dad would quietly visit the pet shop and purchase an almost identical replacement.

By the time the children returned home, Goldie was swimming happily around the bowl, apparently none the worse for having spent the morning floating upside down, practising his backstroke.

The same principle could theoretically apply to Christmas trees.

If yours starts looking a little worse for wear around December 15, simply sneak out, purchase another one and replace it before anyone notices.

There are, however, some practical difficulties.

For starters, finding two Christmas trees that look exactly alike is considerably harder than matching two orange goldfish.

There’s also a lot of admin involved in de-decorating and re-decorating a Christmas tree.

And most importantly, unlike the goldfish, you can’t flush the body down the toilet.

Which brings us back to our original question. When should the tree go up?

I think the most sensible approach is to work backwards from the big guy’s arrival.

Santa is due on December 25.

Ideally, we’d like the tree looking magnificent on Christmas morning, with presents underneath, lights twinkling and enough needles still attached to distinguish it from a besom broom covered in tinsel.

So, if we accept the experts’ estimate of three to four weeks, that puts the earliest sensible date somewhere around the end of November.

But remember, that’s assuming perfect conditions, regular watering and a level of horticultural dedication that most households have never demonstrated.

We also need to allow for the fact that Christmas doesn’t finish on December 25.

There’s Boxing Day, visiting relatives and those strange few days when nobody knows what day it is.

In fact, Christmas doesn’t officially end until leftover ham for lunch and pavlova for breakfast are no longer considered acceptable meals.

So, to be safe, I’m proposing the first weekend of December as the official Christmas tree installation date.

It’s early enough to enjoy several weeks of Christmas cheer, late enough to give the tree a fighting chance of surviving the festivities, and conveniently close to the point when even the most determined Grinch starts accepting that Christmas is actually happening.

Naturally, I don’t expect everyone to agree.

The Christmas enthusiasts will accuse me of stealing precious weeks of festive happiness, while the Grinches will argue that December 24 still makes considerably more sense.

But that’s the wonderful thing about Christmas. We all have our own traditions, our own little rituals and our own ideas about how it should be celebrated.

And as long as there’s a little goodwill, a bit of laughter and someone willing to untangle the Christmas lights, does the exact date really matter?

Although I will say this: if you’re already putting up a real tree, you’d better be very good at watering it.

In March 2026, Māori trust Waipā-Rānui Incorporation started the process to find a new lessee for their 1120ha, steep-to-rolling sheep and beef farm in Waingaro, northeast of Raglan in Waikato.

It was seeking exceptional farmers who would match its mission: “To administer and protect our taonga tuku iho [cultural property], to promote economic, social and cultural development for future whānau”.

PGG Wrightson rural and lifestyle sales consultant Richard Thomson was approached by the board of trustees to conduct the tender process.

“While the goal was to get the land leased, the focus was on the people who would be taking over the care of the land,” Thomson said.

“The response was huge, with 200 inquiries; more than 50 people attended five open days, and I presented 14 offers to the trust board.

“This was shortlisted to four who had face-to-face interviews with the trust board.”

Trust board negotiator Quinton Moore said the board had accepted the tender from Simon Wood and Grace Bradley.

“They had done their homework in researching the land and soil conditions along with the output ratio to what the farm was capable of carrying in terms of stock units,” Moore said.

“We could see that they possessed good values, morals and a work ethic which aligned with our vision and aspirations for protecting and caring for our farm for future generations.

“We are extremely happy with our selection and are looking forward to a great future ahead for all.”

Wood and Bradley originate from Taranaki and were born into dairy farming families.

Bradley has completed some Primary ITO courses.

She was given two working dogs by the late Neil Hadland, which she said gave her a huge step up for her first proper job on a Hereford stud.

She loves the lifestyle, dogs and horses.

Wood has worked on sheep and beef farms since his teens, building experience and knowledge as he went.

He was grateful for ongoing support from Anzco’s Danny Smith.

The pair still have a lease block in Hawke’s Bay and manage both blocks between them and a worker, Henry Cox.

“Henry approached me in Hawke’s Bay for work, and I jokingly said if he found me another lease block, I’d give him work,” Wood said.

“Less than 24 hours later, he sent me a Facebook post of the Waingaro tender.”

Wood and Bradley took over the Waingaro property on June 1 and hit the ground running.

They brought in 2000 breeding Romneys, breeding cows and trade steers “to get animals on the ground straight away”.

Their pride in the land is evident, and the property is stunningly beautiful hill country with 360-degree views, including Whāingaroa Harbour and Raglan.

“The 20-year lease gives us time to spend money and actually see the results,” Wood said.

“We can really focus on the land and improving it and making it more productive.”

The tracks and races are in good condition and extend all through the 530ha of effective land.

Natural springs fill tanks that are gravity-fed to troughs, and there are troughs along all the ridgelines.

While not against technology, Wood prefers to check on stock personally by driving around the farm.

“I’d rather see the stock frequently and regularly drive around the farm so we immediately see issues with fences, gates, water and stock where they shouldn’t be.”

Bradley takes it one step further and, when the job is suitable, she uses one of her four horses, which take her where vehicles can’t go.

The couple have five working dogs each and use different dogs for different jobs.

They also have other young dogs and pet dogs.

Experienced working dog trialist and breeder Kevin O’Connor, Bradley’s cousin, helps on the farms.

She said he has taught her a lot about how to use dogs.

“I’m breeding using his 50-year-old bloodlines, and I love working with the dogs, especially when I’m on horseback.”

Immediate plans include some re-grassing, a summer rape crop, re-metalling some of the tracks, reducing wild goat numbers and tackling gorse.

“Longer-term, we want to move towards stocking with traditional breeds of Romney for the sheep and Angus and Hereford for the cows,” Wood said.

“We look for facial eczema tolerance in our sheep breeding.

“For the beef, we want a quiet herd that is easier to manage, and we want to breed to keep live birth weights low for easier calving.”

There are some areas on-farm that the couple would like to fence off, and they have plans for native planting.

The couple have good communication with the Waipā-Rānui trust board and are looking forward to a long and productive relationship.

I can’t see Christopher Luxon stepping down as leader any time soon – Heather du Plessis-Allan

New Zealand Herald November 14, 2026

I suspect the critics calling for Christopher Luxon’s head are set to be disappointed.

I can’t see him going anywhere in a hurry.

It’s not that the critics are wrong. Richard Prebble and Josie Pagani – to name two – have seen enough election results to know National’s 29% is nothing to be proud of.

The party may have done much better if it wasn’t weighed down by Luxon’s sub-zero popularity.

Also, he allowed a campaign that has been roundly criticised for being too negative, lacking vision and being too nasty. From Harry Mowbray (who is now under police investigation because the Nats narked on him) through to Chlöe Swarbrick (who they obsessed over on Instagram), they might have been more successful in creating enemies than converting voters. Luxon allowed that.

And then, after bringing in the third-lowest National Party result of the 21st century, Luxon read the room on the night like a man with vision impairment. He kept the country waiting until after midnight for his speech, swept up to the stage like he’d done National a favour in bringing home that big old 29%, and then delivered a sermon on horizons.

Between that and his original plan to make Opportunity leader Quilae Wong wait several days for someone in his team to set up a meeting, he was giving presidential vibes when the country barely wanted him to be prime minister.

Everything – from the result to the post-result behaviour – is screaming “roll me for the sake of the party”.

But it’s not going to happen.

At least, not without a triggering event.

Normally, an election is that event. MPs start freaking out that they might lose their jobs because the leader is dragging the party vote down.

That is exactly what happened. They freaked out in November, April and August but never rolled him, and now Chris Bishop, Nicola Willis, Paul Goldsmith and Gerry Brownlee are no longer in Parliament.

But that’s history now. The election is no longer a threat to jobs. The people left in caucus have survived and, short of a strange turn of events, they’re safe until 2029.

They won’t really turn their minds to that election until late 2028, which means Luxon is safe from election-related panic for another two years.

He might yet make a gaffe in the media big enough to get himself rolled. He’s done that before. Sometimes multiple times in one week. That is why the August attempted coup happened.

But this far out from the next election, the motivating factor for the caucus would be embarrassment, and in order to induce enough to spark a coup, the gaffe would have to be pretty seismic.

It may be possible for former National Party heavyweights to pressure him out with a targeted PR campaign. Depending on how you read it, the cryptic open letter from former party president Sue Wood this week might’ve been a gentle attempt at that. But that still requires caucus to feel the same. Currently, they’re probably more stressed about whether they can pull together a coalition than the mechanics of a coup.

Luxon could obviously decide to resign, realising that this is not a game he’s particularly good at. But that would take a degree of self-reflection we have not yet witnessed.

There is also the outside chance things go horribly wrong for him in the specials or the coalition negotiations, and he isn’t PM at the end of this month. That would be definite gone-burger territory. That’s the most likely fate of Chris Hipkins at this stage.

The truth is, Luxon has survived the thing that should’ve put an end to his leadership: the election. And even though it played out exactly as predicted under his leadership, many of his remaining MPs will just be grateful that they’re back.

Which means, if he survived that, there’s no pressing reason for him to go, is there?

De la Fuente adamant there is no racism in Spain despite England reminder to players

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 20:27:02 GMT

England’s first game in Madrid since racist abuse in 2004

De la Fuente tells Tuchel ‘we’re not racists, none of us’

Luis de la Fuente has told Thomas Tuchel there is no racism in Spain after the England coach’s admission that he would remind his players of the anti-racism protocol prior to their meeting at the Metropolitano on Sunday night.

This will be the first time the countries play each other in Madrid since some of England’s black players were subjected to racist abuse in a match at the Santiago Bernabéu in 2004. And although England have returned to Spain three times without incident since then, twice in Seville and once in Alicante, Tuchel was asked on Friday about going back in the buildup to Sunday’s game. The England coach replied that England “will not expect anything [untoward]” but also said: “maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid].”

Asked to respond to those words, and whether Spain still had work to do combating racism after being fined for discriminatory chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt in Barcelona in March, the Spain coach asked for confirmation as to whom they had come from, then said: “I can say the opposite. Tell Thomas there is no racism. As clear as that. Exactly the same as in England. We’re not racists, none of us.”

Tuchel, speaking later on Saturday night, expressed his irritation with the media, accusing journalists of manufacturing a row. “I got asked ‘what will happen if and if and if’, and I said if it happens, we have a protocol in place. That’s it … I never talked about racism in Spain, I answered politely a question about what happens. You create a lot of confusion for absolutely nothing.”

De la Fuente also described Spain versus England as “one of the best games you can see anywhere in the world right now, maybe the best”, and admitted that his team needs to exercise more control than they had been able to do during their 3-2 win at Wembley in September.

Asked to explain how the Premier League could be the richest league in the world and English players command bigger transfer fees than Spaniards despite the national team not winning anything since 1966 while the selección have won two World Cups and three Euros in this century alone, he insisted that it is a mistake to mix price and value.

“There is a song about value and price and it is exactly that,” the Spain coach said. “Someone has to pay it and that’s very welcome but it doesn’t mean it is the real value. I am surprised often when you see the prices paid for our players compared to [the fees] paid in England. I think ‘they’re so cheap’. They [Spanish players] are the best in the world. You can buy a player for half the price of what you pay in England for someone. In that world, in that market, that’s what’s spent. But I’m clear on this: we must not confuse price and value.”

“Between the English model and the Spanish model, I would choose the Spanish model,” De la Fuente added. “It is recognisable and the players have the ability to express it. The English model has developed a lot and I think it is very good. But you have to have the players. We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us.”

Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 20:00:53 GMT

Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago

Magnusson: And your time starts ... now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in a different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016, though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs, and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s.

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director.

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.

Which brings us to Mauricio Pochettino. He has done remarkable things: he may not yet have won trophies in England but he effected such an extraordinary transformation at Tottenham that it seemed not unreasonable they should be part of the Super League project. He found things difficult at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, but most people do. A last-16 exit at a home World Cup with the USA was about par. The question, now he is 54, is whether the sense of drift about his career is an unfortunate and temporary state, or evidence that he is not quite what he was.

Perhaps the United job will revitalise him and he will revitalise them. But this feels like another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago; that United, once again, are answering the previous question.

New Orleans officials file $1m lawsuit after ‘Mississippi miracle’ tanker crash

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 19:54:38 GMT

Port also succeeds in seizing tanker, Atlantic Asphalt, to recoup damages after it crashes into cruise ship

New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit seeking more than $1m in damages from the owner and operator of an asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship on the Mississippi River in the city on Friday.

In some of the first legal consequences of Friday’s crash, the port has also obtained a federal court order authorizing the seizure of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker. The Atlantic Asphalt slammed into the American Heritage cruise ship, causing the river boat to flip onto its side, injuring more than 30 people and setting off a frantic but successful effort to pull people out of the water.

The board of commissioners of the port of New Orleans filed the lawsuit in federal court late Friday, naming the Atlantic Asphalt tanker; its owner, Nave Shipping SA; and its management company, Thome Ship Management, as defendants.

Court documents state that the Atlantic Asphalt struck the American Heritage cruise ship at about 12.30pm Friday while passengers were disembarking at the port’s Thalia Street terminal.

The crash also left the terminal with extensive damage, according to the port’s lawsuit. The port estimates that repairs will exceed $1m, although officials are still determining the full scope of the destruction.

The port – beside repair costs – is pursuing compensation for cleanup operations, inspections and other expenses stemming from the Atlantic Asphalt’s crashing into the American Heritage.

Using a term for when a moving vehicle strikes a stationary object, the lawsuit alleges: “The allision occurred as a result of the negligence, gross negligence, fault or carelessness of the Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping, Thome (and potentially other parties not yet identified with responsibility for the operation, condition, crewing and seaworthiness of the Atlantic Asphalt).”

“As a result of the foregoing,” the lawsuit also states, “the Atlantic Asphalt, Nave Shipping, Thome (and potentially other parties not yet identified with responsibility for the operation, condition, crewing and seaworthiness of the Atlantic Asphalt) are solidarily liable for all damage sustained by the Board as described herein.”

The port furthermore requested permission from a federal judge to have the tanker seized and sold to help cover the costs of the damage. The judge, Wendy Vitter, approved the seizure request on Friday.

In its complaint, the port argued that the tanker and the companies overseeing its operations failed to comply with safety requirements and did not take appropriate precautions to prevent the collision with the stationary cruise ship.

The lawsuit maintains that the port bears no responsibility for Friday’s crash and seeks to hold the tanker’s owner and management company accountable for the resulting damage.

Port officials also indicated that additional defendants could be named in the case – and that the amount of damages sought could increase as further details emerge.

There were 197 passengers aboard the American Heritage at the time of Friday’s crash. Despite the severity of the collision, every passenger was accounted for, and no deaths or critical injuries were reported.

The city’s mayor, Helena Moreno, characterized the outcome as a “miracle on the Mississippi” – and attributed it to an effective performance by local, state and federal first responders.

In a news conference on Saturday afternoon, Moreno said that the American Heritage cruise liner may take several weeks to ultimately be removed from the site of the crash.

She added that members of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) had recently arrived in the city, with more expected to arrive later Saturday. Moreno said that “it took a little bit longer for their arrival” because of Friday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that delayed and canceled thousands of flights.

Capt Melanie Burnham of the US Coast Guard, commander of the military branch’s New Orleans sector, on Saturday confirmed that the investigation into the previous day’s crash was ongoing.

She had said Friday that the Atlantic Asphalt had evidently experienced “some type of loss of steering” before the crash – but that it still needed to be investigated.

“Our top priority now is the safe removal of the hazardous material on board the American Heritage,” Burnham said on Saturday. “It’s still pretty early. We are estimating about 16,000 gallons [of fuel] are still on board the American Heritage.”

Burnham also confirmed on Saturday that the Atlantic Asphalt had been towed to a different location, and added that the scene of the crash would remain a restricted area for the foreseeable future.

Portugal have made a permanent change to the No 7 shirt to honour the legacy of Cristiano Ronaldo and ensure the number remains forever associated with their greatest footballing icon.

The former forward, whose career spanned 23 years and 246 caps in which he scored 146 goals, announced his retirement on 5 November after a falling out with coach Jorge Jesus. His last appearance for Portugal was on 24 September, in a 1-0 home win over Wales in the Nations League.

Before their Nations League clash against Denmark, Portugal tweeted a unique design change to the iconic No 7 shirt to ensure Ronaldo’s version remains immortalised.

The small change to the number 7 is an acknowledgement of the star’s playing career in which he broke the men’s all-time scoring record. He captained his country to their first major trophy at Euro 2016, before adding two Nations League titles in 2019 and 2025.

Portugal will also pay tribute to Ronaldo before and during their Nations League fixture against Denmark in Braga on Saturday.

“Time to debut a new 7. Because there’s one that will be eternal,” the Portuguese national team wrote on social media on Saturday. The post included a goat emoji to signify “Greatest Of All Time”.

Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 19:01:32 GMT

Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok

Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra, to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe.

Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising.

The winner, who performs under the single name Carmelle, finished on 211 points, 41 clear of the hosts Thailand, with Vietnam third. She received the most votes from both the national juries and the public ballot.

Carmelle, 19, grew up beside the railway tracks in the Bicol region of south-eastern Luzon and has been competing in televised talent contests since she was 12.

Sobra-Sobra mixes pop and rap, is supported by traditional Philippine instruments, the kubing and kulintang, and is sung in Tagalog and English.

After her victory, Carmelle said her song celebrated female empowerment and was intended as “a tribute to all Filipino women”.

“I made history, since this was the first time,” she told the Associated Press. “It’s such a big responsibility for me, because this one is a global stage, so thank you everybody who voted for me.”

“It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are,” she told the Guardian before the final. “It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas.”

The show opened with a routine celebrating the host country, in which Muay Thai fighters shared the stage with drag performers on street food carts. The 11 acts were then driven on in tuk-tuks, each carrying their national flag.

Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, a star at home for more than 20 years, performed first, among dancers costumed as lotus leaves. Mang x Daou represented Thailand, a duo assembled for the contest in the host country who performed a duet staged like a musical number.

Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai gave one of the most conventionally Eurovision performances of the night with Ananta Maya, a rock ballad staged with fire imagery and a large heart-shaped structure behind him.

He ended it by appealing for support for his country, which he said was “going [through a] very hard situation”. More than 1,500 people were killed and more than 5,000 were reported missing after a rock and ice avalanche near the Chinese border triggered catastrophic flash floods in August.

Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, originally a nine-member a cappella and beatbox group, sang without a single instrument. Three of their members were left out of the final due to a rule capping each act at six performers on stage.

Nyendra from Bhutan sang dressed in the gho, his country’s national dress for men, against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks. Mongolia’s Beck performed in a reinterpreted deel, also a national costume.

Half the result was decided before the show began. The 11 national juries voted at a dress rehearsal on Friday night and put the Philippines at the top with 93 points, ahead of Vietnam and Malaysia.

The other half came from viewers around the world, who could vote online but not for their own country, and who were given eight free votes each and the option to buy 10 more.

Laos’s entrant, Thinla, was unable to hear her own music during her performance, and her dress rehearsal was aired once all live performances were over. She finished fifth, with the night’s third-highest public score.

Carmelle receives no prize money but does get a trophy presented by Dara, the Bulgarian singer who won this year’s European contest, and will perform at Eurovision 2027 in Burgas.

Organisers have said the right to stage future editions will not automatically go to the winner, on the grounds that smaller countries lack the infrastructure.

Some of the clearest echoes of Eurovision’s camp traditions came through those who announced the votes.

South Korea’s jury points were read by Jo Kwon, a veteran pop star who has played Adam in the Korean production of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert and the title role in Everybody’s Talking About Jamie.

The Philippines’ were read by Vice Ganda, a gay comedian who is one of the biggest stars on Philippine television.

Meanwhile, the guest performer was the Thai singer Jeff Satur, who reached a wider Asian audience through KinnPorsche, a 2022 series in the genre of male same-sex romance dramas that has a large following across Asia.

Organisers intend the Bangkok show to be the first of many regional editions, with the executive producer, Assaf Blecher, saying that 16 or 17 territories had expressed interest in competing next year, among them China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.
