‘I’m still trying to find out who I am’: the little-understood plight of Forgotten Australians

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 19:00:53 GMT

They number more than half a million, yet the ongoing trauma from their time in orphanages and institutions remains poorly known

When Judy Leonard entered the orphanage, she was given a bed with a number. That was how the staff would refer to her. Not by her name, or even by one of the cruel nicknames the other children gave her, but by her allocated space in the dormitory: C2.

“I would like the readers to close their eyes,” Judy says now, “and imagine that it was them at age nine.”

Judy’s early childhood, along with those of her brothers and sisters, was spent playing in the streets and beaches in Melbourne’s west. Then the police arrived.

“We were classed as neglected,” Judy says. “Dirty, unwashed, uneducated.” She was bundled into a car with two siblings. “I remember looking back out of the car and seeing my mum and dad cry. And I’d never seen my father cry.”

For six months, the three siblings were locked away at Turana, an overcrowded accommodation (or “reception”) centre in Parkville for children in the welfare system. It doubled as a remand facility for “problem” children. Police were said to refer to it as “the rat bins”.

A judge later ordered the three children to an orphanage. They could come out again, he said, when their parents’ circumstances improved.

It would be years before Judy went home. In some ways, she never did.

Judy, now 79, is among the Forgotten Australians: more than half a million people who were placed in orphanages, institutions and other forms of out-of-home “care” before 1990. Many were subjected to physical, emotional or sexual abuse, and neglect. Depression and suicidality are among the wounds many of them carry.

Despite multiple government inquiries and a 2009 apology from then-prime minister Kevin Rudd, Forgotten Australians’ trauma and the ongoing effects of it remain little-known and poorly understood. For those facing the prospect of aged care, the horrors of their institutionalised childhood can rear up again, only to be met with incomprehension by those around them.

“I want people to look at me as a human being. Because this is not just my story, it’s thousands of people’s stories. I’m no different to you. But I went through life a little different,” Judy says.

“I had my freedom taken.”

In the orphanage, Judy began wetting the bed, for which she was bullied mercilessly. She had headaches from undiagnosed longsightedness. She also, unknowingly, had dyslexia – and was hit with a ruler every time she misspelled a word.

“You had to be on guard all the time,” Judy says. “When you’re like that, you come out of that orphanage with a type of understanding that is beyond the kids out here.”

Judy was 14 when she was allowed to go home.

Many years later, Judy and her husband, Henry, became carers of a two-year-old boy – the child of a friend in distress. Two weeks before his eighth birthday, he was taken by authorities.

“I swore I’d never have another kid ever again, because it just tore me to pieces,” Judy says. “The same as when I was in the home, when I left my parents.”

Dean Wise only recently learned he was a Forgotten Australian. He was in therapy, during a four-year battle with bowel cancer, when he saw a photograph on his psychologist’s computer of one of the institutions he’d been in.

“That was a confronting day, I must admit. I started bawling my eyes out,” Dean says.

At around age 12, and after repeatedly absconding from their foster home, he was separated from his sister and put into Baltara.

He had been fleeing sexual abuse, perpetrated by a man connected to his school. Being in the “reception centre” didn’t stop it: the man was seen as a trusted figure and allowed in to see Dean or take him on outings.

Dean says he tried to speak up about the abuse. He told his social worker, community services, police and school teachers. But “it fell on deaf ears”. The abuse ceased only when the man suddenly stopped visiting.

Finding other survivors through Open Place, Victoria’s support centre for Forgotten Australians, has given Dean community. But even at 57, “I’m still trying to find out who I am,” he says.

“I’m so tired. I’m physically exhausted. Getting diagnosed with the cancer, that just made it even harder.”

Dean is also angry. That’s partly why he’s telling his story.

“I’m doing it for the kids still going through the system and not being heard. Things have got to change. Simple as that. It’s got to change.”

Toni Brown always wanted to be like her bikie brother. She “took off from home”, hitchhiking from Melbourne to Sydney at age 12.

“There were bikers up there,” Toni says. “They used to park on Darlinghurst Road. That was all I knew.

“So one of them got hold of me – I’m 12, 13 – I fell in love – and I went to work for him on the streets.”

Toni, now 68, isn’t flippant about her experience as an underage sex worker, but her “worst years” came after police caught her. They sent her back to Melbourne and charged her with being “exposed to moral danger” – a “crime” frequently used to send victims of sexual violence to institutions. Toni was sent to a remand centre in Winlaton. It was ostensibly a training and rehabilitation centre for adolescent girls. In practice, it was a prison.

“You walked in the door, escorted by the officer. I had to strip,” Toni says. “They showed me to my room … but it was a cell. I had to sleep on the floor on a mattress because it was overcrowded.” Her bunkmate was a girl charged with the murder of two children.

During her seven months there, Toni was raped by an officer. Another officer witnessed the incident. “She turned her back,” Toni says.

“No wonder I got out and did what I did later. It was almost like I wanted to get back at everybody,” she says.

She returned to Sydney, and to sex work. When she was 16, she moved again and worked on a prawn trawler. “I could sit out and just be totally at one with the ocean … I got a drinking habit, a really bad drinking habit. But apart from that, that was what I think really started to make me stop and think about my life and what I’d done in the past. It started to wake me up.”

She came back to Melbourne in her early 20s, where she managed brothels and escort agencies.

Toni found the abuses of her past recurring later in life. They strained and sometimes fractured her relationship with her two sons, one of whom she was unable to see for many years. Still, she persisted. She drove taxis. She trained as a care worker and worked with kids whose challenges were just like hers had been.

These days, Toni dotes on her 11-year-old granddaughter, who she says once made a perfectly timed phone call that stopped her from taking her own life.

If you spent time in Melbourne’s gay clubs in the late 1990s and early 2000s, it’s likely you saw Richard Payne dancing on a podium. He was known as Grandpa Acid – not for the drugs (he wasn’t into those) but the music. Dancing was how he found euphoria.

After a decades-long career in agriculture, a marriage, a family and a divorce, Richard realised he was gay. It has been difficult for his family to come to terms with.

Richard was born with a cleft palate. His mother, an unmarried flight attendant, put him into care so she could work to pay for his medical needs. He was shuffled between hospitals and foster homes until he turned eight, when she relinquished his care to the state.

Then a wealthy landowner arrived, looking to adopt a child. “He took me down the street and bought me a great big lollipop,” Richard says. That sweet beginning didn’t last.

“He started doing things like making sure I’d wash myself properly. He’d come in the bathroom and he’d start washing me, and he started doing things,” Richard says. It escalated to violent rape. “He actually physically whipped me from head to toe and then penetrated me,” Richard says.

Confused and terrified, Richard fled back to the group home. He was turned away.

At 14, Richard was burnt in an industrial accident at his agricultural college and kept in intensive care for three months. “While I was there, the head doctor came in to see me,” Richard says. “He said, ‘Richard, how come you haven’t had your speech therapy treatment done?’” His adopted parents were “put on the spot and shamed to do it”.

Eventually, Richard confronted his abuser. “I slammed him up against the back of my ute and put my fist up and said, ‘If you ever touch me again, I’ll kill you.’”

At 21, Richard married into a relationship he describes as loveless, but that he committed to because he wanted a family. After the divorce, he went to his first gay club because a girl he had dated invited him. The men didn’t harass her there, she said.

He kept going back.

Then one night, a young man kissed him.

“I fell apart,” says Richard. “I was aching – I’d been aching all my life for somebody to show that they wanted me for who I am, what I am.”

In a letter he shared with Guardian Australia, Richard wrote that he felt his sexuality had been “robbed” from him in his youth. “This in turn resulted in my trying to dismiss the past and bury it,” he wrote.

“However you always know that one day you will have to relive it and that time is now.”

John Pinkard turned 80 this year. He has been attending Open Place for nearly a decade, but identifies as a member of the Stolen Generations. His memory is as sharp as a pin. But while he knows what happened to him in Tufnell Home, he can’t say for sure how old he was when he went in or how long he stayed.

Before Tufnell, John lived on the lam with his foster mother, who he just called “Mum”. His birth mother, a white woman ashamed of having fallen pregnant to an Aboriginal man, had abandoned him at a Brisbane hospital after giving birth.

Ann, the mother-in-law of his nurse, didn’t care about the colour of his skin. But the state government did.

“She told me that they physically tried to take me off her,” John says.

Ann took John home, but a sympathetic official quietly warned her that because she wasn’t married, they would try to take John away. So they fled into outback Queensland.

When things went bad in one place, they’d lob back to Brisbane. As John grew older, he learned how to identify government cars and how to hide. Once, he hid in the bulrushes of a swamp.

One day, John was coming home from school and forgot to look for the red rag on the windowsill that would let him know it was safe. Two men opened the door and grabbed him.

“There [were] lots of tears and carry on,” John says. “[Mum] pleaded with them not to take me like that, but she promised she’d take me up on Monday to the orphanage.”

John is emotional when he describes being left at Tufnell.

“We sat on the steps and Mum said to me, ‘John, I’ve got to leave you at this house for a short while, until I can get you back.’

“I saw Mum walk down the path and I saw her head going above the hedge – and the penny dropped. I made a run for the door and they had locked it.”

Minutes later, he says, “I got my first flogging.”

He remembers nuns erecting a makeshift boxing ring so they could watch the children fight. A priest, who took him behind red curtains, made him undress and sit on his lap. “He’d get me to put my hands down and get me to touch him,” John says. Afterwards, “maybe he’d give me a Mintie.”

He was allowed to return to Ann after she married, when he was about 10. That’s when she told him his father was an Aboriginal man who had raped John’s mother – a story he later learned was false – and said: “Don’t you ever own up to being Aboriginal.”

“I’ve lived a life without identity,” John says. “I’d been brought up as a white person, but I’d been looked upon as a coloured person.”

He also struggled to overcome his time in Tufnell. “I have been insecure with people – my wife, my children. I never told anybody about the abuse I got in the orphanage until I was about 50,” John says. “My wife said to me, ‘It’s like living with somebody in a glass cocoon. I can see you, but I can’t get through to you.’”

John remembers the phone call from his half-brother, about eight years ago, confirming his father was Aboriginal. “I just sat here and cried. Oh, God, at last! It’s out, I know, I know!”

And he found and met his mob: the Bundjalung people.

“I’ve had my recognition. I’m in a good place as far as knowing that I’m Aboriginal, Bundjalung people,” John says.

“I’ve been put down all my life, and now I know who I am.”

In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International

The moment I knew: He quoted my favourite TV show. I blurted out, ‘Marry me!’

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 19:00:51 GMT

On Anthony Ashdown’s first date with Jake, their mutual love of nerd culture felt revolutionary. Then Jake referenced a catchphrase from The Golden Girls.

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

Picture it. Sydney. 2015. I had weathered a nasty breakup the previous year. I had often compromised a lot of who I was and what I enjoyed to keep the other person happy. Post-breakup, I decided I would never change who I was for anyone else ever again.

I got on the apps and matched with Jake, a handsome young man 10 years younger than me. We chatted on Grindr and planned to meet for coffee and then spend the afternoon at Cronulla beach.

Days later, on a hot summer morning, I sat waiting in a coffee shop at Miranda Fair. My heart was thumping. This was the first date I’d been on since the breakup. Sure, there’d been plenty of hookups. What gay doesn’t go through his footloose and fancy-free phase post heartbreak? But this was the first real date. And at 33, for some reason, I felt old. What did this cute young thing see in me, that he reached out to me?

He arrived soon after. We’d already covered some ground when chatting online, so the ice breakers and awkwardness were out of the way already.

I laid all my cards on the table. I had nothing to lose. I was about to become a surrogate father with a lesbian couple. I intended on being a part of this child’s life and I wasn’t going to accept anyone in my romantic life who took issue with that, or didn’t want to be a part of that themselves. He wasn’t fazed in the slightest by it.

I remember how much he made me laugh on that date. We’d been quoting The Simpsons, Friends, Star Wars, even Seinfeld! I was genuinely shocked. Marvel and DC comics might be mainstream now but, in 2015 in my world, meeting another gay who was into nerd culture felt revolutionary.

Before going to the beach, Jake asked if I’d accompany him shopping to use up some gift vouchers that were due to expire. Why not? It was still early in the day.

We stood in a homewares store; I wanted to buy a new beach towel. He started to tell me a story. He smirked and said, “OK, picture it, Sicily, 1922 …”

My head spun. For the uninitiated, those famous words are the catchphrase of Sophia “Ma” Petrillo in The Golden Girls, one of my favourite shows of all time. When I was a kid, my late grandmother and I would cuddle on the lounge and watch it together. I didn’t really understand a lot of it then but it still made me laugh, and I remember my grandmother’s laugh, this chuckle that sort of hissed through her teeth. The show is a source of comfort and joy for me now. It advocated for gay rights and acceptance in a time where the mere use of the word “gay” on TV would see pearls clutched across the nation!

So in that homewares store, I did a double take. And without thinking, blurted out: “Oh my God did you just quote Golden Girls at me? Marry me!”

He chuckled and continued with the story. It might sound like a rather brash thing to say on a first date but there was an element of truth to it. I thought, “I’m gonna marry that boy one day.”

Ten years later, I did. On a beautiful April day in Leura, made all the lovelier and greener as it followed a week of torrential rain. We had tuxedos made but I wanted something special: a ball gown for the bottom half. Jake, having just completed a fashion course, granted my wish, and I walked down the aisle that day in a gown made with his own loving hands. For the first time in my life, I felt like a true expression of who I was.

To this day there is no one on Earth who can make me laugh and smile like he does. Jake is a wonderful stepdad to my two daughters. We’ve always accepted each other for who we are. We never fight. We may disagree from time to time but nary a harsh word is exchanged. He’s so gentle and non-combative, conflicts always resolve themselves so peacefully.

In recent years I was diagnosed with autism with ADHD, and suddenly a lot about why I am the way I am made perfect sense. But Jake is always able to calm me down whenever I become frazzled and overwhelmed – we jokingly call him the Anthony whisperer. It’s a level of sorcery not even Tolkien could write about.

I don’t know how I’d survive without him. I wouldn’t change him for the world. Nor would he ever ask any different of me.

Five-try Will Joseph equals record as England steamroller Japan

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 18:39:16 GMT

England 78-15 Japan

Steve Borthwick’s men score 13 tries

Not every game of rugby can deliver a result for the ages and this one never stood a chance of eclipsing the weekend’s remarkable events in Cardiff and Paris. In terms of one-sided contests at Twickenham down the years there have been few to match it although Will Joseph, England’s athletic new wing, will remember every detail for the rest of his days.

Joseph, playing only his second Test, ended up claiming a record-equalling five tries as his side comfortably topped their previous highest tally against the Brave Blossoms. From the moment he helped himself to a hat-trick of tries inside the game’s opening 20 minutes it was simply a question of how many points England would score and Maro Itoje’s side duly took advantage of the free buffet.

To say Japan finished a distant second is to be polite in the extreme. The home crowd went away talking about Joseph’s eye-catching performance and a barnstorming first-half score by Ellis Genge but, in truth, this was akin to shooting koi carp in a barrel after Japan lost their lock forward Harry Hockings to a subsequently upgraded 20-minute red card in the first minute.

England Steward; Joseph, Slade, Ojomoh, Murley; Ford (M Smith, 57), Van Poortvliet (McParland, 48); Genge (Iyogun, 51), Cowan-Dickie (Dan, 58), Opoku-Fordjour (Heyes, 58), Itoje (Clark, 63), Martin, Coles, Earl (Fisilau, 51), Pollock (B Curry, 57). Tries: Joseph 5, Steward, Genge, Murley, Earl, Martin, B Curry, M Smith, Fisilau. Cons Ford 3, Slade 2. Pen Ford. Sin-bin Cowan-Dickie 53

Japan Ueda; Ishida, Riley, Tua (Kitahara, 70), Tokito (Costley, 27); Kitahara (Komura,48), Saito (co-capt; Fujiwara, 64); Kamimori (Otsuka, 51), Harada (Sato, 46), Takeuchi (Helu, h/t), Hockings (Stolberg, 22), Dearns (co-capt), Gunter (Lee, 57), Shimokawa, Cornelsen. Tries Dearns, Helu. Cons Saito. Pen Saito. Sin-bin Hockings 1.

Referee Damian Schneider (Argentina). Att 81,552.

The visiting head coach Eddie Jones, following the relative encouragement of a narrow loss to Wales, wore a stern expression up in the stands from an early stage on his latest return to familiar surroundings. Afterwards he had no option but to cop the result on the chin. “I’m massively disappointed but you have these days as a young team,” said Jones. “It was a hard lesson today.”

The irony of Joseph’s display was also not lost on the man who handed him his Test debut – “That’s not being very loyal, is it?” – in Australia four years ago. The Gloucester back has had to be patient but has now potentially catapulted himself into Steve Borthwick’s World Cup plans. As a quietly satisfied Borthwick put it: “We want to build a squad not a team and there are people who have really put their hand up.”

It has also made life interesting before the final round of Nations Championship pool fixtures next Saturday, with South Africa and New Zealand both now looking to respond to weekend jolts. Working on the basis that Japan, just seven days earlier, finished within a score of Wales it could be argued England should be regarded as slight favourites to overturn the All Blacks in London this coming weekend.

Even in the absence of some first-choice personnel Borthwick’s reshuffled side frequently attacked with verve and were already 49-10 up by the interval as Japan’s afternoon spiralled from bad to worse. Joseph’s first try in the opening minute was splendidly taken but none of the three defenders left sprawling in the 24-year-old’s wake will be in a hurry to rewatch the tape. Inside the first 20 minutes a neat double-pump pass from Henry Slade and a well-judged cross-kick from Freddie Steward had already served up a hat-trick on a willow pattern plate and an acrobatic dive into the right corner for his fourth try reflected the unfettered joy of a rising talent with serious potential.

Genge’s rip-snorting score, again leaving multiple bodies strewn on the floor, sent an even clearer message about England’s intentions, which only wavered fractionally when they were awarded an early penalty in front of the sticks. Judging by some of the expressions on the faces of certain English forwards, Ford’s decision to kick three points was not universally popular, suggesting there are still differing opinions within the squad when it comes to England’s tactical identity.

Argentina bounced back from last week’s heavy Nations Championship defeat in Ireland as they held on to beat Italy 19-14 in Genoa. The visitors were forced to fight back from behind then breathed a sigh of relief when Alessandro Garbisi’s last-minute penalty kick strayed beyond the try line.

Monty Ioane scored the opening try for Italy who dominated the early stages and were unlucky to reach half-time on level terms after Bautista Bernasconi’s converted effort. Argentina took control in the second half with tries from Rodrigo Isgro and Matteo Carreras helping to nudge them 19-7 clear, before a penalty try gave Italy hope, and the South Americans hung on despite losing both Joel Sclavi and Efraín Elías to yellow cards. Press Association

Not that it remotely mattered on this occasion. Cadan Murley, clearly itching to get in on the act, muscled his way over and while Warner Dearns grabbed one back for Japan there was another five-pointer for Ben Earl before half-time. Within four minutes of the restart George Martin had taken England’s try tally to nine and it was something of a surprise when Opeti Helu crossed for the visitors’ second three minutes later.

Even Luke Cowan-Dickie being sent to the sin-bin offered Japan scant respite, an interception on halfway allowing Joseph, the younger brother of the former England centre Jonathan, to sprint 50 metres for his fifth try. Only Douglas Lambert in 1907, Rory Underwood in 1989, Josh Lewsey in 2003 and Henry Arundell in 2023 had otherwise achieved the feat in a Test for England.

The rest was a matter of dotting the i’s and crossing the t’s, although Marcus Smith and Greg Fisilau will not necessarily see it that way. Smith, on for Ford in the 57th minute, looked in sprightly mood and added dash to proceedings while Fisilau, as well as delivering one crunching defensive hit, could not be stopped as he took a more direct route to the line.

Only England’s goalkicking was below par with Ford and Henry Slade landing just five conversions between them. The missing points could have taken their team up into the nineties but, to be honest, people had stopped counting by the end. Jones reckons the All Blacks will pose a “violent” examination this week. “They’ll be hard and tough around the breakdown … they’ll be back to the old New Zealand,” he said, but England’s captain is eagerly awaiting the challenge. “They’re right up there among the toughest teams to play but I think this is a step up this team is ready for,” said Itoje. “We want to show where this team is going.”

Family of Watford woman set alight ‘desperate for answers’ after attack

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 17:59:12 GMT

Appeal for information comes after Brenda Raymond, 80, was set on fire outside her flat on Monday

The family of an elderly woman who was set on fire outside a block of flats in Watford have said they are “desperate for answers”.

Brenda Raymond, 80, was found set alight outside her flat on Caractacus Cottage View on Monday. She was taken to a nearby hospital, where she is in critical condition.

Hertfordshire constabulary have said a 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit arson with intent to endanger life but has been released on bail with strict conditions.

Raymond’s family said the attack had left them in “complete shock” and that they were confused over why she was targeted.

In a statement issued via Hertfordshire constabulary, they said: “Words cannot describe how distressing the past few days have been for us as a family.

“Our beautiful, chatty, fun-loving and much-loved Brenda, who loves to keep fit and dancing, has suffered catastrophic injuries in the most devastating of circumstances; circumstances which have left us all in complete shock.

“We simply cannot understand why anyone would have wanted to hurt her in this way. Someone out there knows something. They know what happened to Brenda. We are desperate for answers and are pleading for anyone with information to please come forward.”

The family also asked for their privacy to be respected during this “unimaginably difficult time”.

Police believe that Raymond was attacked as she returned home at around noon, with her attackers pouring some kind of flammable liquid on her before setting her alight. Detectives said that an accelerant was also poured through the letterbox of a nearby flat, but they have not officially linked the two events.

The decision to publicly name Raymond was made by police with the blessing of her family on Wednesday in the hope it would lead to anyone with knowledge of the attack coming forward.

DI Adam Bridges, from the major crime unit, said: “This was an appalling and deeply distressing attack on an elderly woman who suffered horrific injuries after being set alight outside her own home.

“Our thoughts very much remain with Brenda and her family as we continue to do everything we can to find out what happened and who is responsible.

“Her family are understandably distraught and have taken the step of releasing her name and photograph to help jog people’s memories around this distressing and highly unusual incident.

“Someone out there knows something. You may have witnessed suspicious activity, heard a conversation, noticed unusual behaviour, or captured something on CCTV or dashcam footage without realising its significance.

“Please do not assume that what you know is too small or unimportant to tell us about. It could be a seemingly insignificant piece of information that provides investigators with the breakthrough they need.

“If you know anything about what happened to Brenda or think you may have information that could assist our inquiries, please come forward. Your information could be crucial in helping us find answers and bring those responsible to justice.”

NHS England on track to miss key cancer treatment target by 10,000 patients

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 17:00:49 GMT

Exclusive: 2,850 more patients a month would need to be treated within 62 days to meet March 2027 goal, as experts warn of failure of leadership

Nearly 10,000 more cancer patients in England will not be treated on time because the government will fail to meet its targets, amid a failure of leadership, focus and resource, experts have warned.

The NHS set an interim target to treat 80% of cancer patients within 62 days of urgent referral or consultant upgrade by March 2027. But with little more than 100 days to go, the proportion of patients starting treatment on time in September was 70.7%, down from 71.9% in August, NHS figures show.

Exclusive analysis of official figures for the Guardian reveals the NHS would have to treat 2,850 additional patients on time each month to get back on track, assuming patient volumes remain consistent.

According to calculations by Radiotherapy UK, 24,400 cancer patients a month would need to start treatment on time to hit the 80% target in March. But the NHS is only treating about 21,500 cancer patients a month within the 62-day target, leaving a monthly shortfall of 2,850 and a cumulative shortfall of 9,490 patients, the charity found.

Prof Pat Price, the chair of Radiotherapy UK and a leading oncologist, said: “The government is going to miss its cancer treatment target because the NHS does not have enough staff or equipment to treat the number of patients coming through its doors. This lack of leadership means thousands more people could die because they don’t get their treatment on time.”

The analysis also found significant disparities between treatment of common cancer types. While more than two-thirds of patients with prostate and breast cancers were treated within two months ((70.1% and 68.8% respectively), only 60.9% of those with lung cancer and 60% of those with gynaecological cancers were treated on time. For head and neck cancers, barely half (56.5%) were. Regional inequalities were also stark, the research found. The Midlands had the lowest proportion treated on time, at 66.6%, compared with 77.3% in London.

Mark Lawler, a professor of digital health and chair in translational cancer genomics at Queen’s University Belfast, believes failures of accountability and focus are to blame. He said: “The whole system is being held together by goodwill glue alone. Lack of leadership is derailing efforts to improve cancer survival. Unless there is accountability for these failures by the NHS, a radical change in mindset and a focus on the basics, we will miss hitting treatment targets for another decade.”

The figures come as analysis of latest cancer diagnosis targets by Cancer Research UK shows that, over the last year, barely half (55.4%) of patients with cancer were diagnosed within 28 days of an urgent referral, against the faster diagnostic standard target of 80%, compared with 79.1% of patients who received the all-clear on time.

Naser Turabi, Cancer Research UK’s director of health policy and evidence, said hospital capacity was not able to keep pace with surging demand for cancer diagnosis – with urgent referrals in England up about 20% over the past four years alone. “While recent investment in diagnostic equipment is welcome, we’re not seeing enough progress to cut waiting times for the 6% of people who go on to receive a cancer diagnosis,” he said.

Dr Hilary Williams, the Royal College of Physicians clinical vice-president and a consultant in medical oncology, said crucial earlier diagnosis was only beneficial if patients could then be treated quickly.

“To close the gap, the NHS needs sufficient capacity across the whole cancer pathway,” Williams said. “That means more diagnostic capacity, including imaging, endoscopy and pathology, alongside the specialist workforce needed to deliver and interpret those tests. It also means enough treatment capacity in surgery, radiotherapy and systemic treatments so that diagnosing people more quickly doesn’t simply move the bottleneck further down the pathway.”

Dr Stephen Harden, the president of the Royal College of Radiologists, said “chronic shortages” of clinical radiologists and clinical oncologists, who diagnose, monitor and treat cancer, were “driving dangerous delays” in diagnosing and treating the disease.

“Perversely, NHS hiring freezes for these doctors have doubled in the last year, making it even harder to keep patients safe,” Harden said. “Technology and new ways of working can relieve pressure to an extent, but fundamentally, rising demand for cancer care has outpaced workforce capacity. The government must now step in to end recruitment freezes and ensure services have the doctors they need to diagnose and treat patients on time.”

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “Cancer waiting times are moving in the right direction, with all three cancer standards better than a year ago, and around 290,000 more people over the last year getting diagnosed on time or having cancer ruled out, compared to the year before the election.

“But we know there is much more to do. Our national cancer plan will help more people to get diagnosed earlier and begin treatment sooner, giving them the best possible chances of recovery and survival.”

Democrat wins Alaska governor’s seat for first time in nearly 30 years

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 16:58:33 GMT

Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins’ victory means Democrats will now hold 30 US governorships after midterm blowout

Democrats have captured Alaska’s governor’s seat for the first time in nearly three decades, marking another major victory for their party in a midterm election period that has dramatically shifted political power across the US.

Former Alaska state legislator Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republican opponents, including a candidate backed by Donald Trump, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Alaska since 1998.

His victory – called by the Associated Press on Friday, 10 days after the polls closed – adds to a growing list of Democratic gains nationwide, bringing the party’s total to 30 US governorships. Democrats have also taken control of governor’s offices in several other longtime Republican strongholds, including Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

Kreiss-Tomkins, widely known as JKT, secured the win having mounted a political comeback three years after departing the Alaska house of representatives.

The 37-year-old traveled extensively throughout the state during his campaign, building support around economic concerns and a promise to change the direction of Alaska’s government.

His platform centered on tackling affordability, ensuring full funding for public education, and requiring all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income taxes. He also pushed for a temporary halt to new datacenter developments until state lawmakers establish regulations governing their construction.

Throughout the campaign, Kreiss-Tomkins sharply criticized the leadership of outgoing the Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, arguing that Alaska had become “broken” during his eight years in office.

“Alaskans are hungry for change,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. “We’ve been running the same campaign since we launched in February, and I don’t take anyone’s vote for granted.”

Among his criticisms was the deterioration of the state’s ferry system, which Kreiss-Tomkins said had been left in disarray as service to numerous communities was drastically reduced. The ferry network serves as a critical transportation link for communities in south-east Alaska that lack road connections, including some with limited access to air travel.

Despite his criticism of the outgoing administration, Kreiss-Tomkins presented himself as a leader willing to work across political divisions. He pledged to assemble a cabinet that includes Democrats, Republicans and independents.

Unlike most states, Alaska allows voters to rank candidates by preference through ranked-choice voting – a system that also permits multiple candidates from the same political party to run against one another.

But Kreiss-Tomkins avoided the need for additional rounds of vote counting after winning more than 50% of first-choice votes, securing an outright victory.

The Alaska result comes just days after Democrats scored another major gubernatorial win in staunchly conservative Kansas, where the Democratic state senator Cindy Holscher narrowly defeated the Republican state senate president, Ty Masterson.

after newsletter promotion

Masterson, who received Trump’s endorsement, faced a campaign in which Holscher repeatedly highlighted his ties to the Republican president. At the same time, Holscher maintained that she would remain willing to cooperate with the Trump administration on issues where common ground could be found.

The back-to-back victories in Alaska and Kansas underscore the scale of Democratic gains in what has become a nationwide electoral shift.

The party’s long-anticipated “blue wave” has now materialized, with Democrats flipping eight seats in the US Senate, gaining more than two dozen seats in the House and significantly expanding their control of governors’ offices after the 3 November midterms.

Such gains have handed Democrats a strong majority in Congress for the latter half of Trump’s second presidency, delivering a major shift in the balance of power in Washington and state governments across the US.

Meanwhile, with few ballots left to count for Alaska’s midterm US Senate election, Democrat Mary Peltola on Saturday was leading Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan, Alaska Public Media reported. That had prompted MS Now to characterize that Senate race as “leans Democratic”.

Beside Alaska and Kansas, the Democratic party won gubernatorial elections over Republicans in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, putting them in control of a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Gina Hinojosa is the first Democrat to be elected governor of Texas in 35 years – and also the state’s first Hispanic governor.

A major factor in the GOP’s midterm defeat is the unpopularity of Trump, whom most Republican lawmakers clung to even as polls indicated voters did not support his immigration crackdown, tariffs, the war with Iran or his signature domestic policy bill.

More cold health alerts have been issued for parts of the UK on Sunday night and next week.

The alerts were issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for the north-west, West Midlands and Yorkshire and the Humber, and will be in place from 9pm on Sunday until 9am on Thursday.

These alerts mean the weather is “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, the agency said. The warning came after forecasters predicted the UK was in for a milder weekend, before another cold snap arrives on Monday.

Paul Coleman, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said: “This is the latest cold health alert of the season and we can expect more as we move further into winter.

“Cold weather can have a serious impact on the health of some people, including those aged 65 and over and those with pre-existing health conditions, so it is vital to check in on friends, family and neighbours who are most vulnerable.”

Coleman advised people to heat the rooms they use most and wear warm clothes.

The Met Office said that on Saturday night, central and easterly parts of England should remain dry with clear spells and a touch of frost, though cloudier conditions are forecast elsewhere as well as some showery rain.

On Sunday, temperatures are expected to not fall below freezing in the morning, with sunshine forecast in the east and across the far north and west as the day progresses.

Conditions are otherwise expected to be fairly bleak with plenty of grey skies, cold breezes and outbreaks of rain, some heavy, and potential hill snow in the north.

On Monday, colder weather is expected to return. Sunny skies will appear in patches across the UK, while cold showers are forecast to rain down in the north of the UK. Light snow is also expected in hilly areas in the north.

Wales bury 73-year All Blacks hoodoo with seismic victory over New Zealand

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 16:01:57 GMT

Wales 35-28 New Zealand

Home side secure first win over All Blacks since 1953

Just when you expect it the least. By what wild logic did Wales choose now to pull off a victory 73 years in the seeking? There may have been only 55,000 in Cardiff’s great stadium for this first win over New Zealand since 1953, but judging by the noise alone, Wales are back. They had managed five wins in 31 Tests since the last World Cup, all of them against teams outside the top eight, and they choose now to beat the All Blacks.

An extraordinary defensive display for the last half-hour kept wave after wave of New Zealand attacks at bay, each feat of heroism greeted as if the most sublime of tries by JPR, Gareth, Shane or JJ. None of those ever tasted this, but now a new generation of Welshmen, still young and hopeful, can add a win over the All Blacks to their CV.

New Zealand will claim top spot in the southern table of this championship, but courtesy of two bonus points, rather than the five-pointer everyone expected. They had made eight changes for this, after dispatching Scotland, for whom a first win over this lot had been considered an actual possibility, if not expected. But the changes made them vulnerable, as did the assumptions implicit, and when each of them turned to the other in hope of the sort of authority and calm that might have applied to previous iterations, there was none. They hammered and hammered away but could not force their tireless hosts into submission.

Wales Murray; Rees-Zammit, James, Llewellyn, Hamer-Webb (Hennessey 54); Costelow (Edwards 65), Williams; Smith (Thomas 54), Lake (capt; Elias 70), Griffin (Lewis 50), Jenkins, Beard (Carter 65), Botham, Morgan, Basham (Plumtree 54) Tries Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons Costelow 5

New Zealand B Barrett (capt); Fineangandofo (Ioane 67), Tupaea, Lienert-Brown, Moorby; Mo’unga, Ratima (Preston 65); Bower (Numia 50), Aumua (Bell 65), Newell (Tosi 50), S Barrett, Lord (Hannah 65; Blackadder 70), Segner, Lakai, Sititi (Fainga’anuku 65) Tries Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons Mo’unga 4

Referee Pierre Bousset (France) Att 55,152

A passerby outside might have thought Wales had scored time after time in the last quarter, such were the roars, but, no, these were greeting the latest scarcely believable display of defence. Eddie James, Gareth Thomas, James Botham, Max Llewellyn – each of them pulled off tackles that might not be recorded in the record books, but that they’ll cherish every bit as much as any try.

The stadium may have been some way short of capacity, but it was soon rocking as of old. Wales tore into their fabled visitors from the off. Tomos Williams, one of an increasing number of world-class players Wales are starting to build this new team around, was over within 90 seconds. His cut-out pass to Louis Rees-Zammit was in itself announcement of that class, but he followed up the latter’s chip ahead and was able to dot the loose ball down for the game’s first try.

Cardiff more than stirred, but the Welsh know only too well that a sucker punch at the start of a match against this lot means not an awful lot. So Wales took it upon themselves to score a second just a few minutes later. They sent a penalty to the corner, where Dewi Lake picked a great line off Williams’ pass to crash over. Sam Costelow converted for a 14-0 lead. We had played barely five minutes.

Within 10, the All Blacks had responded. The way Cortez Ratima was able to break blind from an attacking lineout for his try would concern any defence coach and belied what was to follow. There was a sense of ‘here we go again’ at that point, as there was at half-time, but Wales kept coming, exploiting any misconnections between such a changed team with precision and power. None more so than Archie Griffin, steadily building a reputation for himself in Wales’ front row, an increasingly competitive unit. He barged over from another penalty to the corner to open up a 21-7 lead as the game entered its second quarter.

Argentina bounced back from last week’s heavy Nations Championship defeat in Ireland as they held on to beat Italy 19-14 in Genoa. The visitors were forced to fight back from behind then breathed a sigh of relief when Alessandro Garbisi’s last-minute penalty kick strayed beyond the try line.

Monty Ioane scored the opening try for Italy who dominated the early stages and were unlucky to reach half-time on level terms after Bautista Bernasconi’s converted effort. Argentina took control in the second half with tries from Rodrigo Isgro and Matteo Carreras helping to nudge them 19-7 clear, before a penalty try gave Italy hope, and the South Americans hung on despite losing both Joel Sclavi and Efraín Elías to yellow cards. Press Association

The All Blacks may have rung the changes, but they retained a few points of reference, none more fixed than Wallace Sititi at the base of the scrum. He claimed New Zealand’s second on the half-hour, driving off another penalty to the corner, after Asafo Aumua’s drive.

These two were at the heart of the All Blacks’ best passages. Wales sent another penalty to touch with time up at the end of the first half. That they intended to play with it reflects a growing confidence. Alas, precision at the lineout was lacking here, and New Zealand made tell the final passage of the half, which culminated when Quinn Tupaea put Fehi Fineanganofo over to tie up the scores.

One might have thought the fun was over at that point, but far from it. Wales were over twice again within 10 minutes of the restart. A sweeping attack, All Blacks-style, was consummated when Williams put Eddie James over in the corner. Costelow converted again, from the touchline.

Wales were not done. Jac Morgan won a penalty. Surely Costelow would take the three. No, to the corner again, Lake drove close, and Williams sent Rees-Zammit over this time. A 14-point lead with half an hour to go …

New Zealand took over from there. Peter Lakai drove over from close range after relentless pressure to move them to within a score with a full 25 minutes to go. It only precipitated some of the most heroic defence ever seen on this famous old patch of turf.

After so lean a period, amid such financial distress, a new breed of player announced itself. They have achieved already what their more illustrious predecessors never did, but will this spur them on to match those ancestors with more? Watch this space.

A rapid interest rate rise seems inevitable – and UK households are expected to pick up the tab

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 16:00:48 GMT

Raising borrowing costs too far risks laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy

A head of steam is building up behind the Bank of England raising interest rates again. With the latest forecasts by the central bank showing inflation rising to 5% next spring, another increase in the cost of borrowing seems inevitable, and may come as soon as next month.

A growing number of analysts predict the Bank’s policymakers will don Scrooge masks when they meet on 17 December to deliver a message of austerity and sacrifice.

So sclerotic is the economy, so lacking in flexibility or productive spare capacity, that even the burst of growth experienced by the UK over the last year, defying most forecasters, must be calmed down with higher interest rates or else inflation will rip.

Huw Pill, the Bank’s chief economist, told the Financial Times on Saturday that more than one rate rise was almost certain.

This is not a message anyone who borrows money will want to hear, especially when the festive season is in full swing. If interest rates edge up from 4% to 4.25%, mortgage deals will rise and business loans will become more expensive.

The central bank expects businesses to react to the higher costs of doing business by hitting their customers with price hikes. It is an argument that presumes consumers have money available to pay higher prices, despite plenty of evidence to the contrary. Only households in the top half of the income scale have spent more this year and that has depended on running down their savings.

Consumers are also battle-hardened after the greedflation period following the pandemic that morphed into its evil cousin, shrinkflation. They know about grifting retailers and consumer product suppliers that try to build a narrative about the inevitability of surging inflation to disguise their own price hikes.

The Bank says its business surveys have failed to detect efforts by the corporate sector to increase prices. It’s just that a majority of policymakers are convinced pressure is building and inflation will be more than double their 2% target in a few months.

But if consumers don’t have any spare cash, or have become more savvy about how they spend it, there is still a weak link – a special kind of consumer who could aid corporates in pushing up prices.

The weak link is the state, or government in all its forms. The NHS is a big purchaser, so is local government and the many agencies that are funded by government, from Homes England to National Highways. Government expenditure on goods and services accounts for 25% of overall consumption in the economy.

Everything from concrete and medical supplies to food and furniture will cost more, and sellers will be prepared to justify the rise with a wide range of excuses.

Corporates will blame the war in the Middle East for an increase in transport costs and the impact of climate change that makes growing stuff harder. They will even accuse the government of raising costs by introducing new worker protection rules.

Let’s add another one: contractors will say they can’t get the skilled staff and so must pass on the cost of higher wages.

After 15 years of austerity and job cuts, there is a question mark over whether the public sector has the nous and resolve to push back to keep costs in check.

Budgets on the London to Birmingham high-speed rail line (HS2) have spiralled out of control. The costs of the next largest infrastructure project in England, the 14.5-mile (23km) lower Thames crossing linking Essex and Kent via two tunnels, have more than doubled to £11bn.

Government spending on consultants reached £3.7bn in 2024-25 from £2.9bn in 2022-23 and there seems to be no end to their uses, from advisers on artificial intelligence to strategies for reaching net zero.

The public sector is also notorious for commissioning plans for new town or city developments for which there is no funding, except for the inflationary bill from consultants.

These public sector organisations have huge clout, and should use it. If they do, there will be knock-on effects to inflation deals struck within the business community, which in many cases can only ramp up prices knowing the public sector is the ultimate buyer.

Inside Threadneedle Street, policymakers expect everyone – consumers, government and business – to cave in to sellers’ demands. And that many of the UK’s 33 million workers will subsequently demand big pay rises to compensate.

Yet it must be possible that all three consumer groups will adopt the slogan Can’t Pay, Won’t Pay, limiting the rise in inflation and eliminating the need for elevated pay rises.

Even if the poor, financially bombed-out household consumer is the only one to take a stand against greedy corporates, inflation will not hit the heights forecast by the Bank of England. In the meantime, it might have raised interest rates too far, laying waste to whatever growth there is in the economy.

Chelsea go top of WSL as Sandy Baltimore bullet sees off Manchester City

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 15:36:15 GMT

Pragmatic, resolute and gutsy. Sonia Bompastor showed her ruthless side and delivered a tactical masterclass as Chelsea earned a 1-0 win over Manchester City and leapfrogged them at the top of the Women’s Super League.

Lucy Bronze credited fellow full-back Katie McCabe with firing Chelsea up pre-match, having told them they “had to be dogs” in the game, and a dogged performance followed. Sandy Baltimore’s stunning strike in added time at the end of the first half was the difference as the west London side nullified the threat of a team that had scored in each of their preceding 21 games in all competitions, inflicting their first loss of the campaign.

The task for City got even tougher when goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita received a straight red for clattering into Alyssa Thompson, but despite their numerical disadvantage it was end to end right up until the final whistle.

“It always affects you when you go one player down,” said manager Andrée Jeglertz. “But we handled that and that’s not why we lose the game. I think it’s small details. It’s a tight game, it’s two great football teams, there’s a lot of situations, there’s a lot of battles and they managed to score on their big chance from a great finish. We also have a couple of great opportunities where we don’t manage to score.”

Momentum was with City going into the match after their 5-0 defeat of West Ham the preceding weekend and a 4-1 win against Inter in the Champions League on Tuesday night and they were able to welcome the injured duo Vivianne Miedema and Beth Mead back to the bench to bolster their matchday squad.

At Stamford Bridge the England women’s manager, Sarina Wiegman, the US women’s manager, Emma Hayes, and passionate women’s football advocate and pundit Ian Wright were in the stands. It was a fixture that promised much, and it delivered: the league’s most potent attacks, with Chelsea having scored 28 league goals before this fixture to City’s 27, while Bompastor’s side had the most solid defence, having conceded only five times before kick-off.

Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier marked her 150th appearance for the club with a superb strike in a 2-0 victory over Crystal Palace at the Progress with Unity Stadium. Presented with a framed shirt before kick-off, Le Tissier whipped a low shot from distance into the net in the 18th minute before Elisabeth Terland confirmed United’s win after the hour mark.

United moved up to fourth with the win and they kept hold of the position after Tottenham drew a blank in a goalless draw at home to Everton, whose winless run in the league stretched to five matches. In the day’s late game, Liverpool ended a five-match winless run in the WSL by easing past Brighton 3-0. Press Association

It was a chess match. After a thrillingly frenetic start there was a change for Chelsea just 12 minutes in, with the centre-back Kadeisha Buchanan replaced by Veerle Buurman. There was speculation over whether the withdrawal of the Canadian defender was due to injury and Bompastor unconvincingly claimed it was.

“Yesterday in training, she got a knock to her head during contact with a teammate. She was fine after the training session. She was fine in the evening. We assessed her again this morning and everything was fine,” she said. “I just felt watching her from the beginning of the game, she was not herself. Then I took the responsibility to make the substitution. But for me, I was almost forced to do that because I know my player and I know she was not in the game.”

However, if, as many believe, the defensive switch was a tactical decision, it was a stroke of genius, as Buurman was excellent at nullifying the threat of Khadija Shaw.

“She had a really good performance against a top player,” said Bompastor. “Today was positive. But again, as I’ve told you previously, when it doesn’t work it’s not so positive.”

Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 15:34:54 GMT

PM accuses Tories of burning ‘all our bridges’ and says deal he is pursuing with EU will ‘get food prices down’

Andy Burnham has said the UK has “lost more than we gained” since leaving the EU, the prime minister’s latest in a string of comments criticising Brexit.

Outlining his desire to form closer ties with Brussels, Burnham accused the Conservative party of having “burned all our bridges” with the bloc after Brexit and said a new deal he hopes to secure with the EU next week will “get food prices down” and put more money in the pockets of British exporters.

The prime minister is due to meet European leaders at a summit next week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. He will also “explore options” for a different long-term relationship with Brussels.

Speaking at the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday, Burnham said: “We need to be willing to take difficult decisions to get the cost of living down.

“It’s why, in a few days’ time, I will head to the next UK-EU summit and I will be working hard as we move towards it to get to a new deal on food and farming between the UK and the EU. Why am I doing that? Because I want to help Welsh businesses.

The prime minister added: “I think we’ve lost more than we’ve gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I’m going to lead as prime minister on this issue, and I’m going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.”

Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU, but on Saturday he said voters would ultimately be “the boss” of any changes.

He reiterated his commitment to Labour’s manifesto “red lines” – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement. “People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that’s what makes us who we are,” he told the conference.

“And, yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result. So, that’s the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.”

The government has already made several announcements that would tie the UK closer to Brussels. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported that the UK was prepared to spend up to £450m a year to give EU students discounted university tuition fees, if Brussels allowed Britain access to the Made in Europe industrial programme.

Earlier this week, Hamish Falconer, the cabinet minister in charge of EU talks, said Britain was willing to discuss paying towards infrastructure schemes in poorer parts of the EU in return for access to the European electricity market.

James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 14:00:46 GMT

The singer on his love for Ibiza, the weirdest thing he’s done in the name of romance, and being signed up for Celebrity Traitors against his will

You were a punching bag for such a long time after You’re Beautiful became a massive hit, but your consistent good humour is deeply admirable. Does it ever get tiring?

It was a surprise, at the beginning. I was just a little guy with a dream. And when you achieve your dream, you think people would be happy for you. For them not to be happy for you, but angry with you, for your song, seems irrational, an overreaction. It is interesting how people generally want to tear people down for achieving their little dreams. But I’d had a real proper job before that [as a captain in the British army]. My friends might have been on operations in Afghanistan or Iraq, so if I were to complain to them at the time saying, “Oh, the Guardian said something really horrid about me and gave me three stars for my album” – they would be able to talk about who had lost their lives or limbs that day, and that put it all in perspective. And perspective is everything.

Then you start thinking really clearly. A journalist might say, “Hey, I read something negative about you online” – I can either start defending that or put it in perspective, which is: I’ve just played a concert to 15,000 people and those 15,000 people spent really hard-earned money to buy a ticket and booked hotels or flights to get there and queued up and, if it’s in England, queued in the rain. So am I really going to get upset by one negative tweet when 15,000 people really invested themselves in me? It’s all about perspective.

What is the best thing about owning two pubs?

The beer in my life is always free.

Are you very good at pulling a pint?

The staff in my pubs, because of who I am and the shame they sometimes feel, try to keep me out back doing the dishes rather than front of house. I understand why. It is how we roll.

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Ed Sheeran and Carrie Fisher are the godparents of your children. What wisdom did you hope each of them would impart?

I hoped Carrie would look after herself. That’s why I asked her to be a godmother – I could see a destructive human being and I wanted her to care enough for herself that my son might know her. And it wasn’t to be.

And Ed and I had a very similar journey. We were singer-songwriters inspired by similar musicians, found ourselves managed by the same management, found ourselves signed to the same record label – but he just did it better. If you’re going to have your child be inspired by someone, point them in the direction of someone who does it better than you.

I understand you love a rave. How often do you get to one?

Not as much as I’d like, to be honest. I live in Ibiza and my favourite nightclub is a club called Pacha, which opened in 1973. When I was 13 years old, I was on a family holiday here and I walked past Pacha and told my friend, “I am going to live here, and I am going to go to that club.” The moment my first album, Back to Bedlam, became a hit, the first thing I did was buy a house in Ibiza, which is where I’m calling you from now. I later moved to Ibiza when I was a pariah in my own country and I wrote All the Lost Souls, a pretty dark and miserable second album. But the thing that kept me going was the dancefloor in Pacha … I wrote a song called 1973, the year Pacha opened. And then the DJ Pete Tong remixed it, so I would be in that club, listening to my own song, about the club that I was in – which is kind of mental.

There are other clubs I really love. Ushuaïa is like a Miami pool party and they’ll occasionally ask me to perform there. Sometimes I’ll drive down there, I park out the front, the security walk me to the stage and hand me a microphone, I’ll climb on to the stage, sing, crowd surf, go back on the stage, sing the final chorus, hand the microphone over, walk off the stage and drive home to put my kids to bed. That is either really rock’n’roll or really square, I am not sure which.

What is the best piece of advice you have ever received?

Don’t shit where you eat.

Who taught you that one?

Pretty much everyone I know.

What is the weirdest thing you have done for love?

Obviously I am a purveyor of saccharine songs, so I need to up my game when it comes to romance. So last Valentine’s Day, I hired a helicopter, flew over my house and threw 100,000 red rose petals at my wife in the garden below. I thought that was pretty good. She thought it was OK.

Who would you like to play you in the biopic about your life?

My mother really thought Tom Cruise but, if I’m totally honest, I know it’s more likely to be Alan Partridge.

What are you secretly really good at?

I do a really good gorilla impression. And! [James Blunt uses his brow to wiggle his scalp so it moves distinctly from his face] I actually have a wig that no one knows about. I don’t know anyone else can do that but I literally can move my whole scalp and hair as if it were a wig. It’s real. I haven’t managed to monetise it.

Do you have a nickname, and what is it?

Yes, it rhymes with blunt and it’s a tiny bit shorter. It’s character building!

Actually, it is bizarre that my name later became cockney rhyming slang for that. That’s one of my greatest achievements. I have a few things that I find genuinely an achievement – like I have a ski lift named after me in Switzerland, and a burger named after me. But to have cockney rhyming slang for your own name is amazing.

I have also heard about the James Blunt Museum, in a Herefordshire phone booth.

Yeah, a huge, huge deal for me as well. I have been known to go there just to give it a quick clean from time to time. It’s not too far, just a quick six-hour drive. I go there for the morning, clean it, head back home. It’s worth a visit if you find yourself in the northern hemisphere. I really recommend it.

Final question – you were just on Celebrity Traitors. If you could be on another reality show, what would it be?

I swore that I would never do a reality show. Ever. And I have lived and breathed by that proclamation. My manager doesn’t even bring me those shows. But my wife signed me up to this without telling me. And I really wish she hadn’t.

‘You have to cope’: why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 14:00:45 GMT

The world has become accustomed to concerns about the male loneliness epidemic. But research suggests women are just as lonely

Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

No one would think of Sasha* as lonely, least of all Sasha herself. The 38-year-old from Sydney has close and longstanding friendships, proactively keeps in touch and makes plans, and is engaged with her local community.

“All those things that you read about, about why men might be lonely – they don’t maintain one-on-one friendships, or they’re not good at reaching out, or their conversations aren’t deep and meaningful – none of those issues apply to me,” she says. “I’m a very socially connected person.”

Yet Sasha often felt lonely during her first year of motherhood, even when she was surrounded by other people. (All case studies’ names have been changed.) She attributes it now to the intensity of the experience. “It’s the identity shift of your first child, having no idea of what you’re doing, learning on the fly … You feel alone.”

We’re living through a global crisis of loneliness, with the World Health Organization (WHO) declaring it a priority for public health, but it’s hard to miss that the coverage and conversation has been overwhelmingly focused on men.

Global Google searches for “male loneliness” spiked suddenly in mid-2023, and have since seen frequent surges; interest in “female loneliness”, meanwhile, has remained a trickle.

In 2024, the UK government commissioned research on loneliness in boys and young men, even though – as the final report acknowledged – girls and women were more likely to report feeling chronically lonely. (Paradoxically, researchers suggested this was further evidence of the crisis in men, because they were less likely to speak up and seek help.)

In the media, it has been conceived as its own specific issue: “The male loneliness epidemic.”

“When I tell people that I study loneliness, sometimes they ask, ‘Oh, men’s loneliness?’” says Michelle Lim, a principal research fellow at the University of Sydney, chief executive of Australia’s Ending Loneliness Together campaign and an adviser to the WHO. “I have to say, ‘No, no – everyone’s loneliness.’”

From the relative lack of attention on women and girls, you might assume they’re doing fine, or at least better than men and boys. In fact, studies consistently show similar prevalence between genders. “There’s not really any difference … They’re equally both lonely,” Lim says.

Comparisons of men and women’s loneliness produce mixed, but insignificant results. Meanwhile, a recent systematic review of the current literature on loneliness among men in the US concluded that evidence of a “widespread epidemic … is absent”.

So why do we have the impression that men are especially or uniquely struggling, and why don’t we hear about the “female loneliness epidemic”? In part it reflects a broader misunderstanding, says Lim: “We do see this confusion about what loneliness is.”

Loneliness is defined as the sense that your social relationships are somehow lacking in quality, quantity or both. Social isolation – with which loneliness is often confused or conflated – is more objective, referring to an absence of connection.

Data tends to show that men are more socially isolated than women, meaning “they have fewer people they talk to”, Lim says. Because men also tend to value physical presence and “shoulder-to-shoulder” socialising above emotional intimacy and disclosure, “the assumption is that they are more lonely”, Lim goes on – but that is not necessarily the case, if they are satisfied with those interactions.

Women tend to be more connected, “but they might feel lonely within relationships”, she says. That might indicate interpersonal ambivalence or conflict, but it could also stem from feeling isolated and alone in their individual experience.

Women are more likely to be carers than men are, they earn less on average, are less financially secure and are more vulnerable to adverse life events such as redundancy and divorce. “In many ways, they’re more socially disadvantaged, and that, we know, actually does predispose people to more loneliness,” Lim says. “It’s an equity issue.”

This became clear early in the Covid-19 pandemic, when loneliness started to gain more academic and media attention. Though both men and women reported feeling more lonely, the rise in women was much larger, which experts attributed to their increased workload, such as overseeing children’s schooling.

Spending more time on housework and caregiving not only means women have less time and ability to invest in their social connections; there is also likely to be the added loneliness of shouldering the burden, says Manuela Barreto, a professor of social and organisational psychology at the University of Exeter in the UK. “It’s a very gendered experience.”

Research has found that life transitions, such as becoming a parent, can promote loneliness, but the particular drivers likely differ for men and women, reflecting their different expectations and experiences.

Barreto suggests women are often more affected by children growing up and leaving the family nest, for example, due to the expectation or reality that “being a mother is much more central for women than being a father is for men”.

Menstrual health is another particular – and frequently underestimated – factor in women’s loneliness. A 2022 Japanese study found an association between loneliness and severe premenstrual symptoms in teenage girls. Regular pain can promote loneliness “in a very practical way”, Barreto points out, by preventing women from being fully present with others or even socialising at all.

Conditions such as endometriosis are described as lonely, worsened by lack of mainstream and medical understanding. “You have to cope, and deal with things by yourself,” says Barreto. “That really can make you feel very alone.”

That was the case for Sasha. She has endometriosis and spent two “very difficult years” trying for a baby through multiple miscarriages and ultimately IVF. “That was the first time in my life that I had felt lonely,” she says.

Miscarriage in particular, Sasha recalls as “the loneliest of experiences”, causing her to feel apart from her loved ones and withdraw socially. “It’s a type of grief that is really difficult for people who haven’t been through it to understand.”

By the time she gave birth to her daughter, Sasha was “physically and emotionally exhausted”. The shock of new motherhood – far from the easy, beatific state she’d expected – deepened her sense of alienation and ambivalence. “Particularly having a much-wanted baby you’ve really fought for, you think, ‘I’m not entitled to feel anything except joy,’” she says.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Even her partner could not relate, despite his best efforts. “He’s very involved but … my experience was very different to his,” Sasha says. “He was still going to work; his life hadn’t changed to the same degree.”

Loneliness can also spring from self-comparison and feeling yourself to have deviated from the expected or accepted path – itself frequently gendered. For Laura*, 41, from Auckland, loneliness is “almost like a feeling of panic”.

She recalls going for dinner with a group of school friends and realising midway through that they’d spoken exclusively about their children. Laura was the only non-parent among them.

It wasn’t that she didn’t want to hear about their families, she says, and there was no deliberate effort to exclude her. “It was a simultaneous feeling that no one was particularly interested in what might be going on for me in my life, and also feeling shut out from this experience.”

Laura emphasises that she doesn’t feel lonely often. “It comes and goes, and is very much dependent on mood, what’s happening at work, who’s in my general orbit, the weather – all those factors that I think also affect mental health more generally.”

But her experience of loneliness is tied up with her life circumstances. Laura is single and lives alone, while many of her close friends have families or live far away. “I am in a very different life stage,” she says.

Laura works hard to expand her network and socialise solo, but it feels effortful; she misses the easy, unthinking companionship of a romantic partner or even flatmates. Not having “that default unit” – someone to commiserate or celebrate with and just share in her day-to-day experience – “comes with a sense of doing everything alone”, Laura says.

Sexist stereotypes add another layer of ambivalence, she suggests. “A man alone is self-sufficient, taking this bold, brave step, versus a woman living alone is a failure, left on the shelf … a weird, unlovable spinster.” It’s not that she believes this of herself, Laura adds. “It’s more my concern that that’s how other people will perceive me.”

Men have their own gendered drivers of loneliness, not least that expectation of being stoic and self-sufficient. In fact, that might be driving the attention on the male “epidemic”, Barreto suggests: because, stereotypically, men are supposed to be strong and unfeeling – the fact they might feel lonely is considered surprising and newsworthy.

While lonely women tend to internalise the problem and “get on with it”, Barreto goes on, the potential consequences of loneliness, for men, “can be a lot more severe”. Globally, rates of suicide are higher for males than females.

But there is not necessarily a straightforward association between a man feeling lonely and posing a threat to himself or others. The concept of a “male loneliness epidemic” also suggests a single, sweeping event, rather than a highly individual process. “Loneliness is a subjective experience, so it needs to be assessed in that way,” Barreto says.

Instead of comparing male and female loneliness, we need to augment our understanding of both, and non-binary individuals with them, she says. “We need to look at gendered life experiences, and link those to how they are hindering or facilitating our social connection … What is making men lonely, and what is making women lonely?”

By engaging with the specificity of those (and other) experiences, we may learn how to protect against loneliness and intervene effectively, Barreto says.

Already the data points to a productive path forward. A 2022 study of 30 countries found those that had higher levels of gender equality had lower rates of loneliness, for both men and women; the researchers hypothesised that equality was more conducive “to high-quality, close relationships”.

That dovetails with other research, showing loneliness to be a socioeconomic issue. Instead of looking to treat “male loneliness”, a better strategy might be improving social infrastructure and increasing living standards for everyone’s benefit. In the meantime, sharing individual experiences can help.

When Sasha became pregnant with her second child earlier this year, she knew she did not want to repeat the fraught, lonely time she had with her first. She engaged a therapist to protect her mental health and sought out honest, nuanced accounts of motherhood (she namechecks Matrescence by Lucy Jones) that made her feel seen.

“Happily”, Sasha says, her second postpartum experience has been easier. She has also made a point of speaking honestly about her difficult road to parenthood. Her motivation was to help others feel less lonely, but it eased the burden for her, too. “I found the more open I was, the more connected I felt.”

* names have been changed.
