Corporate Democrats are weaponizing identity politics to smear progressives

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 13:00:46 GMT

House members have responded to legitimate criticism with cynicism. Let’s not have another ‘Bernie bros’ moment

Before we get started, some ground rules. You are, of course, completely free to disagree with everything I have to say here. However, doing so might mean that you’re racist, homophobic and/or sexist. (Not to boast, but I have a lot of oppression cards to play.) So, you might want to tread carefully, OK?

That might sound ridiculous, but I don’t make the rules: I’m just taking a page from the corporate Democrat playbook. From Haley Stevens to Hakeem Jeffries, cynically weaponizing identity politics to ward off reasonable criticism seems to be all the rage.

Let’s start with the soon-to-be-irrelevant Stevens who, as you may have noticed, is an adult human female. The Michigan representative is also a sore loser who attempted to torpedo Abdul El-Sayed’s senate campaign by endorsing his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, at the 11th hour.

But don’t you dare quibble with her about any of that or she’ll cry sexism. In a softball interview with conservative commentator Scott Jennings before the midterms, Stevens seemed to imply that sexism played a part in why she wasn’t invited to an El-Sayed campaign event.

“I gave [El-Sayed] an opportunity ... to unite around something that everyone could agree on, and then I got disinvited instead,” Stevens told Jennings. “This is what happens to women.”

Stevens must have been born with an inability to experience embarrassment because, after El-Sayed won, she doubled down on this cringe weaponization of feminism. “For me, living my beliefs was never measured by who would win at the ballot box,” she posted in a lengthy essay on Twitter/X. “As a woman, I have the right to make a decision and to change my mind.”

As a woman, I have the right to change the subject now and move on to Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to be the next speaker of the House.

Not everyone is thrilled by this for a number of reasons. There is the fact that he is very chummy with Aipac (the American Israel Public Affairs Committee), for example. Not only has he received money from the group, but Aipac has publicly boasted about supporting him. And on Thursday, Jeffries refused to say whether he supported or opposed controversial efforts to integrate the US and Israeli militaries.

Jeffries also said this summer that he opposes Medicare for All, reversing his earlier position, and putting him at odds with a number of progressive Democrats who campaigned on the platform.

He’s been consistently hostile to the progressive faction of his party, refusing to endorse Mamdani for New York City mayor for months. And it was recently revealed that Jeffries met with Jared Kushner in private before the midterms, which did not go down very well.

“The American people demanded impeachment!” one protester yelled at Jeffries during an event on Friday. “Your version of accountability is shaking hands with the Trump family!”

Many progressives view Jeffries as an establishment figure who offers no hope for meaningful change and want someone less beholden to corporate interests to be speaker. Jeffries and some of his allies, meanwhile, have suggested that denying him the opportunity to become the first Black speaker in US history would be, to quote Bloomberg, “racially insensitive”.

During the June congressional primaries, when a picture of Jeffries came up on the screen at a victory party for Claire Valdez, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, the crowd yelled: “You’re next!”

“It was very interesting to me, as observed by others, that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd,” Jeffries said in a CNN interview this week.

I don’t know about that crowd, but there’s plenty of diversity amongst DSA-affiliated politicians. Zohran Mamdani, the first Muslim mayor of New York, is a DSA member. So are Nithya Raman and Janeese Lewis George, who just got elected as the respective mayors of Los Angeles and Washington DC. DSA members David Morales and Yousef Rabhi are going to be the next mayors of Providence, Rhode Island, and Ann Arbor, Michigan.

If we’re going to continue to play identity politics, I should note all six of the DSA candidates elected to the House were Black, brown, or from marginalized backgrounds. You can certainly argue that DSA supporters skew white, but painting it as some sort of racist organization, as Jeffries seems to be doing, is intellectually dishonest.

And we’ve seen this craven use of identity politics to smear progressive politics before, haven’t we? It’s the Bernie bros playbook all over again.

Despite the fact that some polls found that young women supported Bernie Sanders in greater numbers than young men in the 2016 primaries, Sanders’ supporters were portrayed as misogynistic bros. Hillary Clinton’s campaign may not have coined the term, but they leaned heavily into this bad-faith narrative.

Let’s not have a Bernie bros 2.0 moment, please. While a petition to make the progressive Massachusetts congresswoman Ayanna Pressley the speaker of the House reached around 100,000 signatures on Friday, Jeffries faces no real challengers. He is almost certainly going to be the next speaker.

Instead of responding to criticism with identity politics, Jeffries has an opportunity to listen to reasonable concerns about his leadership and build a broad coalition that includes progressives instead of sidelining them. And that’s my opinion as a woman.

“We are proposing a comprehensive package of measures to curb all forms of violence against women, for the safety ⁠and dignity of Hungarian women,” the prime minister Peter Magyar said on Thursday. Magyar put an end to 16 years of soft autocracy by the far-right Viktor Orbán when he won a resounding election victory in April.

“While there is no publicly announced restriction on male dentists treating women, a ban appears to have spread across the country,” the Guardian reports. “In most provinces, male doctors have also received orders and directives from the Taliban instructing them not to examine female patients.”

“It just shows the hypocrisy behind so-called Saudi reform,” the activist Maryam Aldossari told the Guardian. “We know MBS [Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince] has been trying to show the world that Saudi is becoming a modern country that empowers women, yet we see the court sentence a mother to 100 lashes.” Large swathes of the western press have been complicit in whitewashing Prince Mohammed (who has been described as a “psychopath” by an exiled intelligence officer), when it’s always been clear his “reforms” are a hollow PR exercise.

“People describe it as a sudden dysphoria … that follows nipple stimulation,” the Guardian writes. There’s not much scientific research into it, and it’s not an official medical diagnosis, but there are a lot of interesting theories.

“It is all too convenient to cast Netanyahu – wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity – as the bogeyman,” writes Owen Jones. “But the dehumanisation of Palestinians is so extreme that even their youngest, most defenceless members are regarded as legitimate targets by leading figures in both government and opposition.”

Following revelations of Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman thought to be a Chinese spy, that phrase is everywhere. “The story behind the phrase is that a good, hardworking man was minding his own business when a serpent of a woman lured him off the righteous path by dishonest means and propositions he, being a man, simply couldn’t refuse,” writes Laëtitia Vitaud for FastCompany. “Can a 63-year-old billionaire CEO really be supposed to have no say over his sex life? Like a bear wouldn’t be able to resist honey?”

While prenups may be all the rage right now, guess who doesn’t appear to have one? Jensen Huang’s wife.

Remember poor Peanut the squirrel? He was euthanized by New York authorities and turned into a parable about Democratic government overreach by JD Vance. Now the squirrel’s former owner has been detained by ICE and may be deported. Is Vance going to come to her rescue? Somehow I do nut think so.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 13:00:46 GMT

From a bamboo gym in Bali to a house made from earth in Wiltshire, these projects show the beauty in sustainable design

With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful.

Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil

In Tocantins, central Brazil, the Canuanã school is a boarding school whose pupils come from remote farming communities across the region. In 2017, architects gave the school’s 540 boarders two new “villages” of dormitories, one for girls and one for boys.

The buildings are made from locally sourced timber and earth bricks. A vast canopy shades the complex, and perforated brick walls let air pass through, so the bedrooms stay comfortable without air conditioning even when temperatures reach 45C. Under the roof, rooms open on to shady, landscaped courtyards and airy verandas.

David Mikhail, the co-founder of Mikhail Riches, a UK practice specialising in sustainable design, says: “It is absolutely fantastic. So beautiful. It does a lot with little resource, which is the essence of a sustainable approach.” He adds: “I love the economy of it, and the huge sense of place they managed to evoke through such elegant and limited means.”

The architects have said their biggest challenge was convincing pupils and teachers that earth, brick and timber could feel modern rather than old-fashioned. They managed to do so by listening to students through 10 days of workshops to understand what they wanted from the design.

The Arc, Bali, Indonesia

The Green school in Bali is surrounded by jungle and promotes sustainability through learning in a natural environment. Since it opened in 2008, it has been built almost entirely in bamboo. Its gymnasium, the Arc, was completed in 2021.

Inspired by a mammal’s ribcage, the Arc’s bamboo arches span a 760 sq metre sports court without a single column interrupting the floor space. The arches support an undulating canopy, and natural ventilation comes from breezes that flow in at the base, while warm air escapes through vents at the top.

Bamboo is a highly sustainable building material because of how quickly it can regrow; large varieties reach building strength in just three to six years. “It is so fast-growing and sequesters a lot of carbon dioxide very quickly, so using it for building is a bit of a no-brainer if you can make it work,” says Mikhail. “And not only have they made it work, they’ve done it absolutely beautifully.”

Sara Kulturhus, Skellefteå, Sweden

Skellefteå, a small city just south of the Arctic Circle, is surrounded by 480,000 hectares (1.2m acres) of forest, and features wooden schools, a wooden road bridge, even a wooden multistorey car park. In 2021 it added Sara Kulturhus, a 20-storey cultural centre and hotel that is one of the tallest timber buildings in the world. It houses two theatres, a museum, an art gallery, the city library and a hotel.

The building is made of glulam – layers of timber glued together – and cross-laminated timber, a kind of super-sized plywood. The hotel rooms arrived as prefabricated wooden pods and were stacked into place. Building in wood saved a year in construction time compared with steel and concrete, while the timber came from trees harvested within 40 miles of the site, and replacement trees have since been planted.

“It promotes a love affair with wood and timber, and the localism of that in an area like Sweden is fabulous,” Mikhail says. “The lovely thing about cross-laminated timber is that the trees you use to make the panels don’t have to be elderly specimen trees. They can be relatively fast-grown and sustainably farmed.”

The Forest, Hobart, Australia

When the University of Tasmania was planning the redevelopment of its main campus in central Hobart, the architects chose to adapt what was already there rather than demolish it and start again. Two early 20th-century brick warehouses and a heritage-listed glass dome were stitched together into a single campus of classrooms and study spaces, which opened in February 2026.

At its heart is the glass dome, built in 1997. It is filled with about 3,200 native plants, including various species of ferns, and has an integrated watering, misting and fogging system that recreates rainforest-like growing conditions.

“You could argue the most sustainable building is actually no building, and the second most sustainable building is a refurbished old building,” says Mikhail. “That’s what this is: they’re taking existing structures and breathing new life into them, reimagining what they could be.”

Rammed Earth House, Cranborne Chase, UK

On the site of a former brickworks in the Wiltshire countryside, this house has been built from the ground beneath it. Rammed earth, which has been used since the Neolithic period, is a building material made of soil that has been compacted layer by layer into thick walls. Here, clay-rich soil was dug up and mixed with rubble from demolished outbuildings and local limestone.

The earth is “unstabilised”, meaning no cement has been added, which makes this one of only a few UK buildings made that way. Unstabilised earth could, in principle, simply go back into the ground if the house were ever demolished.

Rammed earth’s thermal mass also evens out temperature and moisture indoors, which the architects say will matter more as the climate warms. “As a piece of architecture, I think it’s phenomenal,” says Mikhail. “It’s an architect’s dream, and I’m slightly envious of it, I’ll be honest.”

“It’s like a beautiful piece of jewellery, and it riffs on lots of really lovely sustainable ideas.”

Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 13:00:44 GMT

People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.

Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.

Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.

Devastating floods across much of the world In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.

World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.

Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.

Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.

Ocean heat enters uncharted territory Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.

Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.

West African deluge takes heavy toll Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

Fires choke Canada and Europe Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.

Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.

At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.

Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.

Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.

Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.

Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.

Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.

Roads turn to rivers in Chile After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.

Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.

2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history

Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 12:00:46 GMT

Dylan Thomas’s Under Milk Wood reminded me of my dad’s decency and mischief. I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process

I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him.

But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. Then, when my partner and I rearranged our bookshelves, I found the first edition of Under Milk Wood that my parents gave us on our wedding day. I turned the cover and saw the note: “And all the bells of the tills of the town shall ring for our wedding.” It was my mum’s writing, but my dad’s idea. The man loved literature and poetry and considered Dylan Thomas, along with his dad and the Welsh rugby full-back JPR Williams, one of the best men to ever occupy our world.

I decided to re-read Under Milk Wood. I took in the first few lines and I suddenly missed him so entirely. My dad grew up in the most northerly village in Wales, on the shore of the Irish Sea, a place full of humour and surrealism. It made him a glutton for wordplay. Names in Under Milk Wood felt all too familiar: Dai Bread, the baker with two wives; Evans the Death, the undertaker; Nogood Boyo, the troublemaker. I heard my dad laugh at the Preacher’s words: “Will you take this woman to be your awful wedded wife?”

Thomas, like my dad, leaned into linguistic excess. Consider the sea, the jollyrodgered sea, dab-filled sea, still still sea, seesaw sea, seas barking like seals, seas green as a bean. I read the play in my old man’s voice, that London-diluted Welsh, with rolling Rs and whispering double Ls. It helped me access grief and mine proved a good grief: I laughed as I cried, cackled as I wept. My grief reminded me of all we’d lost, all we’d been lucky to have.

Small towns and villages possess their own mythology, secured by whispers, spread by gossips, growing wilder by iteration. I remembered my dad, sitting with me in the garden, a laugh so laughable it made me laugh, telling his child stories of his own childhood. A woman in his home town once grew a potato so big they had to build a chip shop round it. There was a crab who people knew on a first-name basis. Sledgehammer-wielding men could not break a boulder, size of a house, until my dad’s taid (grandfather), a stonemason, drew a small cross in white chalk. “Hit here,” he said, walking away. The boulder shattered into a thousand pieces.

Under Milk Wood brought the stories rushing back, with its own chronicles of absurdity. A sea-lawyer from Mumbles dies from blisters. It is always opening time in the never-closing Sailors Arms, because the clock has been stuck on half past 11 for 50-odd years. And Nogood Boyo was a fisher who never caught a fish, but did catch a woman called Mrs Samuels. Stories spread in winding whispers, embellished at every turn. The stories are seemingly implausible. But they are without doubt true, ask anyone.

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

I realised, spending time in Milk Wood, that there are no roadmaps for grief, nor a right way to grieve. Mine proved tragicomic: pain laced in laughter. And I’m lucky because next month, perhaps next year, I can pick up Under Milk Wood and it’s as if I get to see my old man again. I’ll listen to his stories. I’ll get to hear his voice. So, with that in mind, best to depart on the best part, Eli Jenkins’s prayer, and a stanza that truly captures my dad: We are not wholly bad or good Who live our lives under Milk Wood, And Thou, I know, wilt be the first To see our best side, not our worst.

‘Don’t lie to me to get free stuff’: how small businesses are fighting back against influencers behaving badly

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 12:00:43 GMT

From diva-like behaviour to freebie requests that never result in a review, ‘entitled’ content creators are a growing blight on small-business owners. Now entrepreneurs are calling them out

Nicole Flanagin remembers exactly the moment an influencer came after her business. It was the early hours of a March morning and the cat cafe owner in Lenoir, North Carolina, got a message. “At 1.37,” she says, “a friend sent me the link to this girl’s TikTok.”

The 41-year-old was already having a bad 24 hours. A mother of four, Flanagin also works at a pet rescue shelter and had spent the previous day unsuccessfully fighting for a dog not to be put down. She got home exhausted and promptly conked out in bed. Then she woke up to the message.

The video began innocuously enough with a local influencer sitting in her parked car. “For those of you who know me,” she stated, “I do reviews of local businesses. One very special thing about me is I don’t make bad reviews – but I’m kinda mad right now!” The woman had just taken her child to an unnamed cafe with “animals you can pet”, only to be coldly turned away because she had got its visiting hours wrong. In the influencer’s telling, she began bargaining with staff to try to let the girl into the area where the animals were kept. No dice. Her daughter started “literally bawling her eyes out … and they were just, like, standing there staring”.

Flanagin knew instantly that the woman was talking about her cafe, Brews and Mews – the only animal cafe in the area. The cats are fosters from local shelters, and children aged six and under can only visit during “Happy Meow-ers” sessions, to safeguard the cats’ time away from customers – particularly small, sticky‑fingered ones.

She looked up the woman’s account: she had more than 170,000 followers, some of whom had already started to comment favourably on the post. Flanagin knew it was only a matter of time before internet sleuths tracked down the name of her cafe. “I was, like, I’m going to get crushed. She’s going to close my business.”

But, amid her rising panic, Flanagin had a nagging feeling that something wasn’t quite right. “She attacked my employee and made out he was just staring at her kid wailing on the floor,” she says. But Brews and Mews hadn’t received an official complaint in its inbox. None of her typically conscientious employees had flagged the incident to her. So Flanagin looked up the CCTV. “I love a good receipt,” she tells me. “I’ve been through a divorce, honey.”

Time-stamped footage from security cameras in the cafe showed the influencer entering and having a conversation lasting less than 40 seconds with a staffer behind the till. She and her child briefly looked at the cats in the window before leaving quietly. There was little visible evidence of a toddler tantrum or, indeed, of a rudely gawking employee. “I started watching, and I was, like, ‘This did not happen.’” Flanagin says. A day and a half later, she decided to post the CCTV on the Brews and Mews TikTok page with an outraged comment about the lies the woman had told. That video now has more than 640,000 views.

The content creator later deleted her review and posted an apology video, where she explained: “I was upset as a parent and clicked that post button before I really thought about what would happen.” But the encounter clearly still rankles Flanagin. “Why is your opinion any more valid or important than mine or somebody else’s?” she says today of influencers. “I don’t regret defending myself.”

It may seem extreme to look up surveillance footage in order to prove a content creator wrong, but Flanagin is not the only small-business owner who has resorted to using CCTV. When singer Kelly Clarkson (a celebrity rather than an influencer) posted about what she regarded as bad service at the Art of Play shop in Brooklyn after being told a $15,000 mechanical bird she wanted to buy wasn’t for sale, it went around the world and surveillance footage was posted in response.

Flanagin’s fight was another skirmish on the frontline of a growing war between entrepreneurs and online content creators. The relationship is a complicated one: many business owners are thrilled to have the attention, and know that a post can make a difference. But, increasingly, they are feeling burned by influencers behaving badly, and are taking matters into their own hands. It has led to a takedown economy where the “fightback” can go as viral as a sponsored post. One such example relates to Binky Felstead from Made in Chelsea. When her assistant asked for a free cake for Felstead’s son’s third birthday, the baker snapped, went public, and caused a furore (and got an apology). Some independent shops are banning influencers altogether – and Borough Market in London has clarified its rules on filming, in a crackdown on the plague. How did we get here?

Before the rise of the creator economy, it was only Hollywood actors, star athletes and supermodels who expected celeb treatment. Now that rarefied circle has expanded to include social media influencers and many wannabes. They have sprouted across almost every sector: there are influencers for lawn care, Minecraft, dairy farming and more. But the nature of fame has fragmented, too. You could be lining up for a viral apple crumble next to the biggest food influencer in London and be none the wiser. Your son might be a fan of a Roblox creator with a millions-strong following and you might never recognise their username.

According to Forbes, the influencer economy is worth $250bn and is projected to almost double by 2027. Influencers can shift mountains of product and drive sales for the businesses they choose to work with. That can be transformational, particularly for those that struggle to afford traditional advertising. “Influencers absolutely catapulted my business to where it is now,” says Lucy Herron, the founder of the British shoe-wear brand Sloafer. “You can sell 50 pairs of shoes in 24 hours, and that is the difference between you being able to put a bit of money in your profit pot and not being able to pay your invoices.”

But depending on influencers as a marketing strategy is a double-edged sword. Diva-like behaviour can grow unchecked. Once, Herron sent a free pair of ballerina trainers (retail price £225) to an influencer best known for appearing on a reality show, expecting the customary thank you post on Instagram. Instead, the woman told Herron that she couldn’t publicly thank the brand because it might come to the attention of the tax authorities (according to HMRC, gifted products count towards your taxable income).

After months of back and forth, she reluctantly agreed to post a photo and tag Sloafer. Herron laughed in disbelief when she saw the picture. The woman had worn the black pumps with an all-black outfit and photographed herself standing at the back of a room, her face shrouded in darkness. “It was like collaborating with a ninja,” Herron says. “It sticks in your throat – they could buy a pair of my shoes in every colour and it wouldn’t dent their bank balance.” Still, Herron begrudgingly left a positive comment on the influencer’s page, thanking her for the post. “You have to keep playing the game,” she sighs. (Like all the business owners I spoke to, Herron didn’t want to name names.)

Influencers make for powerful recommendation engines and equally powerful enemies, adept at harnessing their followers’ outrage and weaponising the language of moral virtue. When Four Winds Craft Guild in Nantucket, Massachusetts, went viral after putting up a “no influencers” sign, some creators accused the owner of misogyny. One suggested that hating influencers was a “socially acceptable way to hate women”. “There are obvious valid reasons to criticise influencer culture,” argued the Canadian influencer Levi Coralynn in her video on the controversy, “[but] the conversation has now moved past hating on the industry and people just seem to hate women who participate in it.”

Herron has also been accused of sexism for calling out influencer culture on her social media accounts – particularly when she posted about unfollowing 250 female-owned accounts because she was fed up with sending shoes to influencers who never wore them. “It’s got nothing to do with internalised misogyny,” she tells me. “I’m trying to run a profitable business, and it’s bloody hard enough without someone taking the piss.”

Josh Wheeler, the founder of PR agency Be Broadcast, has worked with influencers for 15 years, often acting as an intermediary between them and brands and businesses. He says there is no one type of influencer most prone to bad behaviour. “I can think of nightmares and angels in all [categories].”

“The view from talent and people smelling the money around influencers is that [they are] the future, so everything has to be bent and broken around that influencer,” he explains. That can lead to mixed results for businesses who are pinning their hopes on an influencer’s reach. “There might be a campaign landing on Monday and the talent pulls out on Friday,” he recalls. “You’re, like, ‘OK, cool. Well, we’ve just spent three months on this.’ We’ve seen talent say to staff, ‘Don’t look me in the eye.’” Another was blacklisted after making “deeply inappropriate” comments about a member of Wheeler’s team on a briefing call. Still, he says, businesses sometimes treat influencers with kid gloves. “There is often a nervousness,” he says. “It’s like they forget they’re in charge.”

Perhaps because of this overweening power, a backlash is brewing against what some see as an increasingly noxious sense of entitlement among influencers. Big corporations can afford to put aside a budget to cover extravagant freebies and press trips, but small indies like Sloafer are “operating on knife‑edge profit margins”, Herron explains. Every pair of shoes sent to an influencer is one that they could sell to a customer, but “you’ve always got that thing in the back of your mind where you know a post could sell 20 pairs of shoes”, she says.

The tantalising possibility of the post that could revitalise your beloved establishment or save your brand is what keeps business owners coming back, says Hubert Zanier, the owner of Kipferl, a London-based restaurant and patisserie that serves Austrian food. In the hospitality industry, influencers have almost completely supplanted the role of the food critic when it comes to spreading the word about their businesses. “A lot of restaurants are struggling,” he says. “They all hope for that one viral post that makes the whole thing explode and pick up.”

Zanier knows this all too well. In 2024, a well‑known London influencer with 100,000 followers left him in the lurch after totting up a £300 bill at his restaurant. The first hint that something was off came when she asked to bring her family – something that Zanier normally wouldn’t accommodate (most restaurants will cover a plus one, but no more). She turned up with her partner, her parents and their dog – and proceeded to order two £38 bottles of red wine and almost £40 worth of schnapps. “My manager texted me and said, ‘Is that OK?’ I was, like, yeah, whatever – maybe we’ll get good coverage out of it.”

Instead, what happened was a months-long dispute between Zanier and the influencer, culminating in the latter calling him after Christmas to scream at him. “I was perplexed,” Zanier says. Typically, influencers will acknowledge a free meal on social media a few days after visiting a restaurant, he explains. But the creator fobbed him off for months. “She started to write really weird stuff, like ‘at the moment my creative juices are not flowing’.” Nine months on – Zanier is nothing if not persistent – the influencer finally gave up and offered to foot the bill. But when he sent it she phoned him up, furiously telling him: “This is absolutely outrageous.”

“I said, ‘I have a small business,’” Zanier recalls. “You exploited and abused my hospitality. I’ve invited you for lunch with wine and everything. I mean, we’re not friends. What’s the deal here?” The influencer conceded that she might include the restaurant in a write-up of European restaurants the year after – at which point he admitted defeat. “I just mentally wrote it off,” he says today. “But it was really, really unpleasant.” He still works with influencers, but is much more selective about who he invites to his restaurant. “I think they are part of the [food] industry now,” he shrugs. “Just because some of them might be black sheep, it doesn’t mean that they’re all crooked.”

But with such “rogue operators” (as Zanier puts it) circling the industry, it’s no wonder that some establishments are vigorously clamping down. When Borough Market security kicked out the food vloggers Bite Twice for filming there in November, it was said to have marked a “Frankenstein moment” for the hospitality business – the industry had created a monster and was now fighting back. The market now enforces rules against the scourge of content creators clogging up stalls and walkways with their equipment – anybody filming with more than a crew of two (presenter and cameraperson) or with professional-grade equipment must now seek clearance and carry their permit with them. It was hailed as a long-overdue rebalancing of the relationship between businesses and influencers – one that puts paying customers first.

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Halfsies Cookie Company founder David Maffei usually spends seven days a week, sometimes up to 10 hours a day, baking in his New York kitchen – as a team of one. In Maffei’s eyes, influencers can provide useful PR for a small business like his. When the model Amber Lancaster posted about Halfsies to her half a million followers, he says, “We sold out for months.”

But influencer culture, he argues, has also spawned a generation of entitled imitators who believe that having a small following justifies A-list treatment from brands and businesses. The worst, he says, are those who fire off blandly friendly copy-and-paste messages to multiple companies, hoping someone will take the bait. “They’re, like, ‘Oh, I love your product. They’re such an integral part of my daily life!’” He now collates the cheekiest requests, along with his withering takedowns, on a Hall of Fame category on his Instagram.

“I’d love to include your amazing products in my bridal party boxes,” one such email request went. “Are you in for some bridal bliss? Let’s chat!” After Maffei pointed out that she had only 1,300 followers on Instagram, the bride-to-be argued, “I’m a beginner influencer.”

“And I’m a beginner astronaut,” Maffei replied. He posted screenshots of the exchange on the Halfsies Instagram account, where it received more than 17,000 likes and was even covered by People magazine. “Don’t lie to me to get free stuff,” he says.

“When you get those messages, it’s quite disheartening,” Anastasia Powers, a luxury balloon artist based in Essex, tells me. She has created dramatic displays for weddings, galas and corporate clients such as Zambrero and Twickenham rugby club. In other words, she’s not short of work – she is currently in the middle of talks with a celebrity DJ to create a display for his birthday – but still receives up to 10 freebie requests a month. “You’ve contacted me, so you can see the quality of my work – yet you want it for free and you don’t want to pay me my worth.” Powers sighs.

She founded Poptastic Balloon Company three years ago and is a one-woman business, doing everything from designing the display, driving to the location, and sizing and shaping the helium balloons to packing it all down at the end of the day. “Collaborations don’t pay for my petrol, my lights, my stock,” Powers says firmly. “They don’t put food on my table.”

She has a policy of turning down all influencer requests and says that other people in her industry are increasingly coming over to her way of thinking. She is in a WhatsApp group chat with fellow business owners to share intel about the worst offenders. “We’ll screenshot the messages, and we’ll all laugh,” she smiles. “Sometimes we’ll coordinate a reply and we’ll all send it to them, which is quite funny.”

Reshmi Bennett is the Michelin-trained founder of the luxury cake business Anges de Sucre, who made headlines for calling out Made in Chelsea’s Felstead after receiving an email requesting a “gifted” cake for her son Wilder. (Felstead is estimated to be worth between £1.4m and £3m and lives in a £3.6m south-west London house, which is, according to the Daily Mail, largely furnished with freebies.) The former banker turned chef was incensed: “Your whole persona is to be rich and fabulous, and here you are grifting for free stuff to pretend you’re rich and fabulous to your followers.”

Bennett’s cakes are expensive and artisanal work – she runs a team of three full-time staff and one part-timer to make towering creations that are hand‑delivered across London and Surrey. “Even though £100 is a lot for the average person to pay for a cake, the costs involved in us making the cake and getting it to the customer have just ballooned,” she explains.

Bennett took to Instagram to call Felstead out, even creating a joke fundraiser for the influencer to cover the cost of her son’s birthday cake. “Unfortunately,” Bennett noted on the now-deleted GoFundMe page, “our energy supplier is old-fashioned and continues to insist on being paid in actual money rather than exposure or engagement”. (A representative for Felstead later said: “This was a standard inquiry from Binky’s PA, offering social media exposure in exchange for a birthday cake.”)

Bennett, 42, has been burned by working for free in the past. An influencer with about 20,000 followers once asked for a birthday cake for her child. As the influencer was local to the area, Bennett hoped it might lead to more customers in the neighbourhood. But when the pictures were posted on Instagram, Bennett’s cake was one of many treats on a dessert table that included cookies, doughnuts and even cakes from her competitors. Worst of all, she only received a single inquiry as a result. It said: “Oh, hi, it’s my daughter’s birthday. Would you like to collaborate?”

“Piss off!” she laughs. “Work for free to get more free work? No thanks … I’ve set a filter in my inbox to put emails that have the word ‘sponsorship’ or ‘collaboration’ into spam.”

Cynics might observe that calling out these influencers can be a way to drive attention to your own brand. With the Clarkson case, the jury is out as to whether Art of Play’s response – contesting her account and jokily raising the price of the bird to $15m – was the right one. Still, negativity is the life force of the internet – one study has found that negative posts attract twice as much engagement as positive ones. In much the same way that “de-influencing” videos of creators criticising viral products became a trend in and of itself, negative posts about influencers have become their own cottage industry, with content creators on YouTube breaking down social media beefs for their followers.

But Bennett says that a no-holds-barred approach doesn’t always go down well if you’re a business trying to sell people your product. “I have got some stick,” she acknowledges. “It’s, like, you could just politely say no and move on. If I do, they just find someone else to [take my place], and it keeps that cycle going.” The answer, she says, is for small-business owners to speak out and share what it’s like to work with influencers – the good, the bad and the ugly. Wheeler, of Be Broadcast, advises businesses to be clear about their expectations when approaching influencers, including getting what they want in exchange in writing. “That early stage is genuinely vital to make sure that your experience doesn’t go pear‑shaped,” he says.

Back in Lenoir, North Carolina, Flanagin is gearing up for the morning shift at Brews and Mews. While she has received support from all over the world after she posted her video, the local community on Facebook have been firmly on the side of the influencer. Critics have said that she should have tried to handle it privately or not posted footage featuring the influencer’s children. “Locally, we’re the devil, yet we’re the first [place] that people call when they find a cat!” Still, her video is staying up. “I don’t regret it, honey. I said it with my whole chest,” she says. “And I would say it all day, every day, again and again.”

Zelenskyy accuses SpaceX of lying about Starshield – and says US floated Donbas-for-Nato deal

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 11:05:33 GMT

Throttling of Elon Musk’s military-grade satellite system affecting whole frontline, says Ukraine’s president

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system, saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”.

Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones had been in place for five days. They could no longer fly at speeds of more than 161km/h (100mph), he said, with connections at higher speeds lost.

As a result, incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones could no longer be intercepted. Ukraine’s own mid-range strikes against military targets in Russian-occupied territory were also severely affected, he said.

Speaking to the Guardian and other journalists at the presidential palace in Kyiv, Zelenskyy said he had asked his military leadership to raise the issue with Elon Musk’s company SpaceX, as well as with the Pentagon and the US state department.

There was “no clear explanation” as to why Ukraine’s operations were being throttled. He said SpaceX had told Kyiv that there were “no restrictions”. The claim, Zelenskyy suggested, was untrue, with problems detected across the “entire frontline”.

“There have been discussions with the company at the institutional level. The ministry of defence spoke with SpaceX. They replied: ‘We are not imposing any restrictions.’ They say it is some kind of technical issue. We do not believe that is the case,” Zelenskyy said.

He added: “The question is not whether we believe them or not. There may be some further checks. But every day, we test this in different directions. Every day, we get the same confirmation. So these are not isolated cases; they are widespread.”

Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. It follows a similar issue last month and coincided with US-brokered talks last week in Abu Dhabi featuring Ukrainian and Russian representatives.

The Kremlin insists Ukraine give up the entire eastern Donbas region.

But Zelenskyy categorically ruled out giving away further land to Russian “terrorists”. He also revealed that US negotiators, Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate developer Steve Witkoff, had asked if Ukraine was willing to give up the Donbas in exchange for membership of Nato, or Nato-like security guarantees.

Details of the proposal were vague, Zelenskyy said. They did not appear to involve US peacekeeping troops on the ground, he added. He said the war could only end with a ceasefire agreement, alongside meaningful security guarantees, underwritten by western partners.

Zelenskyy also dismissed an offer by Putin for a “humanitarian mission” in the eastern city of Kostiantynivka as a ploy. Russia has called for a five-day ceasefire, modelled on a truce last month in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, from where civilians were evacuated.

“It’s an absolutely primitive move. Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” Zelenskyy said. He said civilians had already fled the area as fierce street-by-street fighting continued, with huge Russian losses.

Zelenskyy said he had proposed repeating the Oleshky truce in nearby Russian-occupied villages and towns in southern Ukraine, along the Dnipro River. Putin rejected this. His true goal was to swallow up Kostiantynivka and the Ukrainian garrison cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Zelenskyy said.

He also called Russian attempts to discuss Europe’s security architecture – a topic raised last week by the Trump administration – “concerning”. The Kremlin has called for Nato to return to its pre-1997 configuration, before eastern European countries including the Baltic states joined the alliance.

Putin first made this demand in 2021, in the run-up to his full-scale Ukraine invasion. Its revival after nearly five years of full-scale war, Zelenskyy said, was an alarming signal, indicative of imperial thinking. “Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact,” Zelenskyy said, stressing: “We cannot turn everything upside down.”

Ukraine’s president said his recent conversations with European leaders who met in Dublin had brought tangible results. They included pledges from Denmark to supply ammunition for F-16 jets – used to shoot down Russian drones – as well as energy support packages for Kyiv and other cities.

Russia was “betting everything” on its winter campaign, he added. In recent months Moscow has escalated its attacks on Ukrainian cities, in an attempt to make civilians capitulate. The US Congress could pressure Putin to de-escalate by passing laws on sanctions and giving Ukraine weapons, Zelenskyy said.

Will Trump’s lame duck presidency push him further beyond constraints of the law?

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 11:00:43 GMT

Midterm elections have defanged the US president – leaving critics to worry about his next move in his ‘fat Elvis’ stage

It was just before 3am when Donald Trump entered a crowded Manhattan ballroom, greeted by chants of “USA! USA” and theme music from the Hollywood film Air Force One. On stage, two red “Make America great again” (Maga) caps were mounted in glass cases like holy relics.

That was the scene 10 years ago this week when Trump, a businessman and reality TV star, stunned the world by beating Hillary Clinton to the White House. A decade later an unlikely president is serving an unlikely second term. But in the wake of a humiliating vote of no confidence in last week’s midterm elections, he now enters an endgame wracked with uncertainty.

“Trump is about to get even weirder and, sadly, more dangerous,” tweeted Clinton, who has been a wry commentator on the Trump years, predicting that the president will deflect blame, become more unhinged, demand even greater loyalty from Republicans and potentially launch fresh attacks on Iran.

Political obituary writers have been swift to describe him as a lame duck, defanged lion or cornered animal in the wake of the midterms. Democrats’ 13 percentage point victory was the second biggest of any midterm election since 1942, and the party conquered the Republican bastions of Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas.

The causes of the Republican rout were plain: an eight month war in Iran that sent fuel prices soaring, persistent cost of living pressures and a backlash against masked immigration raids that turned deadly in Minneapolis.

The 80-year-old president’s response has swung wildly between conciliation, aggression and farce. He told the CBS network’s 60 Minutes program that his deportation push was “too tough” while declaring that no amnesty would occur and appointing immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

He publicly invited the job of White House press secretary to “violent fighter and warrior” Dana White of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), brought him into the briefing room to play out the scenario, then insisted it had all been a joke. He threw his weight behind the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, who survived an impeachment resolution brought by a maverick Republican in Congress.

All the while he has retreated into architectural vanity projects, including a White House ballroom and triumphal arch in Washington, and increasingly wayward rhetoric that included ruminations about men’s posteriors, speeches punctuated by strange guttural sounds and a lengthy social media post about comedian Bill Maher.

Miles Taylor, founder of Defiance. org, a non-profit aimed at countering government corruption and abuses of power, agrees with Clinton’s analysis about the finale of the Trump show. He said: “It will certainly be weirder because Donald Trump was always going to end the administration with the bottom of the barrel appointees.

“Like any wannabe autocrat, you end up in the figurative bunker at the end of the regime with the most hardcore loyalists, which tend to be the people who are willing to contort themselves into whatever shape the leader wants. These are the people who have no scruples and are willing to carry out the president’s most extreme edicts and, in some cases, are the ones who have been goading him for almost a decade to do the most extreme things.”

Miller is the prime example. He has championed expansive presidential power, branded the Democratic party a “domestic extremist organisation”, advocated suspending habeas corpus to speed deportations and asserted that the US has a right to Venezuela’s oil and Greenland’s territory. He supplanted Susie Wiles, whose more measured approach had been seen as a potential restraint on Trump’s darkest impulses.

Taylor, a former chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, said: “In my experience with Stephen, he was a guy that was all too willing to walk up to the line of the law and then leap over it and dare the courts to rein us in. That was literally the type of thing he said to me on multiple occasions.

“One of my biggest fears about this next two years is: will Donald Trump cause the ultimate constitutional crisis by defying judicial orders, including from the supreme court, if he doesn’t get his way? I see it as very possible because he’s got a team around him that might be willing to make the case of why that would be justified.”

There is another way for an embattled president to seek a place in history: foreign policy. Presidents approaching the end of their time in office have often turned to diplomacy and international affairs as a means of burnishing their legacy. After Democrats suffered heavy losses in the 2014 midterms, Barack Obama announced the restoration of diplomatic relations with Cuba, secured a nuclear agreement with Iran and helped broker the Paris climate agreement.

Trump has already placed an emphasis on global affairs since returning to the White House last year. Even as Democrats prepare to rein in the president when they take control of Congress in January, Trump will retain considerable latitude to pursue his ambitions on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China.

Taylor commented: “What he did in the first two years on the foreign policy front could potentially pale in comparison with what he does in the latter two years and that’s saying something because he launched this war in Iran.

“But here are things to look for. Does Nato survive this period? Does the United States actually try to go seize more territory? Both of those are things that Donald Trump has talked about doing and been walked back by advisors on over the course of two terms. I’m not sure that’s the case anymore.

“But then there’s other areas of the world that might be worried about Trump administration inaction being just as bad or worse than Trump administration offensive action, if the Russians try to seize more territory and if the Chinese take Taiwan. On the world stage I would warn our allies, it’s about to get very, very bad. And I would say to our adversaries, this is probably the luckiest two years you’re ever going to get.”

Despite the historic losses, there is little sign of a Republican revolt against Trump. On Capitol Hill this week the party effectively killed the attempt to impeach Hegseth while also electing Jim Jordan, a pugnacious ally of the president, as its minority leader for the next Congress. Most Republicans who survived the midterm bloodbath are from safe red districts and staunchly pro-Trump. The outcome could be more Maga, not less.

Olivia Wales, a spokeswoman for the White House, said via email: “President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years, and a stock market that has hit record highs.

“As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security, and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people.”

Some commentators believe that, given Trump’s ideological fluidity, a deal with Democrats might be possible.

Bill Whalen, a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: “If Trump wants to work with Congress, the question is what do they have in common? If I’m running the Democratic caucuses right now, I might think 70-30 or 80-20 is what I want in terms of a compromise, because the president wants to sign something to show he’s still relevant.”

Whalen suggests an intriguing parallel: “Is Donald Trump at his heart really that conservative, or will he turn out to be a little bit more of a moderate Democrat? Similar to [former Republican governor]Arnold Schwarzenegger here in California, where he gets chastised, and then in his second term, he’s governing very much like a moderate Democrat.”

Others suspect that Trump, who has placed a red baseball cap saying “veto” on his desk in the Oval Office, indicating his willingness to block Democratic legislation, intends to go out with all guns blazing. Newt Gingrich, a former House of Representatives speaker, predicts an aggressive counter attack rather than a chastened administration winding down.

“I recommend everybody read Trump’s book The Art of the Comeback, which explains what he’s like when he’s right at the edge of being destroyed, pivots and rebuilds overnight,” Gingrich said. “You have to assume that he and Stephen Miller are methodically thinking through the comeback. I suspect the State of the Union [address] will be chock-full of things that the American people want that the Democrats will be taunted about passing.”

For Democrats, the uncertainty of whether Trump will offer a fight or flight response poses a conundrum. Speaking at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington this week, congressman Jim Himes said: “We just don’t know which Donald Trump is going to show up. Is it the dealmaker, or is it the Stephen Miller pugilist? On any given day we’re not going to know which president is sitting in the Oval Office.”

For Rick Wilson, a veteran political strategist and co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, the president has crossed a threshold into volatile decline. “The impulsivity has come not only from his age but from the understanding now that he is an island unto himself,” he said.

“He doesn’t have that enormous backstop of congressional impunity to work from. That is going to make him do a lot of lashing out and things like we’ve seen the last few days – going to the podium in the press room and just riffing.”

Wilson believes that Trump has reached his “fat Elvis” phase. “He’s trying to recapture the old magic. He’s trying to get back the old mojo and it just isn’t quite there. The crash out of his approval, the loss of his congressional shield wall and the lack of any adult supervision around him now – it’s a toxic combination where he’s going to feel desperate and angry and crazy.”

While Trump grapples with immediate constraints, political gravity is already shifting toward the presidential succession in January 2029. JD Vance, the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, and Texas senator Ted Cruz were all quick to weigh in with opinions on what went wrong in the midterms. Former state governors Glenn Youngkin and Chris Christie are among other potential contenders.

Can Trump endure sharing the stage in 2028? Wilson foresees a messy spectacle. “He has been the centre of that political gravity for 10 years now. Because he’s the devil, he’s going to go in and piss on Vance one day and raise him up the next. He’ll piss on Marco [Rubio] one day and raise him up the next. He’ll try to be the kingmaker.”

Noel Fielding ‘horrified and deeply disturbed’ by Russell Brand’s crimes

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 10:14:07 GMT

Comedian regrets ‘inappropriate’ jokes he made with Brand during work pair did together in the 2000s

The Great British Bake Off presenter Noel Fielding has said he was “horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand’s crimes” and has had no contact with his fellow comedian “for many years”.

In the early 2000s, Fielding often worked with Brand, who was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

In a statement issued to the Sun, Fielding said: “I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand’s crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice.

“I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

“Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him, I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them.”

Footage has recently resurfaced of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with the TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of the Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007. Brand also joked with Fielding about kissing and holding an underage “grasshopper” on an episode of The Russell Brand Show which aired in October 2007.

Fielding, a frequent guest and co-host on the BBC Radio 2 show, said: “How do you even know if it’s a child or an adult? You don’t even care, do you?”

Brand, who was 32 at the time, replied: “It’s a mistake I’ve made. I’ve had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I’m in it, right, I’m kissing it, I’m holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: ‘I’m 12.’”

The pair had met at the NME Awards in the early 2000s and often performed at charity gigs as a comedy duo known as The Goth Detectives.

Fielding has never been accused of misconduct and there is no suggestion he knew about Brand’s behaviour towards women. Since his conviction, Brand was accused of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women in a new investigation by the Times and the Sunday Times.

‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 10:00:42 GMT

In the first instalment of a new series, four young people reveal the impact of an endless cycle of applications and rejections

Guardian to follow lives of eight young people in their search for jobs

“I’ve been demoralised by the process, just constantly applying, then interviewing. I’ve just been applying to any jobs that I could find. I’d really like to be employed by now. Some companies don’t even give rejection emails … they’re not obligated to reply to the prospective interviewee, but they should be compelled to.”

By Aamir’s estimate, he has applied for more than 1,000 jobs since graduating last year. The 25-year-old has a BA in media and communications and an MA in media studies from two Russell group London universities.

He landed a temporary digital publishing role at a media company, but the contract ended after a few months. Two years later, he is living with his parents in east London, claiming universal credit and looking for work.

“I would like to not be on benefits,” he says. “I would like to have a proper entry-level job in what I studied, but I haven’t been able to get anything. I’m trying.”

Aamir also attends interview coaching through the government’s Restart programme and is completing free Google qualifications to strengthen his CV.

“The universal credit people told me I’d done everything right,” he says. “You can do everything right and still lose.

“I feel like the social contract is broken in Britain. People keep talking about young people not working, but I don’t see anyone asking employers why entry-level opportunities have become so difficult to access.”

Although his focus is on PR and media roles, he has also applied for customer service, retail and receptionist jobs. Recently, he prepared carefully for an interview with a large company that he felt went well, only to spend weeks waiting for an update that never came.

“I just feel really demoralised … I wish they would just give me feedback so it would help for the next interview,” he says.

“I feel like my interviewing skills have improved but it’s still the same. I haven’t found a job yet.

“It feels like a generation of talent is being wasted. We are all desperate to work, contribute to society and get on with our lives. Yet so many people have been unable to get jobs, and when they do, it is often things they are wildly overqualified for and has nothing to do with what they studied.”

When Alice, 24, went from her state secondary school to study at the University of Oxford and then on to complete a master’s degree from Cambridge, she never imagined she would end up living at home, unable to secure a job.

After finishing her studies in 2024 she spent six months working in hospitality to fund an Interrail trip around Europe, returning home to Bristol expecting to begin her career.

More than a year later, she is being supported financially by her parents – supplemented by small amounts earned through ad hoc pet-sitting and dog-walking – while applying for long-term work.

Alice has focused on roles in publishing, museums, heritage organisations, the civil service and retail, but is targeting any sector where she thinks she might have a chance, submitting 50 tailored job applications.

She has reached the interview stage five times and keeps track of every role on a spreadsheet. The process itself has become exhausting. “The worst is when you have to upload your CV, then type out your entire work history again, answer detailed questions and write a cover letter. It just becomes completely mind-numbing.”

One employer headhunted her and put her through two interview rounds before admitting it could no longer recruit anyone. She has volunteered at a charity shop for six months but narrowly missed out on two paid roles within the organisation.

She came second in the process to select a deputy manager role at a different shop and then was encouraged to apply for another similar position. However, despite feeling confident about how the interview went, she was again unsuccessful. It was a huge blow.

“I was encouraged to apply; I made relationships with people at the charity, I had the skill set required, and yet I couldn’t get the job. I feel that if I can’t get this job, I can’t get anything.”

Job hunting has taken a toll on her mental health. “There have been occasions where I’ve not been able to sleep. I’ve cried in the middle of the night and just thought: ‘I don’t want to do any of this.’ Every setback is tricky to pick yourself back up from.

“I assumed I’d have a sort of nine-to-five office job,” she adds. “Maybe living away from home in a different city. Nothing exciting, just a fairly nice, normal thing to do. Instead, I just feel really stuck.”

“The frustrating thing is employers keep saying you need experience. But if you’ve got no experience, they should give you that. Years ago they’d train you on the job. Now it feels like everyone’s looking for somebody who’s already done it.”

After leaving school at 16, Liam, a 20-year-old from Exeter, completed a level 1 qualification in horticulture, followed by level 2 and level 3 diplomas in land and wildlife management, convinced he was building towards a career in grounds maintenance or landscaping.

Instead, he has spent the past two years trapped in a cycle of applications, rejections, short-lived jobs and disappointments.

“I’ve had interviews, rejections, ghosting, you name it,” he says. “I’ve had jobs where they let me go after a couple of weeks. It’s just soul destroying.”

One employer told him he lacked experience after a trial shift. Another kept him on for just six shifts before saying rising costs meant they could not afford to keep him.

Liam, who is autistic, believes some employers also fail to understand the adaptations that would help him succeed. “Sometimes I worry about telling employers because I think it might put them off,” he says. “I just need things explained clearly and a little bit longer to learn. They need to provide reasonable adjustments.”

He now volunteers two days a week at two different community gardens, planting wildflowers, pruning, cutting grass and helping maintain green spaces while building the experience employers say he lacks.

“Volunteering gives me a reason to get up in the morning. It gets me out of the house, builds my confidence and gives me work experience. Outdoor work is therapeutic. You’re surrounded by nature.”

Since January, Liam has also been attending Connect to Work, a government-backed scheme that helps disabled people and those with health conditions move into employment through personalised job coaching and employer support.

“They’ve really helped my confidence,” he says. “They’re very supportive and I think it’s getting me closer to employment, even if I haven’t got there yet.”

Despite everything, Liam remains determined: “It has taken a toll on my mental health. You go up, you go down, but I keep fighting. I want to be financially independent, and I still believe that one day the right opportunity will come along.”

“I got good A-level results and I got a first in my degree, but this hasn’t helped me at all. I’m too young to know what it would have been like a few years ago, but it seems like it was a lot easier then to get work”

When Peter, 21, decided to study computer science at Leicester University, he believed it would give him excellent job prospects. However, the reality has been quite different.

After his course finished in April he initially applied for graduate software engineering jobs in London, figuring it would be easy to commute from his home in Maidstone, Kent, where he lives with his parents.

“Sometimes I would make it to an assessment stage but I have never made it to an interview stage,” says Peter. “With these jobs, I am essentially competing against everyone in the country.

“When I was in primary school, computer science was touted as a high-paying field, desperate for new people. But now that I’ve graduated, it seems that everyone has a computer science degree.”

Peter is also well aware of the devastating impact AI is having on opportunities in the sector. “Why would you employ 10 graduates when you can have one graduate doing the work of 10 with the help of AI. One programmer can do much more than they used to.”

He has applied for more than 50 jobs but cannot afford to move away “to places like Manchester or Edinburgh”. Meanwhile, “there are no graduate-level software engineering jobs locally in Maidstone”.

Peter, who achieved As in maths, physics and computer science, and a B in further maths, believes his lack of any work experience has hampered his search for work.

Yet he remembers at school pupils being “scolded for working too much at part-time jobs when they should have been studying”.

“It seems now that this was actually the correct thing to do,” he says. “I believe that not doing part-time work while I was studying was a huge mistake.”

However, he acknowledges such experience comes at a price: “Imagine if I spent all my time doing part-time work and I got really bad grades, then people would be saying, ‘Oh, you should have studied more.’”

Peter has shifted his focus to look for “entry-level” work at supermarkets and restaurants and has also applied to volunteer at places such as charity shops to build up experience. These applications have been unsuccessful, but he has recently secured two days a week of bar work.
