King Æthelstan founded England in the year 927. Why don’t we celebrate that anniversary?

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 10:00:41 GMT

Nearly 1,100 years ago, the nation’s first king drove out the ‘heathen’ Vikings, declared war on starvation and made ‘Englalonde’ what it is today

On 4 July, the United States celebrated its 250th birthday with all the razzmatazz and dazzle characteristic of an American public occasion. Next summer, on 12 July, England will be celebrating the 1,100th anniversary of the event that, more than any other, marked the founding of the country – but of razzmatazz and dazzle there will be, I suspect, very little.

The great turning point took place on 12 July 927, beside the river Eamont in what today is Cumbria. Here, amid an untamed wilderness of mountains and lakes, the most powerful king in Britain had summoned other kings and lords from across the island to meet him for a summit.

Æthelstan was the grandson of Alfred the Great, the heir to a dynasty that by the 920s had come to rule all the lands south of the Humber. This formidable agglomeration of territories was the fruit of repeated victories over the Vikings: a pagan people, ferociously martial and given to sinister practices such as taking weekly baths.

Back in 925, when Æthelstan had been crowned beside the Thames in Kingston, a Viking still ruled in York, and much of Northumbria – once the most brilliant of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms – remained subject to his rule. But when, in the spring of 927, this Norse king of York died unexpectedly, Æthelstan seized his chance. He appeared before the walls of the ancient city and there was no one to resist him. The lords of Northumbria had duly submitted to Æthelstan as their overlord. For the first time, all the various lands where English was spoken – the lands of the Angles and the Saxons – had been brought to acknowledge a single king. A fateful moment, for it had marked the birth of a new polity: the united kingdom of what would soon come to be known as “Englalonde”.

The summit meeting at Eamont was held to solemnise this new dispensation. So intimidating was Æthelstan’s authority that “all the kings of the island were brought under his rule”. Submission was made; payments of tribute pledged; oaths sworn that no dealings would ever again be had with “the heathen Vikings”. These oaths, in the event, were not to be kept for long. The princes of Wales and Scotland resented the claim of Æthelstan to rule as the rex totius Britanniae – the king of the whole of Britain. His death in 939 enabled them to slip the rule of his heirs.

But the united kingdom of England, secured by Æthelstan in 927, did endure. There was nothing preordained about its emergence. Had Æthelstan neglected to seize his chance in 927, then the political contours of Britain might easily have ended up very different. It is not far-fetched to imagine an Anglo-Viking kingdom ruled from York putting down permanent roots. The heirs of Alfred would then have been confined to Southumbria, and the kings of the Scots to the Highlands. The events of 927 were, in that sense, the making of Scotland as well as of England.

The 1,100th anniversary of that fateful year richly merits commemoration. Æthelstan – mighty warrior though he was – was great not merely as a conqueror. Piety, learning, a passion for justice: these as well were the qualities that drew his contemporaries’ praise. He enshrined in the heart of English governance legal and social assumptions that endure to this day. Æthelstan’s determination that no one living on his own lands be permitted to starve led him to issue repeated ordinances. Officials responsible for his estates were warned by their master that fines would be levied on those who failed in their duty to the needy, and the proceeds donated to charity: “My wish it is that you should always provide the destitute with food.”

Is the mood in England today really so buoyant that it would not be improved by marking – and perhaps even celebrating – the country’s birthday? The story of how Æthelstan’s royal dynasty went from near-oblivion at the hands of the Vikings to fashioning a kingdom that still endures today is among the most remarkable in British history.

It was quite as stirring an achievement as the American Revolution, and quite as epochal in its consequences – and it featured, unlike the signing of the Declaration of Independence, a founding mother. This was Æthelflæd, Æthelstan’s remarkable aunt, who in her role as ruler of the Midlands won back swathes of territory from the Vikings. Remarkable characters, dramatic success against the odds, and the most remarkable feat of state-building in early medieval Europe: there is so much to celebrate.

after newsletter promotion

And those who had witnessed the emergence of England as a unitary state knew it. They appreciated that the joining of different peoples in a shared sense of identity was not something that had been easily achieved. Two and a half decades after the death of Æthelstan, a bishop called Æthelwold, who had served as one of the king’s closest advisers, paid tribute to a man who was “mature in age and very prudent, and farseeing in wisdom, and hard to overcome in any strife”.

Bishop Æthelwold spoke for all those who, enjoying the order brought to lands that only decades before had been scenes of carnage and devastation, felt due gratitude to those who had achieved it. He, close enough in time to Æthelstan’s reign to have been the great king’s protege, understood the full scale of his debt. We, at the remove of 1,100 years, could perhaps remember it better.

Tom Holland is a journalist and author

From Ukraine to Gaza, this is why we need to tell better stories about war

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 08:00:38 GMT

Artists’ acts of remembrance about destruction and violence defy the dominant narratives of heroism and sacrifice

The way stories are told about wars really matters. It is a point powerfully made by the classical scholar Alice König who, in her work on ancient and modern warfare, points out that the way war is depicted and narrativised feeds into the way wars are actually conducted. Creating and absorbing a story (whether that is told in prose or poetry, or offered by an artwork or memorial) is more than packaging or reflecting on the past; it is about generating images and expectations, and about envisioning the future. Stories, she argues, influence real-world behaviours.

The war correspondent Christina Lamb has also made this connection in relation to sexual violence in conflict: depictions of war from Homer onwards show that women have always been trafficked and raped, used as bargaining chips and spolia, their bodies made battlefields. But stories told for centuries, for millennia, have taken this violence for granted, looking blindly past the experience of women. Rape was recognised as an independent war crime and a tool of genocide only in 1998. And so it goes. Rape becomes a brutal and cheap weapon in every new war.

The powerful create wars; wars create power. Unless, that is, the wars go terribly wrong and reality butts into the intended narrative – see the US’s midterm elections, when the story Donald Trump wanted to tell about the Iran war was turned back against him by the irreducible fact of prices at the fuel pumps. The most bald contemporary example of the war-power feedback-loop is perhaps that of today’s Russia, where the second world war (or the great patriotic war, as the acceptable discourse has it) is constantly invoked by Vladimir Putin, seeded liberally into the wider culture and the education system; the invasion of Ukraine is then claimed as, essentially, its extension. For Russian propaganda purposes, the violence against Ukraine is a “denazification”, as if the years between 1945 and 2022 had been magically collapsed.

All of which is why new stories about war are needed – ones that are more truthful and more complete than the dominant patriarchal narratives of heroism and sacrifice. Not that the official narratives are always malign: the processions and the solemnity and the medals brought out on Remembrance Sunday have a dignity and a respectfulness that are of deep value. But there must be a truthfulness, too. The old lies, as Wilfred Owen knew, do no one any good. Poets like him have been the real truth-tellers in war. Instead of lighthearted, invulnerable warriors, or bronze heroes posed on plinths, he brought us the truth of men on the battlefield “Bent double, like old beggars under sacks, / Knock-kneed, coughing like hags.”

War and the act of storytelling are deeply intertwined. Stories about war, such as the Iliad, were among the earliest to be written down. Embedded into that ancient Homeric epic is perhaps an even older form of song: the lament for the dead. The Iliad ends with the corpse of the Trojan prince Hector mourned by Andromache, Hecuba and Helen – his wife, mother and sister-in-law. One veteran of the Russo-Ukrainian war, the artist Bohdan Bunchak, once told me how he and his fellow soldiers, those who survived a terribly dangerous task in the deadly forest in 2023, stayed up for hours into the night, though exhausted, talking about what had happened – who had survived, who died – as soon as they had returned to the relative safety of their base. The storytelling begins at once. In the wake of battle, you tell stories to prove you are alive, and to mourn the dead.

But wars are too jagged and incomprehensible for the whole story of them to fit into the inherited forms. And it is doubtful, too, whether “story”, with all of its implied neatness and coherence, could ever be adequate to the dark demands of describing war. The poetry of Paul Celan (who was born in Chernivtsi, then part of Romania, now Ukraine) almost breaks form itself in its anguished straining to express the darkness of the Holocaust. Ukrainian artists and writers, as the war drags on, are finding their own new forms.

The writer Sasha Dovzhyk, for example, in her new book, Apocalypse Baroque, has stories that might be described as “documentary fairytale”. These tales of real people are melded with motifs from folklore that give them a strange, off-kilter feeling, an unnerving quality that, paradoxically, connects them more closely to the actual texture of life under an invasion than straight documentary could achieve. Alisa Kovalenko’s films – Traces, about survivors of wartime sexual violence, and My Dear Theo, made as a letter to her small son in case she failed to survive her year in the armed forces – are rigorous and thoughtful, but incredibly intimate first-hand records of war. They are completely shorn of false heroism.

There are plenty of conventional memorials being created in Ukraine, some more successful than others, but the most moving I can think of are the “situational gardens” that the artist Dasha Chechushkova has been making with friends – humble flowerbeds, not meant to be grand or permanent, but small plots of growing things made in honour of the dead. The quiet, communal work of their creation – in defiance of so much brute destruction – is as important, perhaps, as the result. This year, she made one in Edinburgh when she was on a residency in the city. Her etchings after Goya’s blackly satirical Los Caprichos can be seen in a new exhibition, titled The Rupture, at Edinburgh’s Talbot Rice Gallery. They express not jingoistic fervour but the inner bleakness – feelings of depression and helplessness – that the war has brought with it. Also in the show is a simple artwork by Taysir Batniji, a Palestinian artist who was born in Gaza, which is nothing more than a stack of bars of soap on a shipping pallet near the exit. The soaps – visitors may take one as a parting gift – is engraved with the Arabic phrase, “dawam el hal men al mahal”, meaning “nothing is permanent”, or “this too shall pass”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

An act of remembrance in the guise of a bar of soap would be inexplicable to those who built the great bronze men of more bombastic times and places, but it is, to me, more effective and more honest. It is a friendly offering. You might think about the circumstances that led to its creation as you complete the ritual of washing your hands. The soap itself and its motto wear down over time. Its small message, nothing will last, is both a promise and a threat.

Charlotte Higgins is the Guardian’s chief culture writer

Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 07:00:40 GMT

Russia and US approach potential summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice, as Putin hopes to find consensus on new global order

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, is among those who have expressed concern that the world will witness a Yalta 2.0 moment if Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet trilaterally, as expected, on the sidelines of the Apec summit in China next week.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.

Putin has long proposed this re-enactment of the greatest wartime summit, held in February 1945 at Joseph Stalin’s insistence in a rundown Tsarist resort on the south coast of Crimea alongside Franklin D Roosevelt and Winston Churchill.

Trump has cast himself in the role of the enthusiastic guest while Xi acts the bashful host, ever reluctant to embrace the status of a traditional global superpower.

No one quite knows what will happen if the three men meet or even if China will allow more than a stiff protocol-driven exchange of statements. China is already trying to push nuclear disarmament off the agenda.

It may prove to be little more than abbreviated geopolitical theatre that Putin can retail domestically to show that Russia – even with an economy seven times smaller than that of the EU – still plays with the big boys.

But if Putin has his way he will try to ensure that this becomes the first of a series of meetings in this format in which the big powers organise a new world order on a set of security oriented principles in which liberal values play little part.

As Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, told Russian TV: “The task is to create a comprehensive system of comprehensive security in Europe that will become a new modern Yalta or Potsdam. If we manage to create such a security system then we will ensure peace in Europe for decades, perhaps even centuries. That is our main task.”

Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, said the summit could mark “the start of a return from this slide into absolute chaos to stabilisation”. For Zelenskyy, the concern is that almost any time Putin and Trump converse, it is Kyiv that suffers.

The original Yalta is widely remembered, outside Russia, as a moment of cynical trade-offs, even ignominy, to rival the appeasement of the 1938 Munich agreement. It was eight days that shaped the postwar world in which absent countries were discarded or divided by the imminent wartime victors.

FDR, months from death, was intent on enlisting Russian support for a new League of Nations organisation and for Russian participation in the war against Japan. In return, he accepted the fait accompli of Russia’s presence in Poland, and covered his treacherous tracks by persuading Stalin to sign a declaration that affirmed the principles of “sovereign rights and self-government” should prevail in countries freed from Nazi rule.

Few thought the dictator had any intent to honour the agreement. Indeed, honour was somewhat absent throughout the eight days. When Churchill told Stalin it was a “matter of honour” that the independence of Poland, Britain’s original casus belli, was preserved, Stalin replied the issue for him was “a matter of life and death”. Churchill had no means to confront Stalin since by then he was the victor of Stalingrad and Kursk, and the commander of an army that had crushed Germany.

The subsequent sense of shame about the betrayal of Yalta accumulated mostly in America, so much so that in May 2005, before a trip to Moscow for the 60th anniversary of Victory in Europe Day, George Bush told an audience in Latvia that Yalta had “consigned millions to communist captivity. When powerful nations negotiated, the freedom of small nations was somehow expendable. Yet this attempt to sacrifice freedom for the sake of stability left a continent divided and unstable.” It was a view shared across Europe.

The Republican tradition expressed by Bush has been expunged by Trump. In his 2025 national security document, Trump lauded the sphere of influence geopolitics championed at Yalta. He named the western hemisphere as America’s domain. It remained deferential to Russia and China’s spheres.

Unfortunately, Trump took little notice of the strategy prepared for him. He retained his respect for Putin and Xi, but indulged himself, and Israel, in a disastrous imperial overreach elsewhere, notably in Iran.

after newsletter promotion

As a result, the US and Russia are approaching the summit seeking China’s help to extricate them from wars of choice that have wounded them. Xi is cast in the role of Stalin, hosting two countries in need of his beneficence.

It leaves China somewhat wary, reluctant to use its leverage if it helps the US, or is seen to run counter to the Chinese narrative of being a force for stability and coexistence. Speaking at the Emirates Policy Center conference in Abu Dhabi, Prof Minghao Zhao from Fudan University gave a classic exposition of Chinese non-interference. “The Russia-Ukraine war is the strategic mistake made by the Russian president. The Iran war is the strategic mistake made by President Trump. China is managing the consequences of those conflicts.”

By contrast, Dr Wang Huiyao, the president of the Center for China and Globalization and an early advocate of a trilateral summit, argued China was needed. He referenced the Kindleberger trap – a period of chaos caused by too little global leadership. He said China was trying to be helpful by propping up multilateralism and might provide guarantees in Iran, something the Iranian leadership favours, but even he saw China’s stabilisation role largely through the prism of developing the global economy.

In short, China might help extricate Trump in the Middle East. After all, open waterways are necessary to meet its insatiable demand for oil.

But China sees Ukraine as a strictly European security issue in which it is not willing to betray Putin, or endorse a settlement reached without Europe’s agreement. China is in the midst of repairing relations with Europe after China’s industrial overcapacity in 2025 flooded the European market, risking its deindustrialisation. China’s embrace of Putin’s vision of a new European security architecture would infuriate Germany and the European Commission.

For some, such as John Ikenberry, the theorist of liberal internationalism, the sight of the US president carving up the world with autocrats is anathema. He thinks there is a viable alliance of democracies.

But Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, says more Yaltas are the future. “We have to learn to work across the geopolitical and ideological dividing lines,” he said. “We are now in a world in which the US and its democratic allies are no longer the preponderant coalition.

“Who is coming up? China, India, Indonesia, large countries of the global south – all of then playing the field and most of them have closer economic ties with China than with the US.

“We are going to have to learn to work with autocracies and to live with them more comfortably. Is there a downside risk? Sure. Might Trump throw Taiwan and Ukraine under the bus? Possibly, but I doubt it. But we need to break the ice. These conversations have to start now and I give credit to President Trump for starting it.”

Five Great Reads: Sleep paralysis, parakeets and problematic laundry

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:21:43 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

If you’ve spent any time looking at the big headlines this week then you’ll know it’s high time for a good old break from the news. Take a breath, and bliss out with some long reads (mostly) a long way away from the doom cycle.

The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has spent his life studying the unfathomable depths of the human brain. His passion is sleep paralysis, “a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma”. While one in five people have experienced this frightening experience, very little is known about why the brain creates such terrifying images in the subconscious. Jalal has experienced sleep paralysis himself, and he thinks it may be a pathway to a deeper understanding of our minds.

What does it feel like? Some describe it as “the moment of peak fear in a horror movie”. Others describe being frozen in their own bodies while some evil force approaches them in their bed. It’s not uncommon for people to be able to open their eyes, which can often heighten the fear.

Around the world: Stories around sleep paralysis are more common in some countries and cultures than others. “Your grandmother might say: ‘There’s this monster that comes at night. It looks like this,’” Jalal says. In countries like Italy and Egypt, there is a long history of the phenomenon, which can cause it to happen more and for longer.

Notable quote: “When you are paralysed, and you can’t speak, your thoughts will go to a potential predator, somebody trying to hurt you. You feel very vulnerable.”

How long will it take to read: About five minutes.

Further reading: Do you like sleep? Try lazymaxxing.

Their existence is loud – and myths abound as to how these Himalayan birds came to be a common feature over London’s skies. Loved for its green plumage, the ring-necked parakeet has been making itself at home in Britain for decades. But more recently the birds have been recast as an ecological threat, prompting deeper questions about the idea of invasive species.

‘Invaders’: Evidence from Belgium and Spain suggests parakeets may outcompete several species, most significantly the Eurasian nuthatch, leading to local declines in areas with large parakeet populations

Opinions are split: They might be a nuisance to fruit farmers, or to nesting nuthatches. But to many Britons the birds are a welcome addition to otherwise grey cityscapes. “Everything is about diminishment and decline, but the parakeets are thriving, and they’re doing it in style. It’s a joyous thing to witness,” says Nick Hunt, the author of the 2019 “gonzo ornithology” work The Parakeeting of London.

How long will it take to read: You’ll have your beak in this story for nine minutes.

Further reading: This volunteer army is plotting to wipe out Britain’s grey squirrels.

For the past few weeks, fridges and freezers across Europe have been encountering the same problem. Temperatures inside the ice boxes have shot up, some reaching as high as 50C. Alex Pearce, who owns a fruit and vegetable business in London, discovered the malfunction was a cyber-attack when he walked over to the cable connecting the units to the internet and pulled the plug. As the rise of AI makes it easier to hack IT systems, experts say cyber-attacks could become more common.

Notable quote: “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited.” – Richard Horne, the head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), says we are in the “foothills” of a new hacking landscape.

Not just fridges: Blood banks in France, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, even Ukraine’s emergency alert app. And by 2028 the NCSC predicts AI-powered malicious software will “highly likely” be used to hack UK power stations, airports and hospitals.

How long will it take to read: About four minutes.

Further reading: The fridge hacks provided fairly little disruption, but what would raise the stakes?

Bluey, the Australian series about a six-year-old dog and her sister Bandit (and, of course, their ridiculously unflappable and time-rich parents), has become a worldwide hit. Now one of the founders of the studio behind it is making headlines of his own.

Packed with nostalgia: Daley Pearson, co-founder of the Brisbane production company Ludo Studio, has created a new Netflix family film called Allen, which by his own account is topped to the brim with his own childhood nostalgia, including the things that feel impossible to let go. It centres on a character called Petey who befriends, for one blissful month, a bug-eyed extraterrestrial – Allen. But decades later, Petey is trapped in a state of arrested development and obsession.

Notable quote: “I was using the stuff that I love to tell the story of not being able to let go of the stuff you love, and how it maybe holds you back,” Pearson says.

How long will it take to read: Just over two nostalgia-filled minutes.

Further reading: The Bluey composer shares the trick to music that “hits you in the feels”.

The news cycle can be depressing at times, but that doesn’t mean your wash cycle has to be. Could there be hope for your washing in an online rabbit hole? Victoria Turk tumbled down the r/laundry subreddit in search for answers to 10 stubborn laundry problems.

Sud-based science: We’ve all been there. A coffee stain on a white shirt. Pasta sauce on a new pair of pants. Try as we might, wash after wash, stain remover, baking soda – nothing works. Eric Thompson, better known by his online avatar KismaiAesthetics, preaches a science-based approach to cleaning clothes. TikTok trends and Instagram hacks are out. Green chemistry and “the magic of water and time” are in.

Take a spa day: Thompson’s answer to persistent stains and lingering odours sounds relaxing. Famous online for its efficacy, his “last-ditch effort” to save an essential wardrobe item is described as a “spa day”. The power comes from heat, time and the enzymes in bio-powered detergent (click through for detailed instructions).

How long will it take to read: Six minutes. You can read it while folding your laundry.

Is it finally OK to be frank about 2000s pop culture? ‘It was profoundly, cheerfully horrible to women’

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:00:42 GMT

The imprisonment of Russell Brand and allegations against David Walliams have prompted scrutiny of a culture that encouraged male transgression

In a 2008 episode of BBC Two’s comedy panel show Never Mind the Buzzcocks, the choreographer Arlene Phillips – the only woman on the programme – was told by the host Simon Amstell: “You look like you run a good whore house.” In reply, Phillips told a story with what appeared to be faux sincerity: while working with big stars, she explained, she would sometimes be asked to find dancers with “very special abilities” who might want to party after filming. Another panellist, the TV presenter Dermot O’Leary, mimed picking up a phone and said: “When you’re dancing tonight, do you mind having sex afterwards?” Everyone laughed.

Russell Brand’s imprisonment for rape and sexual assault this week, and allegations of sexual misconduct against the comedian and children’s author David Walliams have prompted scrutiny not only of the men involved, but of those who appeared to enable them. The chatshow host Jonathan Ross has apologised for a 2004 joke, in which he described the 15-year-old British comedy awards as being “like most 15-year-olds: drunk, unpredictable and probably going home with David Walliams”. The latter has denied the allegations made against him in reporting by the Guardian and ITV News, but is now the focus of an investigation by the Met police on separate sexual misconduct claims.

On the face of it, Phillips’s story had nothing to do with Brand or Walliams. But as clips like this have resurfaced they have been viewed in a different light. Were they simply jokes, or symptomatic of a wider culture in which women’s bodies and sexuality were routinely used as entertainment? Were they merely knockabout fun, or did they stand alongside the ubiquity of topless models on Page 3 of tabloid newspapers and so-called “lads’ mags”, which mixed lifestyle and often tasteless humour with overtly sexual images as a backdrop to something darker? Did the atmosphere of the time make more serious misconduct easier to overlook?

“The popular culture of the 2000s was profoundly, openly, cheerfully horrible to women,” said Sophie Gilbert, the author of Girl on Girl: How Pop Culture Turned a Generation of Women Against Themselves. “The shift from third-wave feminism to postfeminism during the 1990s enabled an environment where women were supposed to own their own objectification – to enjoy it and profit from it, and never complain.”

Gilbert cited Geri Halliwell and Kylie Minogue kissing on the chaotic entertainment show TFI Friday as a “surprise” for host Chris Evans, and Victoria Beckham being asked to step on a scale weeks after giving birth.

Throughout the late 90s and 00s, young female celebrities were relentlessly pursued by paparazzi, subjected to scrutiny over their weight and photographed in compromising situations. Upskirt pictures were published in magazines. In 2004, the highly successful celebrity magazine Heat devoted an entire special to celebrity cellulite, circling supposedly offending patches of skin on the legs of women including Beyoncé and former EastEnders star Martine McCutcheon.

When the singer Charlotte Church was 15, a website ran a countdown to her 16th birthday, when she would reach the age of consent – which was reported by the Sun. The Radio 1 presenter Chris Moyles, then 28, spoke on air about wanting to take Church’s virginity when she turned 16. Similar countdowns targeted other young celebrities, including Harry Potter star Emma Watson.

“I was made into this caricature: sexualised, patronised, ridiculed,” Church recently reflected. “I feel my character, the narrative of who I was in the world, was taken from me, and made into something salacious, or something to be ridiculed.”

Britney Spears faced similarly intrusive scrutiny as a teenager. In her memoir, The Woman in Me, she recalled reporters asking whether her breasts were real and “whether or not my hymen was intact”.

Ben Widdicombe, a former New York gossip columnist who examined the era in his memoir, Gatecrasher, recalled how the aftermath of 9/11 created an appetite for frivolous celebrity coverage; a phenomenon felt far beyond the US. “I saw an insatiable hunger for light, ‘sexy’ stories. This elevated a generation of young starlets into ‘pop icons’. However, the cruel logic of the tabloids is that they build you up only to knock you down,” he said.

The treatment of Spears particularly troubled him. “I genuinely feared that we were going to hound Britney to her death.” But, he said, audiences shared responsibility: “There’s no media without an audience – the public was baying for Britney to be humiliated, and the tabloids obliged.”

Of course, the era’s misogyny did not go completely unchallenged. Many women objected, but their voices were often drowned out by the all-powerful entertainment industry.

“It was only acceptable to the men who were being loud and dominating TV,” said the comedian Jo Caulfield. “As a woman who was around then, it wasn’t acceptable then or now. They did and still do protect the stars.”

Anna Tippett, an academic who specialises in the sexualisation of popular culture, said the idea that it was simply “a different time” overlooked the women who were actively challenging the culture. In a 2012 survey, Tippett found that 57.8% of respondents classified lads’ magazines as “soft pornography”, despite their mainstream acceptance. “Women who objected risked being labelled prudish, humourless or outdated,” she said. “There was considerable pressure either to appear ‘in on the joke’ or to remain silent.” Perhaps Phillips’s anecdote should be understood in that light.

Nowhere was that dynamic more visible than in comedy, an industry that blurred the line between provocation and intimidation. Brand’s public persona, and vast success, was built around sexual excess and outrageous stories about women.

“This was the nature of his appeal,” Gilbert said. “If TV and radio bosses didn’t want to call him out for his behaviour, it was because they knew his transgressions were what made him popular.”

In 2007, a 21-year-old Lily Allen appeared on Channel 4’s The Big Fat Quiz of the Year; again the only woman on the panel.

In another resurfaced clip, Ross suggested moving her away from Brand and the comedian and now Great British Bake Off presenter Noel Fielding so that she might “go home with her dress still on”. “How dare you? We’re not rapists,” Fielding said. “What if, horror of horrors, he ain’t even done a rape? You could ruin his reputation,” Brand quipped.

Even Allen laughed. But rewatching the footage years later made her uncomfortable, she said in 2023. “In retrospect, that’s really horrendous. I don’t think I felt that at the time, because it was the culture.”

During live performances of the TV sketch show Little Britain, Walliams played Des Kaye, a former children’s entertainer and sex offender who pulled down audience members’ trousers on stage and attempted to kiss them.

In 2008, the journalist Mary O’Hara described how comic Johnny Vegas had brought a young woman on stage at a London gig, where he groped her and repeatedly pulled up her skirt as she tried to cover herself. “Most disturbing, perhaps, was that around half the audience seemed to find this really funny,” she wrote. In a complaint about O’Hara’s article at the time, Vegas’s solicitors said that the young woman from the audience had told them she went along with the joke willingly and did not feel intimidated, scared or abused. His representatives have been contacted for comment for this article.

“I can’t tell you how toxic that culture was back then,” said the comedian Josie Long, who had her own backstage encounter with Brand.

“He would bite my face and I would tell him I didn’t like it and he would chase me around,” she recalled this week. “I would giggle because I was 22 and it was overwhelming.” Looking back, she said, she understood the behaviour as physical assault.

“Even at the smallest end of this spectrum, the culture was designed to tokenise and sexualise women,” Long said. It allowed “a kind of blokey camaraderie” that readily included “rape jokes and jokes about brutalising women”, while excluding different perspectives.

According to the TV writer Jack Seale, the rise of panel shows – at the expense of sitcoms – helped create a more adversarial form of comedy, dominated by “big, aggressive” male personalities. “Women – beware panel shows!” read the headline to an article by the comedian Jo Brand in the Guardian in 2009.

“Post-Britpop, post-Oasis, post-Cool Britannia, post-TFI Friday, you had the exuberance of the late 90s but with a nasty, lairy edge that certainly included misogyny,” Seale said. “Men on TV were like: ‘We know we shouldn’t be doing this, but we just have anyway.’”

Jessica Toomey, the director of the Live Comedy Association and the Women in Comedy festival, pointed to the lack of formal reporting procedures and the relatively small number of women in positions of power during the period. “The most frustrating sentence I keep hearing recently is: ‘Why didn’t they report it back then?’, when many victims just wouldn’t have felt empowered, informed or supported enough to know how to.”

So, how much has actually changed? Plenty, if you consider the rise of feminist blogging, an increase of women in positions of power in the industry and the ability to use social media to demand accountability.

“What has changed is not simply our recognition of misogyny, but the cultural willingness to confront it – and this is something to be celebrated,” Tippett said.

But other features remained, Tippett said, referring to the current era as “lad culture reimagined”: online abuse, “incel” culture and the prominence of figures such as self-professed misogynistic influencer Andrew Tate. Others point to the ubiquity of platforms such as OnlyFans as a contemporary successor to the influence of lads’ magazines such as Nuts and Zoo, and argue that widely available pornography, often seen by teenage boys, is more extreme than ever.

Meanwhile, some doubts remain as to whether greater awareness has translated into greater institutional accountability. This week, the comedian Lucy Beaumont, who revealed herself as a whistleblower in the investigation into Walliams, said she was struck by the lack of any obvious route for raising concerns. “There is no HR department in TV, there is no proper duty of care.”

She said she feared that speaking publicly about powerful figures could end her television career. “The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work. No one wants to mess that up.”

In an article for the Guardian, she argued that the harmful actions of some men were seen and often ignored. “What happened to the women and girls wasn’t done in secret,” she wrote. “I think this is what the very national outcry is about – because it could have been called out, stopped, and women could have been prevented from being in dangerous situations with these men.”

Tara Joshi, a co-host of the 2000s pop-culture podcast Twenty Twenty, cautioned against treating the 2000s as a closed chapter. “Lad culture, tabloid culture, diet culture and misogyny all still exist, they’re just manifest in slightly different, perhaps more insidious ways,” she said.

Joshi acknowledged that conversations about abuse were now more open, and that more people may feel able to speak out. “But the reality is that Russell Brand was working in major film and television productions into the 2020s,” she said. “This conviction has only really been able to happen because there were an indisputable number of people coming forward with allegations.”

Seale said: “Celebrities behave that way when they feel untouchable, which comes from them recognising their own financial clout: everyone around them is earning their living from the star’s good reputation.

“Even now, unfortunately, it is still difficult to get someone to call out abusive behaviour if their salary depends on them not doing so.”

Support for anyone affected by sexual abuse issues is available in the UK from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse and childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 06:00:38 GMT

The arguments have been endless and they are fatuous. Wales and Scotland stopped conflating national identity with race: why can’t England?

In 2021, the then shadow justice secretary, David Lammy, asserted his Englishness on the Saturday LBC programme he hosted, only for a caller named Jean to insist that his African-Caribbean heritage disqualified him. He could be British, she maintained, but “never be English”. Jean defended Englishness as though it were a possession she would never surrender to the country’s Black populace. Lammy’s entreaties to recognise it as a civic identity were ignored, as Jean attempted to demarcate its racial boundary live, on air.

After cross-party condemnation of Jean’s nativist screed, Lammy would go on to appeal for census options that would allow him, his children and other Black people building lives in England to identify as English, but the Office for National Statistics (ONS) stood firm. A spokesperson responded: “The evidence did not support a change to include Black English in England.” This was despite the ONS having recommended Black Welsh and Asian Welsh categories, with equivalent options available in Scotland. In Wales, the change followed criticism that census categories recognised Welsh identity among white respondents but not ethnic minorities; Scotland’s approach was informed by research and consultation showing that Scottishness was integral to the identities of many people from ethnic minority backgrounds.

The Liberal Democrat MP for Eastbourne, Josh Babarinde, has now brought the argument Lammy was making five years ago to parliament, introducing a 10-minute rule bill to extend English identity to people of all ethnic backgrounds. He is backed by a range of MPs including Lammy and the Conservative James Cleverly, and support for his proposal has been signalled by the prime minister.

“Polite society” and recent polling largely agree that Blackness and Englishness are compatible. In 2025, a study by YouGov found that only 13% of adults in England thought someone had to be white to be English, while 43% of UK-born ethnic-minority adults described themselves as either “British, not English” or “more British than English”.

The more interesting resistance, then, is coming from within Black communities. To be called English by another Black person is never a neutral descriptor. The designation is often used by relatives or Black friends, humorously or caustically suggesting that we have drifted from the cultures we inherited.

The same dynamic follows us to the countries our parents or grandparents left, where it becomes shorthand for the cousin changed by life in England. “To be colonised in the Caribbean,” wrote Sam Selvon, author of the 1956 book The Lonely Londoners, “celebrating Christmas with images of snow or pastoral interludes with daffodils – was to live with a kind of permanent unreality, for reality always seemed to be elsewhere, in London or in the metropole as a whole.”

That invasive identification bound colonial subjects to the mother country. As Anne Spry Rush notes in Bonds of Empire, West Indians were taught to think of themselves “not as conquered people, but as conquerors”. The repudiation of this supposed bond on arrival in post-second world war Britain partially explains the suspicion towards Englishness carried by their descendants.

That particular betrayal belongs to a Caribbean history. Black African communities arrived in England through different routes and with distinct relationships to Britain, but they encountered the same racial and institutional forces that marked Black people as conditional members of national life.

If Englishness felt like a gated identity – culturally alien and difficult for us to recognise ourselves within – Britishness offered a broader, more abstract way of reconciling ourselves to the country. Forged as a political and diasporic identity, Black Britishness provided solidarity and a means of asserting belonging.

But its very success deserves closer scrutiny. Jean, the LBC caller, had no issue with an arrangement that recognised Lammy as British while refusing him Englishness, as neither position troubled her increasingly anachronistic worldview. Seen in this light, Black Britishness may also have functioned as an identitarian kettling pen: capacious enough to contain all of us while leaving Englishness the preserve of the country’s white population.

Babarinde’s bill arrives amid continuing attempts on the hard right to equate Englishness with whiteness, even as Reform MP Suella Braverman’s recent denial of a Black audience member’s Englishness on BBC Question Time inadvertently staged a public referendum on the proposition that left her on the losing side.

Where Lammy invoked his attachment to recognisably English sensibilities, Babarinde speaks proudly of his Englishness, arguing that skin colour should have no bearing on who can claim it. Their feelings shouldn’t be dismissed, but their pride is not necessarily shared by the Black population of England, whose relationship with Englishness has yet to produce a settled consensus.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The ancient presence of darker-skinned people – from Cheddar Man to soldiers of African descent guarding Hadrian’s Wall – has moved neither reluctant Black Britons nor the ethno-nationalists who have long defined the debate.

Celebrated Black Britons are held up as evidence of inclusion, although the honours bestowed on them can have the opposite effect, distancing them from the communities they are made to represent owing to their historical association with an empire built on colonial exploitation and slavery. Representation in sports poses its own problem: infographics designed to highlight how much weaker the England national team would be without Black migration suggest that Englishness is earned through exceptional achievement.

All these arguments render Black Englishness a perpetually conditional identity, at odds with the reality of how it is experienced. The census should have offered a Black English option long ago, but Black Englishness has already arrived without announcement, and needs no manifesto. It can be recognised in the things mistaken for mundanity: the places we identify with so deeply that they become part of us; the streets and areas we mythologise; the neighbourhoods where memories accumulate and the Black English vernacular that has travelled far beyond the communities that birthed it; and older relatives born ‘back a yard’ who nevertheless regard burial here as obvious, joining generations of West African and Caribbean dead already committed to English soil.

Sociologist Paul Gilroy – who told the Guardian in 2021 that he has always regarded himself as English – understands such transformations as “the fissures, stress cracks and structural fatigue in the edifices of Englishness [that] become more interesting and acquire their own beauty”.

After England’s World Cup victory over Mexico in July, Sky News found two Black children huddled beneath a flag of Saint George in the morning sun, having stayed up beyond bedtime to support their country. The image felt jarring because nothing about it appeared that way to them. They seemed free of the self-consciousness with which older Black generations have approached Englishness: no qualification, no argument and no need to negotiate the terms of their belonging.

Calum Jacobs is the author of A New Formation: How Black Footballers Shaped the Modern Game and the founder of CARICOM magazine

Guilty or redeemed? Our critics’ verdicts on this week’s UK cinema releases

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 05:00:35 GMT

From Cynthia Erivo’s bravura barrister to Johnny Depp’s surprisingly good Scrooge, take a quick glance at this week’s new films

In a sentence Screen adaptation of Suzie Miller’s international stage hit stars Cynthia Erivo as a lawyer whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience.

What our reviewer said “A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers the movie.” Peter Bradshaw

In a sentence Director Vincent Munier takes his father and son into the Vosges forest in France in an emotional study of human-animal interaction.

What our reviewer said “A subtle, tender work that evokes the need to pass on interest and engagement in the natural world to younger generations, but which manages to avoid feeling too preachy or sanctimonious.” Leslie Felperin

I saw how brightly stars like Russell Brand could shine, but there is darkness in the shadows

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 05:00:35 GMT

After years of celebrity interviews, I have learned not to be fooled by the allure of fame. We never really know them – we know what they want us to know

As I sat in Southwark crown court, listening to the final day of Russell Brand’s trial, there was one subject that came up repeatedly, invoked as often by his defence as the prosecution. I don’t mean sex or coercion, but fame. It ran through every victim impact statement and loomed so large in the courtroom that it felt as if it was almost on trial itself.

I’m an entertainment journalist who has been covering celebrities for more than 20 years – as long as Brand has been one – and I have written about him at various stages of his career. But I went to Southwark crown court as a member of the public who wanted to see justice done. For the women he had hurt, for the ones who couldn’t get as far as the courtroom, and for all of us who came of age at a time when rape culture was so fast and furious that young women mistook it for a joke that we were in on. In the age of lads’ mags, sex felt cheapened, yet somehow we were the ones who ended up paying for this. So it was doubly strange to sit in court and feel somehow complicit in it - in how this media culture had encouraged Russell Brand.

I interviewed Brand in 2011 for a glossy magazine when he was promoting his remake of the film Arthur, with Helen Mirren. They were to be interviewed together, and an editor told me that if I accepted this freelance commission I would need to “muck about a bit and basically be into Russell Brand’s humour”.

When I played back the tape this week, I heard the me of 15 years ago asking Mirren if she had read his book (“No,” she hadn’t). Brand and I both pressed her. Had she really not read the chapter in Booky Wook 2 in which he outlines what he would like to do to her with her Oscar. “You have, I read it to you, the chapter’s called ‘Mummy Helen’,” he insisted. On the tape, he and I are both laughing while she is not. She was too dignified to play the game, saying she hadn’t been sure about joining his film project “because Russell is intimidating”. Yet we both ploughed on at her. I struggle now with how inappropriate this behaviour was – it’s mortifying. But it was what the job entailed.

Fast forward to Brand’s sentencing in court, where I listened intently to the victim impact statements from the women he was found guilty of attacking, each one stressing that recovering from his attacks had been rendered almost impossible by seeing him doing things such as joking about his sex drive every time they turned on the television or picked up a paper. I shuddered again. No, I’d had no idea what darkness he was capable of.

By 2014, when he turned to politics, I did at least write a piece about him in which I said he had, by now, “grabbed a thousand women as if they were lifeboats made of tits” and was trying to overthrow democracy “with a revolution fashioned from leftover bits of the internet and some string”, so at least my judgment had improved somewhat.

But he’s not the only interviewee whose darkness has been right there in front of me, hiding in plain sight. In 2007, I spent the day with Jared Leto, an actor who would go on to win an Oscar but who was then playing with his emo-rock band, 30 Seconds to Mars. I spent the day with him, his bandmates and various young women, some of them teenagers, who had flown into London from across Europe to see their hero play live. The girls who got to meet him seemed unworldly, wildly overexcited and close to fainting in his presence, and while I found his vibe intense to the point of weirdness, I never imagined he’d have any interest in these geeky fans. In 2026, he was accused by four women of criminal sexual conduct, with the alleged offences taking place when the women were teenagers. These are allegations he vigorously denies.

And now the spotlight is on David Walliams (who I’m relieved never to have worked with), after this week’s accounts from the women who had relationships with him as teenagers and now consider it grooming. He, too, denies any wrongdoing, beyond hurting their feelings. Walliams had sold £156m-worth of books in the UK alone, which is presumably why his industry protected him for so long.

Celebrities are surrounded by layers of people. When you interview one, people often imagine that you would have their phone number, but this is rarely the case, as that meeting will have been set up by a whole paper chain of intermediaries, which often include the star’s publicist, agent, manager and assistant. If there’s a photoshoot, you’ll be given a callsheet with numbers of the hair and makeup people, the styling department – and even drivers. Basically everyone apart from “the talent”, as their number is kept private every time. No wonder impressionable young fans were made to feel special by stars such as Walliams getting in touch directly from their own number.

I once interviewed a deeply charming celebrity at her home in West Hollywood, where we shared jokes about us both being chocoholics. As soon as I left, she called her agent to say I should be fired. I thought we’d got on well – but she was, as my editor subsequently reminded me, “a trained actress”. This is why the first rule of interviewing is to remember the maxim: “Why is this lying bastard lying to me?”, and that the star is never your friend. You are their conduit. And sometimes you are their cover.

Sophie Heawood is a feature writer and commentator

‘Stinks of a cover-up’: David Warner fans flames with new sandpapergate claim

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 04:17:36 GMT

Former batter said Hazlewood, Lyon and Starc not interviewed in 2018

Ex vice-captain claimed Cricket Australia ran ‘shoddy investigation’

David Warner has further fanned the flames on Australian cricket’s civil war as he claimed three of the bowlers who played in the third Test against South Africa in 2018 were not interviewed as part of a “shoddy” investigation into the sandpaper scandal.

The former Australia vice-captain said the ball tampering investigation “stinks of a cover-up”, as he claimed on social media that the trio weren’t interviewed by Cricket Australia in the wake of Cameron Bancroft being spotted handling sandpaper on the field in Cape Town. The three players were part of a bowling quartet with Pat Cummins at the time.

“As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” Warner posted on Instagram on Saturday.

“If that’s correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn’t know? It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover up.”

Warner made the claim a day after he said Cummins had thrown Usman Khawaja “under the bus” when the current Test captain fired back at his former teammate in a marathon press conference earlier on Friday.

CA has backed its investigation at the time and said each player still has an opportunity to share their version of events from the tour of South Africa in 2018.

Warner, Bancroft and Steve Smith were the only players sanctioned after a CA investigation found the trio had prior knowledge of the scheme to use sandpaper as a ball tampering agent in Cape Town.

“As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since,” a CA spokesperson said.

“Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players right to provide their own version of events.”

The controversy was reignited by Khawaja’s allegations in his memoir Sabr, and during interviews to promote the book.

In a wide-ranging press conference that lasted more than an hour, Cummins said that he “did not know” that sandpaper was being taken on the field at Newlands.

“When he says ‘we all knew’, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out on the field he’s 100% wrong,” Cummins said on Friday. “I’ve said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening. But, I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that.

“He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That’s complete and utter nonsense. I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper.”

Warner hit back just hours after Cummins spoke to media at Cricket New South Wales headquarters in Sydney, when speaking on Kayo Cricket during the build up to the first one-day international between Australia and England in Perth.

The former Australia opener said he would “stick by Uzzy and what he’s written in that book”.

“It’s the truth and I really, really support him,” Warner said on Friday. “I actually feel for him at the moment. I actually feel that the captain today actually threw Uzzy under the bus, and I’m very, very disappointed about that.

“All three of us [Warner, Bancroft and Smith] have paid a big price in this. I hadn’t spoken about it in eight years. But at the end of the day, we’ve got to live with these consequences daily and we’ve been served a life punishment.

“It’s been very difficult, because the way that it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and actually give more evidence. I felt like it was a botched investigation. It was a quick one to get it over and done with.”
