Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?

The Guardian Sat, 14 Nov 2026 04:00:34 GMT

One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight

What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.”

He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks.

In one of the early hearings, he also receives some words of support from a court security guard, “just some normal geezer, patting me down for weapons or sharps”, who whispers: “All right, Russell. The whole country’s behind you, mate. The whole country’s behind you.”

Brand takes solace from these words. “I felt very, very encouraged.”

I’m not a mind reader, so how do I know all this? Usually we know nothing about the thoughts of defendants in trials because they stay silent for the duration, but Brand finds it hard to stay quiet. At the start of his trial, he was putting out podcasts combining prayers with updates on how he was feeling about the experience. His broadcasts were joined by podcasts about the case from at least five media outlets, including the BBC, Sky and the Times, making this probably the most scrutinised rape trial in British legal history.

For much of it I was there, too, part of this pack of journalists, watching proceedings during the day, listening to the podcasts at night, particularly fascinated by Brand’s own updates, which he recorded alongside Laura, who attended court most days. Inexplicably, they have chosen to express their thoughts dressed in loosely belted dressing gowns, and Brand’s robe, troublingly, keeps flapping open to reveal his naked chest.

In the second mid-trial update, he and his wife compliment each other on the outfits they’ve picked to wear to court.

“You’ve looked absolutely beautiful and spectacular,” Brand says to Laura.

“That’s so kind. You’ve looked wonderful, too,” she replies, laughing.

In another episode, they pray for people who are enduring difficult times. “We pray for all people that have suffered harms. May we experience deep, deep love,” he tells his listeners, before it seems to occur to him that members of the media may be tuning in. “There may be people watching to find mean things to say,” he says. “We pray for them, too.”

One hundred and eight journalists are here to cover the case. Are we all just trying to find mean things to say? And if not, why are we all peering so intently at the trial of a comedian and actor whose career has waned? What are we hoping to understand with this exhaustive focus on a case examining whether Brand raped or sexually assaulted half a dozen women over a 10-year period from 1999 to 2009?

People are fascinated by Brand, now 51, because he has been so unflinchingly frank about how he has used women for sex – in his books, in his comedy. For years, this was a core part of his appeal; many of the millions who listened to him and read what he had to say just laughed indulgently at his anecdotes about shagging women and treating them badly. His persona pre-empted criticism: if you weren’t smiling at him, it was because you had no sense of humour.

Alongside Brand, the era that spans my early adulthood looks set to go on trial – an era of rampant sexism masked as ironic laddishness, which made it so tricky to argue with because every insult was just a hilarious joke.

By now, anyone who has listened to the news, or scrolled on their phones over the last few weeks will be familiar with the charges against Brand made by six unconnected women: that he raped one of them at the Labour party conference in 1999, that he orally raped another in the toilet of a bar, that he attempted to drag a receptionist to a toilet at MTV, that he anally raped a woman who had gone to his home for consensual sex, that he pinned a radio employee against the wall and kissed her while a colleague laughed, that he placed his face in the groin of a television production worker and demanded a massage. Brand denies all seven charges – three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of attempted indecent assault.

As the trial begins, the journalists who have managed to secure a seat in court 3 are taking notes on laptops, trying to keep up with the complexities of the case. Whenever a particularly disturbing fact is revealed, about 30 journalists start typing in unison. It becomes very loud. When one witness notes how Brand “went from someone who was quite affable, jovial, and turned into a wild-eyed maniac”, it sounds like a tropical rainstorm drumming on a tin roof. Even the judge has remarked on the disruptive noise of the furious typing.

By day four, I am beginning to wonder what I can add to the collective thoughts of dozens of journalists and podcasters, and Brand himself, on this trial. So the following morning I turn left instead of right out of the tube, and make my way to a different rape case starting at another court, a 15-minute walk in the other direction.

This is the story of two rape cases; one that the whole world is paying attention to and one that has attracted no attention at all.

As Russell Brand listens to the evidence of his six accusers, a mile away in court 9 of Inner London crown court, Michael, a 32-year-old data analyst, sits in the dock as a prosecution barrister outlines what happened during the afternoon of 17 June 2025, shortly after this defendant, who was driving through London in his BMW, on his way to get a hair cut, spotted a 17-year-old girl, whom he found attractive, and stopped his car.

I’m the only journalist here; the creeping extinction of local newspapers has prompted a stark decline in coverage of most court cases. This morning, there were no lines of police and photographers outside the court, there was no jostling for a seat in the courtroom, no artists sketching the scene. The defendant is wearing a new light-grey suit, the slit at the back still tacked together. He is accompanied by his father and a friend. His father is silent and looks morose, but as the defendant is taken to the dock to be locked in for the duration of the hearing (something Brand is not subjected to), he reaches out to brush his son’s hand in a wordless gesture of support.

The jury at Brand’s trial is made up of eight men and four women. Here there are nine women and three men, who take notes as the prosecution barrister explains in her opening statement that the complainant, who had just turned 17, was walking home from college with a 15-year-old friend, when the defendant saw them, and pulled up by the kerb, and asked for her number, suggesting they should all go to a restaurant together later. Not long after, he messaged her and they arranged to meet in a nearby Morrisons car park. The defendant said he would collect a friend so they could go on a double date. In due course, the two girls were picked up, and they all stopped to buy some alcohol. The 17-year-old chose a chocolate BuzzBallz cocktail (a milkshaky alcoholic drink that costs about £4.50), of which she only drank about half. They were all driven to a nearby flat, where the defendant said they would stop for a while “to get to know each other”, before going out to eat. They did not end up going to eat. In the flat, the other man took the 15-year-old to a bedroom, and Michael sat with the complainant on the sofa for a while, before – she says – he dragged her on to his lap, and then over the course of around an hour raped her four times.

Later, she and her friend were dropped by the defendant at the bus stop. The next day, she visited the police station to report that she had been raped.

All rape cases are different, of course, but there are similar themes that run through these two trials, which are happening at once, at opposite ends of Borough High Street in south London. In both cases, the defence rests on consent. No one is denying that intercourse happened, but the defendants’ lawyers are arguing that the sex was wanted by both parties. This is the classic “he said, she said” conundrum. It feels illuminating to sit through this case in parallel, to observe proceedings, stripped of the drama unfolding around Brand’s trial, to understand the process, the core challenge of determining if consent was given, of persuading a jury of guilt or innocence.

Both cases involve a power imbalance: in Brand’s, celebrity; in this courtroom, the fact that the defendant is almost twice the age of the alleged victim. In both cases, the defence barristers acknowledge that their client’s behaviour was either “ungentlemanly” or “distasteful”, possibly even immoral, but argue that behaving badly is not illegal.

Both courtrooms are tired: the chairs are frayed, revealing yellow foam innards; in Southwark crown court the lifts are temperamental; in the neighbouring court the tech doesn’t always work, and the heating veers between sweltering and icy.

It is a peculiar experience spending three weeks at two rape trials. To begin with, hearing the explicit content feels awkward, but quickly it becomes totally normal to be listening to detailed discussions of vaginas, penises, ejaculation, fingers, rectums, orgasms. But the judges in both cases still have to encourage the defendants not to use euphemisms. Even Brand has to be reminded to speak plainly. “Don’t be too coy or shy,” the judge tells him. “We are all grown up here.”

The jury watches a recorded interview with the complainant, filmed a few days after the alleged rapes. She is calm and articulate, sitting on a sofa in the police station, hugging a cushion to her stomach as she sets out what happened. She doesn’t cry, but looks very young, her knees touching and her feet in big trainers turned inwards, pigeon-toed. She says she told the defendant, “I don’t want to do this” and, “You’re moving too quickly.” “I was not enjoying myself,” she says. “The whole thing was rough and fast.” The defendant did not use a condom. When she told him it was painful, he made shushing noises. “I was in such a state of shock, I didn’t know what was going on.”

When she got home, her mother sensed something bad had happened. “She said, ‘What’s the matter? What’s the matter?’ But I wouldn’t tell her.’” Instead she told a cousin later that night, who told her to go to the police.

In the afternoon, the girl, who is now 18, is brought into the court via an unseen corridor at the back of the courtroom, and gives evidence from behind a reddish velvet curtain pulled across the witness box so the jury, judge and lawyers can see her, but the public and the defendant cannot. As she answers the prosecution barrister’s questions, she sounds sure of herself, unfaltering.

“Did you go to that address thinking that you were then going to go to a restaurant?”

“Yes.”

“Did you at any time want to have sex with him?”

“No.”

“Were you expecting that to happen?”

“No.”

When the defence barrister stands up to argue that, contrary to her account, the sex was consensual, she remains composed for a while.

The broad process in both courtrooms is the same: interviews recorded by the police with the complainants when they first report the rape are played on several screens. The prosecution barrister (in both cases a woman) questions the complainant about the alleged assault, and the defence barrister (who in both these cases is a man) cross-examines her. Even though we know the experience of being cross-examined in a rape trial is often shattering, and even if we understand that it needs to be rigorous in fairness to the accused, it still feels brutal. None of the women in either case is asked about her sexual history, and the defence barristers acknowledge that victims of rape can behave in unexpected ways – they may not scream, or resist, or try to run away – but, despite this preamble, the women are then subjected to intense questioning about their decisions and their responses.

The teenager is asked many questions about whether and at what point and how she said no, and why she accepted a lift back with him. Every step of their encounter is interrogated.

“It is right, isn’t it, that he asked you if you wanted to sit on his lap?” the defence barrister asks.

“No.”

“I suggest that he asked you to sit on his lap.”

“No, he asked me to move closer to him.”

“You said to police that he dragged you.” “Are you suggesting that I’m lying?”

“I’m suggesting that he didn’t drag you to sit on his lap. It would be very difficult to. He asked you to sit on his lap and you agreed.”

“No.”

“When you were on his knee, he was touching you in a sexual manner.”

At this point the complainant begins unexpectedly to howl, from behind the curtain, a loud, uncontrolled cry. The court clerk gets up to rummage around for tissues, and takes them behind the curtain. The judge asks the girl if she needs a break or if she is able to compose herself. She apologises and says she will try.

“You don’t need to apologise. It’s about getting the best evidence from you, and we can’t do that if you’re very distressed.”

She calms down and the defence barrister continues.

“After that, you had sex on the sofa.”

“I didn’t have sex. I was raped,” she says firmly.

“You may have regretted this very much afterwards but while it was happening you participated,” the defence barrister says.

“No.”

“You may have got very upset with yourself later for having had sex with someone you have only just met.”

“No.”

“You didn’t say stop.”

“That’s incorrect.”

“You didn’t say it was hurting.”

“I did. I did say it was.”

“And it was a relatively short time before you had sex again.”

“We didn’t have sex again. I was raped.”

Michael’s father gets a string of rosary beads out of his coat pocket and appears to be praying.

Brand is also praying as the women give evidence against him. On several days, I get the last available courtroom seat for journalists, a chair in the friends and family section, to the side of the court, with a side view straight into the dock, which is left unlocked and open, so I can see Brand in profile. I see how he stands, with his eyes shut for more than a minute at the start of the morning before the jury comes in, and how he falls quickly to one knee before taking a seat, discreetly crossing himself.

His faith is a recent development, emerging, perhaps coincidentally, around the time of the allegations against him. He said his 2024 baptism in the Thames, which television adventurer Bear Grylls assisted with, was “an opportunity to leave the past behind and be reborn in Christ’s name”.

Brand calls the glass box where he sits, with most of the press seats behind him and the court in front, the “aquarium dock”; say what you like about him, he has a talent for words. His expression is fixed and blank; he is remarkably still, except for the fingers of his right hand, which move along the beads of a rosary, dangling between his knees. Very occasionally, if a witness says something that is potentially helpful to him, he turns to glance at his wife, Laura, sitting in the seat behind me.

His father, Ron, is also here to offer him moral support. In apparent deference to his celebrity status, Brand and his team have been allocated court 6, along the corridor, to retire to during breaks. Ron is not invited to join them, so spends his breaks perched on the corridor sofas that have been used by thousands of nervous defendants over the decades. In his 2007 memoir My Booky Wook, Brand recounts how his father took him on a trip to Asia when he was 17 and paid for him to spend the night with a sex worker in Hong Kong. Perhaps this is why Laura appears a bit brusque with her father-in-law.

Outside the courtroom, Brand seems at pains to signal that he is a changed man, a decent, devout individual. On day one, when one journalist shouts out (not especially politely) to ask him how he is feeling, he replies: “I feel, of course, concerned, but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everyone involved. That’s my prayer. And thank you for the polite way that you asked the question. I appreciate that.”

Commending the journalist for politeness seems an unsubtle attempt to reveal himself as someone who values manners and sensitivity. I think: let the jury be the judge of that, rather than attempting to sway people before proceedings have even begun. I feel the same way about the Bible sometimes in his hand when he is photographed, with multicoloured Post-it notes marking different pages, and the Christian studies book by an American writer, Praying the Names of God for 52 Weeks. Isn’t this also an obvious attempt to convince us of his purity and goodness?

On arrival, he goes through the court security arch, setting off the alarms so the lights flash red. “Once more,” he is told, but it happens again, until he yanks out a large silver crucifix from under his shirt, wondering if it might be the problem. He stretches out his enormously long arms so the guard can sweep over his body with a handheld scanner. There’s something about the position he takes that makes me wonder if he is deliberately echoing Jesus on the cross. He looks silently towards the ceiling in a martyred attitude. I think I’m imagining this until I later hear barristers, working on a different case, laughing about his crucifixion pose.

At the courtroom cafe, Brand is friendly to his team of half a dozen supporters, helping carry water and cups of coffee upstairs, balancing three double espressos in one hand (although he lets one of his sidekicks, an American man who looks like his strangely shrunken twin, with the same long black hair, greying beard, stacked boots, skinny grey jeans and crucifix, pick up the £34.65 bill). He even gives a cheery thumbs up in my direction when I catch his eye as he steps back into his black people carrier at the end of the day.

But, as the weight of the allegations stack up against him, day by day, his defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, doesn’t bother trying to paint Brand in a saintly light or even in a particularly positive way. In a nutshell his defence goes: “Disgusting, distasteful, immoral. Who cares?” Brand’s behaviour during this period might well have been exceptionally gross, but that doesn’t mean he has broken the law.

The prosecution barrister, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, sounds sad and regretful, as she paints a picture of Brand as a man on a mission to sleep with 5,000 women, a man for whom women were disposable, a man who was “rampant in his desire to have sexual contact whenever he wanted, whenever he pleased”. She quotes a 2017 interview where Brand describes women as “amusements in his playground of orgasms”. She tells the jury that in his comedy shows he would invite members of the audience to have sex with him afterwards. “If you have a vagina and a heartbeat, we’ll be at this pub afterwards,” he told them. He said his age range was “16 to death”. We hear from a former friend who says Brand would select members of the audience to be invited back to his dressing room for consensual sex. We hear that sex in toilets was not unusual.

The defence barrister says all of this is irrelevant; all that matters is whether consent was given. Winter is very critical of the six complainants for the long delay in coming forward with their allegations, a delay he describes as “monstrous” and which he says has contributed to the “poisoned well” of evidence. Brand’s accusers each say they have different reasons for not reporting the offences at the time: they felt no one would believe them; they wanted to forget about what happened; they blamed themselves for not having prevented the attacks; one woman felt guilty for having willingly gone to his home for sex. They have taken years to come forward, finally prompted by a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary in 2023 that profiled his behaviour towards women.

The passage of time does make things difficult. Some of the evidence dates back to events 27 years ago and memories are hazy. One witness, a former flatmate of Brand’s, demonstrates how hard it is to be certain. “I think I almost remember him saying he raped her,” he tells the court, unhelpfully.

Michael is called to give evidence on the second day of his trial. His suit looks more crumpled. As he walks to the witness box, he has sweat on his face and trails a faint smell of aftershave. His defence lawyer asks him to describe what happened in the flat, and how they came to be having sex. He clearly finds the lawyer’s requests for graphic details excruciating, and his responses become steadily inaudible.

“I know it is embarrassing, which may be why you are mumbling,” the judge says. At one point, he doesn’t have the words to describe how the sex happened, so he mimes the action, thrusting backwards and forwards in the witness box. His friend guffaws; his father frowns at his feet.

The prosecution lawyer is briskly efficient, highlighting the speed with which Michael progressed from seeing the girls in the street to getting them into a flat. She asks how he can possibly have decided so quickly that he was attracted to the 17-year-old as he was driving along the road. “How long had you observed them before you pulled over?”

“I couldn’t tell you.”

“I suggest it could only have been a few seconds.”

The prosecution barrister wonders if he stopped his car because he thought the girls looked young.

“Were you attracted to her or did you think a younger girl might be easier to manipulate?”

“No.”

She reminds him that the complainant had told him that she needed to get home to babysit her younger brother at seven that evening. She asks him if he noticed that the girl had braces on her teeth. His answer is evasive, so she reminds him that in his initial police interview he acknowledged that the oral sex had not continued for a long time because the girl’s braces hurt his penis.

“Your behaviour was predatory, wasn’t it?” the prosecution barrister says.

“I see now that I shouldn’t have spoken to them.”

“They are children – do you accept that?”

“I accept that now.”

But he argues that the complainant told him she was older than 17 and is “lying about everything” because “she might feel embarrassed”.

“Are you saying that she is so annoyed with herself that she had sex with you that she reports you to the police for rape?”

“I am baffled,” he says. “She was calm, she spoke nicely, we shared a vape.”

“Why on earth would she go to the police if she was so happy?” the prosecution barrister asks.

“Perhaps she was just so annoyed with herself. If she had told me no, I would never have carried on. I know what no means. I know what consent means.”

Brand is in the witness box a few days later and the experience instantly strips him of his starry sheen. He has been arriving at court looking Hollywood-ready each morning, each day in a different theatrical approximation of a staid court outfit. He makes a nod to wearing a tie, without wearing an actual tie. One day, it’s a long white silky ribbon. On another, it is a brownish stringy strip. Today, it is a silk scarf wrapped around his neck, between piratical turned-up shirt collars. He has a wide array of different sunglasses he puts on for maybe four seconds for the few steps between the minivan and court door. I’m puzzled by the sunglasses. This is late October in London, so most days it’s not sunny. Are they to signal that he is a celebrity, on a different plane from everyone else? Why would he want to do that?

Even his gait is that of a famous man. He walks along the long corridor from court 6 to court 3 with the slight strutting, loping sway of a model on a catwalk, stepping over the areas of the dirty red carpet that have been stuck together with yellow and black striped tape. After Brand has walked past, I hear a barrister congratulating his client as they wait for their own hearing to begin. “Look, see, you’re in good company. That was the Hollywood film star.” His client does not appear to know who Brand is.

The celebrity buzz seeps into the room. It feels like theatre, or a TV courtroom drama. There’s no space for the public in court 3, but people keep turning up, hoping to watch. A few find their way to court 15, the overflow room for journalists who haven’t found a seat in court 3. On one morning I’m sitting next to a man, probably in his late 70s, wearing a beige mac and eating his way through a packet of Halls as he watches discussions of sexual assault, the smell of the cough sweets wafting potently around the room.

When Tommy Robinson’s trial begins one floor down, the media scrum outside the court intensifies, as citizen journalists and supporters (one wearing a union jack suit) line up outside. There is a noticeable absence of people declaring themselves to be Brand fans, although his mid-trial podcasts attract messages wishing him and his family well, which he and his wife read out.

Brand’s lawyer encourages him to address the way his supporters have melted away following the accusations of sexual assault. Brand says it has been “devastating” and that when his son was having heart surgery in Great Ormond Street hospital, the doctors barred his “attendance and presence” because of the material published about him.

“Were you able to persuade a single person with relevant evidence to come and give evidence on your behalf?” Winter asks.

“I have not.”

“Would they touch you with a bargepole?”

“No.”

To begin with, he barks out his answers, his hands behind his back, like a soldier responding to a sergeant major. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, who throughout the trial is a friendly, avuncular presence, compliments him for his powerful projection. “Mr Brand, that is nice and loud.” His answers are monosyllabic, as if he has been told to keep them succinct.

“Did you marry Katy Perry, who I believe is a popular music singer?” the barrister inquires (implying that he himself is too important to know anything about such matters), asking him to add “in just two words” how this changed his life.

“Staggering fame,” Brand replies.

We hear an analysis of whether Brand pranced around the hotel room of one complainant, topless, in the manner of an ostrich. We hear how Brand has clear memories of one evening at a nightclub because he met a group of “attractive women” from the X-rated TV channel Babestation. We also hear he saved the number of one of the complainants in his phone, with the letter T next to her name and two asterisks. The T stood for tart, he says. “That was what I used to denote casual hookups.”

We hear about the speed with which he moves to the lavatories with a woman, whose name he does not know, for what he terms “kissing, touching, fondling”, “canoodling”. He concedes: “It is possible that I could have taken my penis out of my trousers.” But he adds: “I recollect that the environment was unsuitable for the goal that I went in there with, which was getting off.”

The judge is uncertain if he has heard correctly, questioning “getting off”.

“I did say that, my Lord, but I could have said ‘achieve an orgasm, climax’.”

He tells the court that he believes “consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and indeed in many ways more important than sex itself”.

In the afternoon when the prosecutor, Karmy-Jones, takes over, she questions whether Brand has really lost all his friends as a result of the televised allegations.

“It’s not the case that because of Dispatches, you have been rejected by everyone you know.”

There is a long pause, so she asks: “Is that a difficult question?”

“I’m not sure I understand it,” Brand says.

“This is not a case of ‘poor Mr Brand’. You have a platform of 6 million followers.”

Brand says nothing. He becomes increasingly truculent as the afternoon progresses; his answers sound sulky and surly, he pauses after many of the questions, thinking at length about what to reply, then just asking for the question to be repeated. Brand is normally a dominant presence in the room, so tall his head is a hand span from the top of the courtroom door, but he seems suddenly diminished. His answers become harder to hear; he moves his hands from behind his back, and shoves them in his trouser pockets; his shoulders sag.

Sometimes his answers are a bit unclear, and the judge intervenes to clarify: “Are you saying you don’t drag people to lavatories who don’t want to go?”

“Thank you – yes, that’s right.”

He is no longer the articulate star who opens his mouth to deliver 1,000-word orations. He becomes like Michael, just another defendant in a rape trial.

Karmy-Jones asks him whether it’s true he used to say that he never liked to leave any interaction with a woman without a conquest. He affects to be offended.

“The way that has been characterised is so nefarious, unpleasant and ugly that it is difficult to answer in earnest,” he says. Later, he says that what he probably meant was just a version of a Woody Allen line: “… when he said the only advice my dad ever gave me on his deathbed was ‘Always try and fuck the waitress’. It was a joke.” It is interesting that Brand reaches for Allen, another cancelled comedian, to justify himself, as he leans on the just-a-joke defence.

Before he leaves the witness box, he makes an acknowledgment, as Michael did, that his behaviour doesn’t look so great in hindsight, but insists he has done nothing illegal.

The final stages of the rape trial seem the most fraught for the defendants. The judges sum up the evidence, and give the jury a series of questions they need to work through in order to get to a verdict. (Are you sure the complainant did not consent? Are you sure the defendant did not reasonably believe she was consenting?)

In the last days, Brand has looked increasingly withdrawn, sitting unmoving, trancelike, listening to the closing arguments, so pale that he looks as if he is drawn in black and white, black hair and eyebrows, greying beard, grey skin. He sits bolt upright for hour-long stretches. As he moves between courtrooms, he seems robotic. A friend greets him with an enthusiastic: “Hi, Russell.” He pauses, disconcerted, and then responds: “Blessings,” before turning away. He and Laura have stopped doing their podcasts.

Concluding her case, Karmy-Jones notes that the complainants had no hidden ulterior motive, but were “six women who have nothing to gain, who have not sought the limelight, who have not looked out for some form of publicity, who have not taken part in a documentary, not made claims for compensation”.

Winter makes his closing statement to the jury on the Monday morning of the fourth week of the trial. He reiterates that Brand is a promiscuous man. “So what.”

Down the road, Michael’s lawyer’s defence covers some of the same ground. “You may think this was deeply unattractive behaviour by Michael. But this case is not about morality; it’s not about whether older men should be sleeping with younger women, or should have sex with younger women having known them for a short period of time. This is not a court of morals. It is a case of consent,” he says. “Sex on the sofa with a young girl may be shameful, but it is not a rape case.”

Giving directions to the jury, the judge, recorder Samantha Presland, says it is important to dispense with preconceptions about how someone ought to behave after being raped. “Any person who has been subjected to any form of sexual assault will have undergone trauma. Some people will show obvious signs of distress. Others will not. Some will be angry and display their anger, whilst others will remain completely calm. Every person has their own way of coping.”

She adds that “experience has shown that different people can respond to unwanted sexual activity in different ways. Some may protest and physically resist throughout the event. But others may be unable to protest or physically resist. This may be out of fear or because they are not a very forceful person.”

She is addressing standard rape myths, hard-to-shift preconceptions that people hold about how a victim should behave during and after a rape. The jury retire to deliberate for a couple of hours, before being sent home. The next morning the judge says, if need be, she will accept a majority verdict, since they have indicated that they are struggling to come to a unanimous conclusion.

Michael, and his father and friends have been told they can leave the court building, but no further than Starbucks, a two-minute walk up the road, but it is raining so a couple of friends offer to go out to bring him a takeaway.

What is going on inside Michael’s head as waits for the jury to decide? Mostly, he is worrying about the large number of women on the jury.

“I think it’s stacked against me because of how many females there are. Some of them might have daughters that age. They might be mums. Nine females. That’s just not fair. Men, they might have children, too, but men might understand where I’m coming from more. Obviously, I can’t do anything about the composition of the jury. If God wants it to go well, it will go well.” He is exhausted because he has been having difficulty sleeping and can barely bring himself to eat because the stress has made him lose his appetite.

How do I know this? Again, I’m not telepathic, but this time the defendant has come to talk to me, during a break. He is curious about why I’m covering his case, and makes a special plea for his name not to be mentioned in the article. He is worried that his children, a seven-year-old girl and a 16-year-old boy, might be targeted at school if his name appears in the paper. “I don’t care about myself. I don’t want them to be bullied.” I agree not to print his surname.

I ask if he has spoken to his son about the case. He says he has. I wonder if he has talked to him about the notion of consent; I’ve been reading about the Cornell fraternity case and the allegations of gang rape at the US university, and am thinking a lot about parents’ responsibility to teach their children about consent. But Michael is not inclined to talk to me about this and just says: “He’s a smart kid. He knows no means no.”

Instead, he wants to say that he has thought hard about his own behaviour, by which I assume he means the wisdom of an older man organising things so he can have sex with a teenager he has only just met on the street. “I’m very changed. If this goes well for me … my life will change for the better. I will focus on my work, and my kids and my missus.” He says he is a devout Catholic. “I’m praying in my head all the time. I’m praying while I’m in court.”

He wants to be feel confident that the jury will find in his favour. “They have to be 100% sure in order to find me guilty. If there is a slight thought that I’m not guilty, then I’m not guilty … My lawyer is confident. What’s your opinion? You’ve listened through it all.”

I say I find it impossible to know, and he returns to his friends, who are chatting, laughing and scrolling on their phones. He hunches over his knees, holding one arm across his stomach, as if the stress of waiting is causing him physical pain.

I am the last woman he speaks to before being sent to prison for a number of years.

After six hours and two minutes of deliberation, a majority of the jury has found him guilty of two of the four rapes and of assault by penetration (fingers/vagina). He is found not guilty of oral rape and another rape. It is a confusing verdict, suggesting that the jury have believed both the defendant and the complainant’s accounts in part but not in full. I feel shaken at being present at such a critical moment in both their lives. The jury gather their coats and bags and file out of the court without making eye contact with the defendant.

The corridor outside is full of the hot smells of his uneaten takeaway, which a friend brought back just as the jury returned their verdict. Another of his friends disappears to find a large, unzipped Sports Direct carrier bag with some belongings and hands it to his lawyer to take to him.

One of his friends turns to the dock to ask: “Are you OK, bruv?” Michael says nothing.

Brand’s jurors take eight and a half hours to find him guilty of one charge of rape, and three charges of sexual assault; they find him not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Metropolitan police Det Supt Andy Furphy says outside court that this marks a “watershed moment”, a final reckoning for the laddish culture of the 90s and 00s (an era that saw Brand named “shagger of the year” by the Sun three times in a row).

But the trial down the road, relating to events from just last year, suggests that if laddishness has become unfashionable, it is only because a new manosphere-driven era of male entitlement has replaced it.

Only 9% of adult rape allegations that are reported to the police ever make it to court. There is a high level of attrition because of the psychological toll for the complainants, and the challenge of gathering sufficient evidence to convince the Crown Prosecution Service that there is a realistic prospect of conviction, especially in “he said, she said” cases. Around 3,000 rape cases are heard every year in England and Wales; for those adult rape cases that get to court the conviction rate is around 53%.

Brand closes his eyes as the first guilty verdict is announced. His lawyer asks if he might be given bail over the weekend, until sentencing, as “an act of humanity” to allow him to say goodbye to his wife and children. The judge declines the request. He tells Brand that he is likely to receive a lengthy custodial sentence.

“Yes, my Lord,” Brand replies.

On Monday, Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from Rape Crisis on 0808 500 2222 (England and Wales), 0808 801 0302 (Scotland), or 0800 0246 991 (Northern Ireland), or visit 247sexualabusesupport. org. uk In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio. org/rcip/internl. html

The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:01:46 GMT

From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers

Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October, resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month.

Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions.

On Monday, Russia finally succeeded in silencing the famed Novaya Gazeta, which had spent decades battling growing repression. Six of its journalists, including Anna Politkovskaya, paid for their coverage with their lives. But the newspaper continued until, stripped of its newsroom, donation platforms and right to publish, it was forced to turn the lights off. (The separate Novaya Gazeta Europe, founded by many of its alumni, continues.)

These cases are part of a wider pattern. Press freedom is at its lowest ebb for a quarter of a century, Reporters Without Borders said this spring, judging more than half of the 180 countries it surveys to have “difficult” or “very serious” conditions for journalists. The rising tide of war worldwide is also increasing the pressures and dangers: the Committee to Protect Journalists recorded a new peak of 129 deaths of reporters and other media workers in 2025. Unesco said last week that almost nine out of 10 killings of journalists go unpunished.

High-quality journalism has never been more necessary in a world of rising conflict, AI slop and malicious fabrications spreading on platforms run by big tech firms who barely nod to ethical responsibilities. As Ms Attalah herself has pointed out, the disappearance of professional media organisations enlarges the space for conspiracies and disinformation.

Yet while the US previously pressed the case of threatened journalists overseas, sometimes helping to ease their conditions, it is now led by a man who has called news media “the enemy of the American people”, whose FBI raided a correspondent’s home in January, and who is currently pursuing a $10bn lawsuit against the BBC. Donald Trump has also sought to dismantle federally funded organisations which were an important source of independent reporting on many repressive nations.

This week, an appeals court panel ruled that the administration had illegally fired the head of Voice of America. VoA, Radio Free Asia and Radio Free Europe have all struggled on thanks to dedicated staff, though hugely diminished. Recent elections in Serbia, Brazil and the US are evidence that journalism, alongside activism, can stem the erosion of democracy. Thousands of people protested in Turkey last month against Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s media crackdown. Large parts of the public still want the truth and, against the odds, courageous journalists worldwide persist in finding it out and sharing it. That authoritarians target them so relentlessly only testifies to their importance.

The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 18:00:56 GMT

The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past

“Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize.

Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t want to break out of the ghetto; he wants to break it down. “I really hate categories, and I really hate being categorised,” he said.

Set in an unnamed seaside town in an unspecified future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain after the invasion of an alien species called the iGhettis, rumoured to have “come out of the internet”. Capitalism, ecological disaster, AI, Brexit – the cause of “the crisis” is unclear. All we know is that “it’s ongoing and unresolved. It never ends.”

Ahead of Cop31, Ed Miliband this week claimed that “the scenarios once of science fiction are now regular occurrences”. With news of Microsoft outages, cyber-attacks on supermarket freezers, not to mention national stockpiling, the Booker judges’ decision couldn’t be more timely. As Atwood has said, science fiction is “always about now”.

From Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein to Isaac Asimov’s Robot series to Nobel laureate Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (a new film adaptation of which has been panned by critics), writers have been fascinated by non-human intelligence. Science fiction responds to anxieties about the impact of scientific and technological discoveries on society and the human psyche. Harrison’s great hero, JG Ballard, described his move away from classic sci-fi as a rejection of outer space for “inner space”.

Harrison has dismissed science fiction’s world-building as “the great clomping foot of nerdism”. The End of Everything is about a world breaking down, and as rationality and communication have collapsed, he had to break down the rules of fiction, including science fiction. There are no explanations or solutions, no salvation. He wants the reader to feel as confused and destabilised as his characters.

For some, this lack of answers is bewildering, and will confirm the Booker’s reputation for tricky winners. Others have an alien aversion that no amount of fine writing can overcome. The Wasp Factory author, Iain Banks, published his science fiction novels under the name Iain M Banks to distinguish them from his mainstream work. This is no longer necessary.

Whether the novel’s win marks a new frontier for publishing and literary awards remains to be seen. One thing is certain – there will be no shortage of fiction confronting a bleakly precarious future. As Harrison has said, we are living “in an age of fantasy”. The End of Everything is a novel for our times. Today’s polycrisis demands a polyphony of genres. Be it speculative fiction, science fiction, horror, fantasy, satire, dystopia - or a mix – the question of whether such fiction deserves a capital L belongs to a bygone age.

Toxic media industry must face a reckoning

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:53:10 GMT

Readers respond to an article by Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett in which she questions why it took so long to unmask Russell Brand and David Walliams

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is correct when she talks about the toxic 1990s in the media industry (Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal, 11 November). This abhorrent sexualised behaviour from celebrities and channel executives has been going on for much longer.

When I worked in the media as a makeup artist in the 1980s we were warned never to be alone if working with a certain Mr Savile or Mr Harris. Men like those two were the majority, not a minority. They were directly enabled by those managers and directors who sanctioned their behaviour through inaction. If you complained, you were seen as trouble and hounded out.

If the Russell Brand case has taught us anything, it should be that those in power are equally culpable through inaction and refusal to upset the so-called “talent”. Until these enablers are rooted out, the TV industry will remain a ripe hunting ground for sexual predators who are excused because they make money.

I long for that day to come, as it is obvious that the safeguarding laws today are completely ineffective in the face of power, money-making and obstructive management structures.

There are many more of these cases both present and past that will now surface. How offences are reported will influence how the victims are perceived. I cheer from the sidelines each time a vile, entitled abuser is held accountable. It would be far-reaching to hold TV executives accountable, too. Claire Parkman Brighton, East Sussex

Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s article gives a thoughtful perspective on young womanhood for those of us who experienced the early to mid-1990s and 2000s as teenagers and young adults.

I would like to add that not only were young women subjected to the appalling lads’ mag culture that no doubt enabled sexual assaults through constant objectification and dehumanising language, but women were also hoodwinked into thinking that mimicking poor male behaviour was somehow empowering, only to find that so-called ladette culture was subjected to harsher judgment.

It often led woman to be complicit in their own dehumanisation and objectification. “We’re only having a laugh, love – have another beer!” What a thoroughly depressing time. Kirsty Lees Mont-Joli, Canada

While it’s true that misogyny and lad culture were applauded and rewarded in the 1990s when I was young, I don’t believe for a minute that my daughter is growing up in a safer, less toxic environment.

In a world where drink covers are available to buy online to prevent your drink being drugged while out, let me assure you that girls and women are still in danger every day, everywhere. Domestic violence is on the rise, and the comments yelled at my daughter and myself are still as vile and threatening as they’ve ever been.

It would be lovely to be able to walk down the street without some man my age saying he wants to F my daughter. It’s great that women are speaking up, but quite often that just makes them more of a target. Ask any female politician or public figure about the abuse they receive on a daily basis. We have a shockingly long way to go. Sarah Wolf Elwood, Melbourne, Australia

I have every sympathy with Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett’s experiences of growing up with “lad culture” and rape myths. I was born in 1961 and it was all alive and thriving when I was growing up: the miniskirt myth, the “she had it coming” view of rape victims, the trivialising and the jokes. All the more reason to applaud the victims – and the journalists – who challenge the culture that women have endured for too long. Melanie Tuck Abingdon, Oxfordshire

How it feels to battle with a flood of AI-generated complaints

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:53:05 GMT

An investigator writes that a human-written grievance at least gets to the heart of the issue immediately. Plus letters from Dexter Jandoo and Pete Bibby

Re your article (‘AI clog’: UK public bodies battle onslaught of chatbot-generated complaints, 8 November), I’m a complaint investigator for a housing association. I’ve worked here for nine years, and the scope of my job has completely changed within a few months. I am well-versed in policy and legislation, and I love my job, but it can be unbearable sifting through hundreds of pages of extremely wordy complaints.

You only need to look at the awful case of Awaab Ishak to know how important it is that a housing provider’s complaints process is accessible to tenants, but AI-generated complaints don’t help with this. Sending a complaint can be intimidating and time-consuming, and using AI can give someone confidence, but when we speak to customers in person or over the phone, and reference the same technical language that’s in their AI-generated complaint letter, they often don’t understand what we are saying.

It is much better to receive a human-written complaint (even with spelling mistakes and expletives), because at least it comes from the person, and gets to the heart of the issue. It means we can help you to the best of our ability, because you have told us exactly what you need. Additionally, AI enables our regular complainants.

“Frequent flyers” are part of any complaints role, but receiving multiple, massive, AI-generated complaints a month from someone makes us feel as if they don’t see us as people worthy of respect. Our organisation is considering classing this as a form of harassment, and it can’t come soon enough. Name and address supplied

I am wholly unsurprised at the AI clog phenomenon, though I view it through a different lens. Using AI as an assistant to seek support or remediation for crumbling public services should not be seen as a nuisance. It is the democratisation of recourse for wrongs that would normally be reserved for those with the time and resources to pursue them. Public bodies, especially councils, need to face their problems and start using AI assistance (with a human in the loop) to work through the likely legitimate complaints, regardless of how they are written. Dexter Jandoo Transformation consultant, London

The fact that AI has been used to write a complaint doesn’t necessarily invalidate it. It might be that AI enfranchises those who by reason of lack of education or inarticulacy have until now been unable to express a grievance. The “clog” might just be a metric of previous powerlessness. Pete Bibby Sheffield

Monty Don was the best teacher and presenter imaginable

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:52:52 GMT

Saul Abbott says his pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him, Jane Bates values Gardeners’ World immeasurably, while Joe Mackenzie shares a poignant memory

I started my professional gardening career in 2004, a year after Monty started presenting Gardeners’ World (‘It’s the final goodbye’: Monty Don bows out with a blissful last Gardeners’ World, 6 November).

To say this great man taught me much of what I have learned since is a gross understatement. Not just about the principles and practices of gardening itself, but the understanding in a greater sense of what a garden is, what it gives to us both in bounty, tangibly, and nourishment of something far greater, internally.

His pace of presenting matched the pace of the world surrounding him. I truly believe he has been the greatest presenter of a TV show in a generation.

I had a tear in my eye at the end of his final episode. As a novice, I would sit and watch the show with a pencil and pad every Friday night and make notes of every plant shown and every method of gardening, so that I could go to work the next week and put that newfound knowledge into practice. My friends couldn’t believe that I was giving up Friday nights out for a gardening programme. Honestly, I wouldn’t change that for all the Camellia sinensis in China.

I can’t express how much I will miss him on the show. Thank you, Monty, for being the best teacher imaginable. Saul Abbott Saul Abbott Garden Design, Essex

Monty Don’s struggle with depression has always been a part of his presenting of Gardeners’ World. The programme hasn’t focused on mental health, but it has always focused on the benefits that gardening, fresh air and plants bring to anyone experiencing the ups and downs of living.

Friday nights with Monty and his team of gardening experts have given me an hour every week to look at what is real and relevant to my own internal life and enjoyment. My life is decidedly the better for it. I value the programme immeasurably and look forward to its continuation in a new form for years to come. Thank you, Monty. Jane Bates Macclesfield, Cheshire

I was sad to hear about Monty Don’s last episode on Gardeners’ World, not that I was an avid watcher. In fact, I only learned about the show during Covid when I was quarantined with my granny, who watched it religiously. She was an avid gardener herself, regularly took part in her village flower competitions, and in the summer of 2020 spent more time outside than in. She wasn’t that interested in TV, but she never missed Gardeners’ World. I think it was Monty (who I’m sure she had a huge crush on) who inspired her to allow part of her garden to grow into a wildflower meadow to attract bees and insects.

The week of my wedding, my granny went into hospital, and the night before, worrying about her and the big day, I turned on the TV in our hotel and Gardeners’ World was on. My granny died a week later, so she got to see the flowers from my wedding, but not Monty’s final episode. Joe Mackenzie Lewisham, London

The folly of just-in-time supply chains

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:52:48 GMT

Hannah Walker says systems designed to minimise expenditure in the name of efficiency can end up less capable of fulfilling their actual purpose

The article by Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend on the dangers of excessive optimisation identifies a problem extending far beyond mathematics and artificial intelligence (The efficiency trap: why optimising everything can backfire, badly, 8 November).

The widespread adoption of just-in-time supply chains illustrates it perfectly. By eliminating inventories and spare capacity, businesses reduced costs and improved efficiency, but frequently transferred those savings into risks that remained invisible until something went wrong. The disruption of global manufacturing during the pandemic exposed the consequences.

The same thinking has shaped public services and national defence. Hospital beds, experienced staff, strategic stockpiles and redundant infrastructure can all appear wasteful when measured against immediate demand. Yet their value lies precisely in their availability when circumstances cease to be normal.

Europe’s dependence on American military capabilities provides a particularly troubling example. What appeared financially efficient in peacetime has created strategic vulnerabilities as the reliability of US commitments comes into question.

The fundamental error is not optimisation itself, but optimising the wrong objective. A system designed to minimise expenditure may succeed brilliantly at doing so while becoming progressively less capable of fulfilling its actual purpose. Resilience is not inefficiency. It is a form of insurance. Like all insurance, the value only becomes apparent when it is needed – usually in a crisis. Hannah Walker Wymondham, Leicestershire

Don’t just blame the culture for keeping powerful men’s dirty secrets. Blame the law too

The Guardian Fri, 13 Nov 2026 17:43:03 GMT

It is important to understand just how effectively perpetrators of abuse have used lawyers as their shields. A challenge to that can’t come soon enough

There will be empty shelves in many bedrooms this weekend, where the David Walliams books once stood. For parents of a certain era, there was no escaping that particular publishing-industrial complex, and I certainly did my share of wearily reading Gangsta Granny or Mr Stink on repeat. At his peak, Walliams was the bestselling children’s author in Britain for 100 weeks straight, to say nothing of the spin-off theatre productions, Christmas specials, countless World Book Day costumes, and that family-friendly stint as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent during which we now learn he was reportedly inviting teenagers to his dressing room.

“What I try and do most of all in my books is encourage reluctant readers,” he told breakfast TV’s Lorraine Kelly in 2024, the year before publisher HarperCollins finally dropped him after allegations over his behaviour towards junior female staff. But it’s parents who would have been reluctant to bring his books anywhere near bedtime had we known earlier about the young girls claiming that Walliams exploited his fame to prey on them, and then threatened legal action if they tried to speak out.

One 19-year-old was left “shaking” in fear by a missive from Walliams’s lawyers, Schillings, warning that she risked committing a serious civil offence if she talked publicly about her experiences with him, and requesting a signed legal undertaking not to do so. (Schillings maintains it was acting on its client’s instructions that she might sell “untruthful” stories to the press.) If it takes an agonisingly long time to bring some stories to light – the Guardian has been investigating Walliams since 2022, while the Sunday Times started piecing together its separate case against Russell Brand in 2019 – then don’t underestimate the herculean effort required now to build the evidence and to win the trust of frightened young women. They are not just afraid of having to relive a trauma in court, or being outed and harassed on social media, but of being personally sued for everything they have.

This isn’t just about Walliams, who denies the allegations and was eventually named after failing to secure an injunction against publication sought on the grounds that he might attempt suicide, however. Shortly afterwards, Private Eye reported that another male celebrity accused by multiple women has secured an injunction preventing the magazine from publishing. And even now, some women are still reportedly gagged by so-called non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) from sharing what they know about the convicted rapist Russell Brand. Publicly and privately, in our increasingly angry conversations about how exactly toxic men get away with it, women are starting to ask some very pointed questions about the law’s role in protecting them.

Twenty years ago, celebrities facing embarrassing stories about their sex lives might have asked their PRs to lean on a friendly tabloid editor and get it spiked. But that doesn’t work in an era of girls whistleblowing independently on TikTok, which means reputation management is increasingly now the preserve of lawyers, and in particular privacy specialists.

Why risk suing for libel in open court, if you can stop things long before that? Five times as many women as men have signed NDAs, according to the campaign group Can’t Buy My Silence – whose co-founder, Zelda Perkins, bravely broke her own to help get her former boss Harvey Weinstein convicted of rape – while Slapps (so-called strategic lawsuits against public participation, essentially designed to intimidate and exhaust the target rather than necessarily to win in court) are becoming increasingly common in allegations of sexual misconduct.

Even better than hushing things up afterwards, meanwhile, is ensuring confidentiality before they have even happened. The celebrity stylist Lou Teasdale posted on Instagram this week that it’s now routine in television for girls left alone with male stars to be asked to sign NDAs and surrender their mobile phones first. Though ostensibly to protect the celebrity from sneaky recordings, an agreement “to remove the woman’s voice and the device that would keep her safe” hardly incentivises men to behave well, Teasdale argued.

Everyone, of course, should enjoy the right to protect themselves against malicious claims, libellous gossip and unjustified intrusion into private life. But that doesn’t explain why two years ago, an inquiry by parliament’s culture, media and sport select committee accused the music industry of using NDAs to get victims of sexual harassment to leave quietly, while keeping the perpetrators in their jobs.

It doesn’t explain the rape victim bound by a gagging order that stopped her even discussing the attack with medical professionals, whose case was raised in parliament by the then backbencher (now cabinet minister) Louise Haigh during her successful campaign to curb the worst abuses of NDAs. It doesn’t explain the solicitor-turned-MP Sarah Russell’s memories of dealing with companies where everyone knew the boss to be a pervert but “the board can give the women 20 grand to go away, they sign an NDA and that is the end of that”.

And it certainly doesn’t explain the late Harrods boss and serial rapist Mohamed Al Fayed’s routine use of NDAs to silence and intimidate his victims. (Though legally such orders can’t stop someone reporting a crime, women were warned that Harrods’ feared head of security, John Macnamara – a former Met police officer – would find out if they contacted the police. Alison Kervin, author of a book about Fayed’s crimes, heard of one survivor who emerged from giving a police statement to find Macnamara waiting outside.)

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

At long last, the tide may be turning. The equalities minister, Bridget Phillipson, is considering new curbs on NDAs, to prevent “a system where rich and powerful men are able to silence women”. Later this month, parliament will debate the former Tory minister John Whittingdale’s backbench bill aiming to stop the weaponisation of Slapps against journalists and whistleblowers.

But nine years on from the mass reckonings of #MeToo, both its successes and failures are now clicking into sharper focus. Young women are thankfully far more vigilant for predatory behaviour than my generation was, and as Brand discovered, so increasingly are juries. (Though still too low, rape conviction rates are rising, with completed prosecution rates at their highest for a decade.) What we didn’t foresee when the old barriers crumbled, however, was that new ones would rise so fast. It’s true there has been for too long a culture of impunity for powerful men, and shame for women. But it isn’t just “the culture” – that vague, amorphous soup for which nobody is clearly responsible – that keeps men’s dirty secrets: sometimes, it’s also the law. Too bad for predators, then, that the latter is by far the easier to change.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

My Mother Has Dementia. These Sounds Help Bring Her Back.

The New York Times November 12, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Op-Docs

Video by Taliesin Black-Brown

Text by Hank Lentfer

Mr. Black-Brown is a filmmaker and photographer. Mr. Lentfer is an Alaskan author and sound recordist.

If our eyes are the front door of perception. Our ears are the back door.

We open our eyes to a familiar world of shape and color, streets and homes, faces and bodies. Sounds can slip in unannounced, rearrange our emotional furniture and let themselves out before we’ve even realized they were there.

There are voices far older than any human tongue.

Demoiselle cranes, for instance, called from African skies for millions of years before our ancestors descended from the trees and eventually set forth on two legs. Sandhill cranes greeted the first humans to find their way to North America. Along with robins and chickadees, rain and surf, elk and wolves, whales and gulls, they form a gorgeous, unending chorus. These ancient voices can, for a keen listener, help unlock memories we didn’t know we had. They remind us we are part of a lineage of sound that will continue long after we are gone.

We titled our short documentary “Listen” for a reason. We’re inviting you to slow down and really listen to what’s there. Use headphones if you have them. Better yet, grab a friend, hook up the best speakers you can find and let these wild voices rearrange your furniture.

Taliesin Black-Brown is an Emmy Award-winning filmmaker. Hank Lentfer is an author and sound recordist based in Alaska.

Tech Leaders Rally Behind Jensen Huang

The New York Times November 14, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia.

By Kalley Huang

Reporting from San Francisco

Many of Silicon Valley’s executives and investors are rallying behind Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday after revelations that he had affairs with an employee and with a woman whom U. S. officials believed to be a spy for China.

In social media posts and letters to Nvidia’s board of directors, Mr. Huang’s billionaire peers described him as a singular leader who could not be replaced at Nvidia. Mr. Huang’s exit, they argued, would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race. And they blamed Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive and the richest person in the world, said in a social media post on Saturday. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

The support put a spotlight on Nvidia’s role as the linchpin of the A. I. boom and on Mr. Huang’s leadership as the company grew into one of the most valuable in the world. Nvidia, which started making computer chips for video games, now controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the advanced chips used in the big A. I. projects that are driving the U. S. economy. Along the way, Mr. Huang became Silicon Valley’s consummate dealmaker, turning Nvidia into a central banker for start-ups that needed chips and funding.

“We believe the board should avoid a rush to replace Jensen that undermines and thwarts the best interests of shareholders,” Brad Gerstner, the chief executive of Altimeter Capital Management, and Gavin Baker, the chief investment officer of Atreides Management, wrote in a letter sent on Friday. The investors, whose firms are Nvidia shareholders, asked the company’s board to consider “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”

An open letter to Nvidia’s board, titled “Stand With Jensen,” asked the board to reinstall Mr. Huang as chief executive, to conduct an independent investigation and to explain its actions. As of Saturday morning, the letter had nearly 100,000 signatures, including by current and former employees of Nvidia, business partners like Mr. Musk, and start-up leaders and shareholders including Garry Tan, the chief executive of the venture capital firm Y Combinator.

Some executives and investors struck a more confrontational tone.

“Jensen made a rookie mistake,” Pavel Durov, the chief executive of the messaging app Telegram, said in a social media post on Friday. “Founders: Don’t have a board. Be the board.” (Mr. Durov’s app has been accused of enabling terrorism, crime and disinformation.)

Tim Sweeney, the chief executive of the video game maker Epic Games, said on Thursday that Nvidia’s board had “serious corporate governance issues” and that it had been “gaslit” into pushing out a “once-in-generation visionary.”

On Wednesday, before Mr. Huang’s resignation, Mr. Sweeney said that if Nvidia’s board removed Mr. Huang, the action would be “an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy.” Apple’s board ousted Mr. Jobs in 1985, and he returned to the company and became its chief executive again in 1997.

Elad Gil, a venture capitalist, said in a post on Thursday that Mr. Huang’s resignation was a “good reminder for all founders to revisit who is on their board.” He advised founders to “reset your board during good times to avoid sudden action during bad times.”

Among the chorus was Travis Kalanick, Uber’s co-founder and former chief executive. In 2017, Uber’s biggest investors asked Mr. Kalanick to resign from his position as the company faced growing legal and ethical scandals. Mr. Kalanick stepped down and did not return to Uber.

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

Here’s Why It Could Take Days for Flights to Return to Normal

The New York Times November 14, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

With hundreds of planes out of position and crews out of hours, restarting the nation’s flight system is no easy task.

By Niraj Chokshi

Aviation reporter

The near-total shutdown of the nation’s airspace ended on Friday evening, but its ripple effects continued into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights.

By Saturday morning, almost 15 percent of the day’s flights had been scrapped, and the number was still climbing. The recovery will most likely last for days as airlines work to juggle their schedules, rebook passengers and reposition planes.

Aviation functions like a relay race. To work well, many things have to align in the same place at the same time, including the availability of planes, crews and an open airport gate.

On Friday, thousands of planes were pulled from the air, filling up limited space on the ground. Many returned to the airports they had just left, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. Jets at crowded airports weren’t allowed to depart and sat idle while flight crews quickly hit their legal working limits.

Pilots are generally limited to eight or nine hours of flying and a total shift length of 9 to 14 hours, though union contracts and airline policies often shrink those windows. Flight attendants are also governed by limits on the length of their shift. Both must receive lengthy breaks in between shifts, too.

For instance, a pilot who was scheduled to fly from New York to Miami on Friday night could easily have timed out while waiting for the ground stop to end. That would have left the airline struggling to find replacement pilots not only for the flight from New York, but also for the flight that pilot was scheduled to operate out of Miami on Saturday. Multiply that by hundreds and airline schedules can quickly implode.

Take N865DN, the tail number for a Boeing 737 operated by Delta Air Lines. It started Friday flying from Charleston, S. C., to Atlanta. From there, it made round trip flights to Louisville, Ky., and Norfolk, Va., returning to Atlanta, according to Flightradar24, a flight-tracking service.

The plane was supposed to fly on to Savannah, Ga., back to Atlanta, and then to Chicago, where it would start the day on Saturday. But it never made those last three flights.

Delta rebuilt its Saturday plan, with the plane scheduled to fly from Atlanta to Spokane, Wash., and on to Salt Lake City and Raleigh-Durham, N. C.

For minor disruptions, airlines can play catch-up by restarting flights and trying to make up for lost time. But bigger disruptions, such as the one that occurred Friday, often require resetting the network by proactively canceling many flights.

Niraj Chokshi is a Times reporter who writes about aviation, rail and other transportation industries.

How Some Flights Were Exempt From the Ground Stop

The New York Times November 14, 2026

U. S. Flight Disruptions

Advertisement

Supported by

Dozens of international flights departed from the United States during Friday’s nationwide ground stop. Some planes also left for Hawaii from the West Coast.

By Emmett Lindner

Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order.

Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage.

Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered.

More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

But more than 60 flights bound for overseas left the United States during the stoppage, according to Flightradar24, an aviation tracking site.

There are 21 air traffic control facilities, 20 in the contiguous United States and one in Alaska, that oversee swaths of regions throughout the country, according to the F. A. A.

As some of those centers recovered, flights were “allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center,” the F. A. A. said in an advisory less than two hours after the ground stop was ordered.

Flights departing for Europe from the Midwest or the East Coast can communicate with the Canadian authorities, said Dan Bubb, a former commercial pilot and an aviation history professor at the University of Las Vegas, Nevada.

Additionally, air traffic over the open ocean is less congested compared with that of the contiguous United States, he said.

Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, said that for planes traveling such a large distance over oceanic airspace, “they have process procedures, different standards of separations, than what we do to run the volume of air traffic” in the lower 48 states.

At 3 p. m. Pacific Standard Time on Friday, about two hours before the nationwide ground stop was lifted, San Francisco International Airport said that Pacific-bound flights, including to Hawaii and Asia, had been cleared for departure.

Why were passengers flying west so fortunate?

Those pilots generally will talk to one of the regional centers until reaching cruising altitude, Dr. Bubb said.

Centers handling air traffic headed to Hawaii or Asia are outside the contiguous United States, and therefore could avoid long delays from the ground stop, he said. At a certain altitude, a pilot could swap communications with California controllers for those in Hawaii or Alaska, he added.

Flights within Alaska, those from the West Coast to Hawaii and international flights from Honolulu were also exempt from the ground stop, Alaska Airlines said in statement.

Areas like Alaska, Guam and Hawaii are far enough removed that they can remain stable even as systems are affected in the contiguous United States, Mr. Daniels said.

“If they would have seen any kind of risk in the system there as well, then they would have reacted the same to reduce the capacity,” he added.

Generally, yes.

During ground stops and delays, emergency and medical aircraft are given clearance to take off.

Life Flight Network, a medical transport service, said in a social media post on Friday that “EMS aircraft are exempt from this restriction,” and its services were operating normally.

“Above all is medevac and law enforcement,” Mr. Daniels said. “They get a priority movement throughout the system, and we move other aircraft out of their way, versus, they need to get in line with everyone else.”

Pilots and controllers have many tools to communicate, Dr. Bubb said.

Pilots can talk to one another, their companies and ground control through different messaging systems even if one fails.

“There are redundant systems where pilots can talk to each other, and we can sequence ourselves, but we follow the instructions that we were given by air traffic control,” Dr. Bubb said.

Emmett Lindner is a business reporter for The Times.
