After Relative Silence, Joe Rogan Said Trump’s Policies Have Lost the ‘Podcast Bros’

The New York Times November 14, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The nation’s top podcaster addressed the midterm election results, days after declaring that he thinks politics is “gross.”

By Jesse McKinley

In the aftermath of the midterm wipeout for Republicans, Joe Rogan, the nation’s top podcaster, has not had a lot to say about politics, instead focusing his program on topics such as Hobbit-like hominids and dinosaurs, which he wanted to assure people were real.

But on Friday, Rogan, who endorsed Donald Trump in 2024 and was seen as crucial in his winning over young male voters, had a harsh assessment of the president’s policies, as well as, seemingly, his place among male podcasters like himself.

“They didn’t just lose the podcast bros,” Rogan said. “They lost most of the country.”

He continued, saying support had frayed when the Trump administration got “into a war that no one wants to be in,” referring to the war in Iran, and put “militarized police in the streets wearing masks,” a reference to the ongoing crackdown by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Rogan’s remarks came just two days after he expressed disgust at politics in another broadcast — “It’s all gross; I hate it,” Rogan said Wednesday, adding, “I don’t like politics at all” — and had largely avoided discussing the midterm elections.

His relative silence had been surprising given the level of influence he and other “manosphere” influencers were credited with in the 2024 election, when young men banked to the right to help carry Republicans to victory in what some called “the podcast election.”

Theo Von, another popular podcaster, who hosted Trump on his show in August 2024, had also been largely mute on the election. This week’s episode of his show, “This Past Weekend,” for instance, featured a happiness expert.

The same was true of Andrew Schulz, whose podcast, “Flagrant,” hosted the president just a month before the 2024 election, allowing him to attack President Biden about sleeping too much and praising Trump’s sense of humor.

Schulz’s shows since the 2026 election have been on other topics: oral sex after marriage and an episode entitled “What Hasidic Jews, Amish and Native Americans Know That We Don’t.”

In some ways, the manosphere’s seeming shift away from explicitly political content is a return to form for a coterie made up of comedians with wide-ranging curiosities and an audience that often just wants to be entertained.

But it also may mirror a broader shift occurring in the Make America Great Again movement. In September, The Wall Street Journal reported that conservative podcasters were “tuning out Trump,” in favor of other topics, including the Lindsay Clancy trial and the Senate candidacy of James Talarico, a young Democrat who won his campaign in Texas.

Initial data about the election also bore out a profound change of heart in young men, showing men ages 18-29, a prime audience for manosphere broadcasters, moving more than 30 points to the left, according to The New York Times’s estimates of voter trends. Male voters as a whole also moved left, some 17 points.

Clay Travis, a conservative broadcaster who often also discusses sports, another mainstay of some manosphere shows, suggested — like Trump himself did — that the election, and the attention paid to it by podcasters, came down to who was running.

“I can’t speak for those guys when it comes to their show decisions, but I think when Trump isn’t on the ballot the stakes feel far lower with most of the audience,” Travis said. “2016, 2020 and 2024 felt like existential battles over the fate of the country. The midterms feel like scrimmages in comparison.”

Some members of the manosphere have been uneasy about Donald Trump and Republicans for months, as the war dragged on. That included Rogan himself, who expressed shock in March after the United States and Israel launched their first attacks, at one point amounting it to a betrayal.

“It just seems so insane,” Rogan said. “He ran on no more wars: End these stupid, senseless wars. And then we have one.”

Von also started to question the motives for the war, telling Rogan in April that he was “sick of rich people not putting” their children “over in these wars.” He also said if simply obtaining oil was the goal, “I’d rather walk.”

Schulz had also been alienated from the Trump administration after the killing by federal agents of Alex Pretti, a nurse who was protesting an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis in January.

Some podcasters popular with young men had already spoken out about Nov. 3’s results. Tim Dillon, a sunglass-wearing comedian who has some 1.3 million YouTube subscribers, had already started to turn on the Trump administration, suggesting earlier this year that Trump was “obviously here to destroy Earth.”

And shortly after the election, Dillon jumped into the debate, discussing Trump’s reaction to his party’s losses (which he called “wistful”), while devoting an hour to a dissection of the midterms.

“I remember two years ago everybody was like, ‘Will the Democrats ever win another election?’” Dillon said, later adding that the results were easy to predict.

“People can’t buy things. They can’t own things,” Dillon said. “People in America exist in two states, broke or not broke.”

A battery of more resolutely conservative male influencers had been outspoken about the election, attacking the president and his party for big losses at the ballot box, with once-loyal social media surrogates voicing demands for change.

“The Trump chapter is finished,” said Matt Walsh, a right-wing pundit who has argued for a subservient role for women in society. “Trump is an extremely unpopular 80-year-old lame duck with no credibility with the voters, no future, and now, no real power.”

Other die-hard conservative podcasters such as Ben Shapiro, Michael Knowles and Steve Bannon were also critical of Republicans, with Bannon predicting a “civil war” inside the party.

Some manosphere figures even linked the Republican losses to the party’s position on men.

“A party that hates its own men is destined to lose,” said Myron Gaines, an influencer who has frequently made anti-female and anti-gay remarks, in a lengthy, 10-point treatise he posted on X shortly after the results came in.

“Men built this country,” Gaines wrote, “and they are not the enemy.”

Pollsters like Gallup have grouped Rogan into “right-leaning influencers,” alongside the likes of Tucker Carlson, the formerly avid Trump supporter who has broken hard with the president over the war in Iran.

After the election, Rogan had made a few passing comments on the results. In an interview last week with Calley Means, a former adviser to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a leader of the Make America Healthy Again movement, Rogan said that Republicans “got destroyed” in the midterms, noting that some of the president’s policies were “deeply unpopular.”

But his remarks on Friday went further, noting the war and an immigration crackdown he said went too far, targeting “nice, good people that are loved by the community but they just don’t have the right paperwork.”

He did praise certain elements of the Trump agenda, saying that “they closed the border and then crime dropped significantly. Those are good things.”

But Rogan, who signed a deal with Spotify reportedly worth up to $250 million in 2024, also seemed bothered by being grouped in with right-wing influencers, after being asked by another guest what he was “angry about.”

“A lot of it is people that don’t really listen to you: They just listen to a narrative about you or they listen to a clip,” Rogan said on Friday, adding that “in a lot of people’s eyes, I represent the right or the far right.”

At the same time, he also downplayed his influence, and seemingly that of other podcasters, saying that they are not “press people.”

“It’s a sickness of our society,” he said, “that people take our opinions so importantly.”

Jesse McKinley is a Times reporter covering politics, pop culture, lifestyle and the confluence of all three.

Did the midterm election save it?

Supporters of James Talarico on election night. He became the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Texas since 1988. Credit... Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Supported by

By Emily Bazelon

Before the midterms this month, experts who measure the health of democracies saw the United States experiencing “the most dramatic decline in American history,” in the words of one global index.

Warnings also came from judges ruling on election-related cases. In late October, Judge David O. Carter blocked the Justice Department from ordering California officials to segregate the ballots of 20,000 voters who were on a list of suspected noncitizens that Carter found to be unreliable. “If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” he wrote.

Against the backdrop of such fears, the November election became not just a referendum on President Trump, but also a crucial test of American democracy. In the end, the country passed. Turnout was the second highest for a midterm in more than a century, and Republicans, including Trump, have accepted the results. Even last week, when Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner of the tight race for Senate in Mississippi, there were no challenges or protests in the historically Republican state.

Does one free and fair election mean the concerns that preceded it were overblown? There’s little question that Trump’s hyperaggressive use of presidential power and his family’s self-enrichment have served as a shock to the county’s democratic traditions. But the election suggests that American democracy has the resources to heal. The point is not that Democrats were the victors. It’s that the popular will won and reflected a wholesale turn against the administration in power.

Leading up to the midterms, scholars debated whether the country was sliding into a soft form of authoritarianism in Trump’s second term, akin to Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban. The answer was yes, the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan A. Way argued in an article published in October. They cited Trump’s leveraging of federal power to cow law firms, prosecute political opponents, pressure news media outlets to alter their coverage, and steer political donations toward his own super PACs. It was all an effort to entrench himself and his party in power, Levitsky and Way wrote, as was Trump’s mid-decade gerrymandering push.

On the other side of the debate, Kurt Weyland, a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin, said that while Trump was transgressive, he was not transforming the U. S. government into an authoritarian regime. For the most part, the laws and traditions protecting free expression and civil society blocked his undemocratic initiatives. The United States was not turning into Hungary under Orban or Turkey under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. “The mayor of Istanbul is sitting in prison” for opposing Erdogan, Weyland said. “James Talarico isn’t in prison.” In fact, he is headed to the Senate.

To amass power, authoritarians need people to rally behind them, either through popular support or fear. Trump has tried both but has hit limits. With Republicans running 13 points behind in the national vote, it became implausible to contest the midterm results, much less seize ballots or voting machines, as Trump said he had regretted not doing after he lost in 2020.

It’s easy to imagine a close election ending with a fight for control in the House and Trump trying to force that outcome, as he did in 2020. As it was this year, he had no chance. “The voters freed this country from what has felt, for many years now, like a doom loop,” Mona Charen, policy editor at The Bulwark, said.

But it’s not just the size of the Republican defeat that safeguarded the election from interference. So did the nation’s constitutional design. States and Congress, not the president, set the rules for elections, which are run by as many as 10,000 local offices around the country. The structure serves as a buffer against presidential manipulation. “Election officials are committed to this highly decentralized system under state and local control, and voters by and large trust it,” writes Bob Bauer, a lawyer who traveled the country this year to support local leaders in defending the voting process.

The courts also checked presidential overreach, as the Constitution provides. The Justice Department brought about 30 lawsuits demanding access to state voter rolls but won none of them. The Trump administration also lost at crucial moments at the Supreme Court. The justices blocked the administration’s plan to restrict the delivery of mail ballots through the U. S. Postal Service in September. And the day before the election, they rejected the Justice Department’s emergency request to set aside the 20,000 ballots in California.

The role the judges have played reflects in part the time that it takes for a president to transform the courts. “It took Orban three years to capture the high court in Hungary and blunt the effect of the other courts,” said Kim Lane Scheppele, a Princeton sociologist who lived in Hungary while studying its courts and focuses on the rise and fall of democracies.

Trump packed the Supreme Court in his first term by appointing three justices, Scheppele said. But a majority of the court has held the line on election administration, even as the justices have elsewhere adopted an expansive theory of presidential power in line with Trump’s wishes. And popular will, expressed in the midterms, also blunted the effect of the court’s decision this year that cleared the way for states to erase majority-Black districts. Black voters turned out in high numbers in the South, estimates show. The number of Black Democrats in the House rose by one. In this way, too, the Constitution gives voters the means to check the courts or another branch.

Even Trump’s tactic of claiming elections were rigged fell flat this time around. Researchers found that this type of disinformation didn’t get the traction on social media that it had in the past. “We went into the midterms aiming to show these rumors to be old, played out, predictable & boring,” Kate Starbird, who helped found the Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington, said on social media. “Seems their audiences felt that too.” After Trump amplified claims of an election conspiracy this week, Megyn Kelly, the former Fox host, posted: “Just stop.”

Maybe Trump will be remembered for trying to distort American democracy but ultimately proving that it was stronger than him. The United States has an advantage over more vulnerable democracies — its wealth and the capacity of civil society. The private sector, universities, unions, foundations and nonprofit groups, along with state and local governments, create a countervailing force. Consider the threats that petered out. The chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, Brendan Carr, urged ABC’s affiliates to drop Jimmy Kimmel, a move that Trump applauded. But Kimmel was back on the air days later after widespread protest. Law firms bowed to the Trump administration’s demands, but lost lawyers and clients. Elon Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars on Republican candidates and came up empty.

Still, it remains true that the president, whom the Constitution obligates to “take care that the laws be faithfully executed,” has often undermined the rule of law. Trump’s Justice Department has defied hundreds of court orders. His executive branch has spent or withheld money without regard for Congress and its power of the purse.

The health of a democracy ultimately depends on the commitment of all the major parties to play by the rules. It’s instructive that after Watergate, Republicans helped push President Nixon out of office — but have done nothing so far to signal that they’re ready to hold Trump accountable.

The president and his advisers have effectively reduced parts of the federal government to rubble, Scheppele said. “They’re destroying things, like the National Weather Service, so Democrats can’t use them either when they’re back in office,” she added.

Voters may become frustrated with the next president — Democrat or Republican — because of the difficulty of rebuilding. In Poland, Scheppele pointed out, the high court filled by the previous illiberal government vetoed measures that the new government tried to take, like restoring the independence of the judiciary or granting abortion rights. That and other factors have made it hard for the liberal centrists elected in 2023 to deliver.

As long as democracy remains damaged in the United States, would-be autocrats have more opportunity worldwide. And huge hurdles loom, at home and internationally, including the challenge of governing artificial intelligence. “The midterms opened up people’s imaginations,” Scheppele said. “There’s a horizon you can see beyond now. But we’ve just taken the first step. What comes out of the rubble, and how do people respond?”

Emily Bazelon is a staff writer at The New York Times Magazine.

Goodbye, Mr. Chips

The New York Times November 14, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Maureen Dowd

By Maureen Dowd

Opinion Columnist, reporting from Washington

My home is full of honey pots.

In the front hall hangs a vintage poster from World War II, a sultry blonde at a cocktail party with three British officers leaning over her and the warning: “Keep mum, she’s not so dumb! Careless talk costs lives.”

I also have a Cold War honey trap: a photograph of the bewitching Tatiana Romanova, wearing nothing but a black velvet choker and black stockings, looking up saucily at James Bond after sneaking into his bed in “From Russia With Love.”

On my TV at night is the new season of “Black Doves,” the Netflix thriller in which the comely Keira Knightley is spying on her husband, the British prime minister, and working for a spidery organization that sells state secrets to the highest bidder.

And on my coffee table is a DVD of the 1946 Hitchcock spy noir, “Notorious,” in which Ingrid Bergman honeytraps a Nazi played by Claude Rains. When the Rains character is forced to confess to his Nazi mother that he married an American spy, the mother sneers at him: “We are protected by the enormity of your stupidity.”

Suffice it to say, Jensen Huang was not protected by the enormity of his stupidity.

Sexpionage in Silicon Valley looks too easy. It barely requires any real tradecraft. All it takes is a smile from the sort of femme fatale these nerdy brainiacs couldn’t get when they were young — before the billions, the makeovers, the personal trainers, the yachts and Huang’s ubiquitous Tom Ford black leather jacket.

Some Silicon Valley executives have warned their scientists and engineers to beware if they find themselves dating women who are “out of their league,” as one tech leader put it to me.

For a 2023 New Yorker profile, Huang told Stephen Witt that he was anything but a player, noting: “I did not have a girlfriend” in high school. His future wife, Lori, was his college lab partner in an introductory electrical engineering class.

Our future is being molded by a sketchy pantheon of stunted tech bros. Many of these boys with toys are immature, awkward and hubristic, high on their own supply, believing themselves to be the gods of a new religion, the creators of a new species.

And Trumpworld is not reining them in — just the reverse. In return for lavish flattery and donations to President Trump’s inaugural fun and pet projects, they’re getting all kinds of leeway, creating threats to national security and a glide path for artificial intelligence to conquer us.

As Julian Gewirtz wrote in The Atlantic, “American strategy has come to depend, to an extraordinary degree, on powerful private-sector actors whose incentives the government cannot simply assume will align with the national interest.”

Though Huang once said at a summit at Stanford that “greatness comes from character,” the lords of the cloud often seem clueless about character, motivations and, indeed, human beings. That’s how Elon Musk threw away close to half a billion dollars on the midterms.

Huang, who went from video games to crackerjack chips that fueled the A. I. boom, dismissed the risks of A. I. and lobbied Trump to lift export restrictions on selling advanced chips to China. Asked if it mattered whether China or the U. S. won the A. I. contest, he said, “I don’t think it does.”

In April, at a $1 million-a-head Mar-a-Lago dinner, Huang made his case to Trump to allow Nvidia to do business with China as the administration weighed an export ban on its chips. The administration shut down sales days after, only for Trump to reverse course a few months later and allow the company to sell certain chips to our chief adversary, provided the government got 15 percent of the revenue.

Trump brays that America can’t slow the pace of A. I. because we have to stay ahead of China. But then he makes perverse moves that will help China catch up to — and maybe overtake — us.

It’s hard to believe Huang wasn’t suspicious of the woman he was involved with, Alice Huang, whom U. S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy. After all, over a year ago, The Times reported on their cozy friendship, noting that Alice Huang’s firm, Megaspeed, was getting its mitts on billions worth of Nvidia’s most advanced products and distributing them to data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia, and perhaps passing them on to China.

This is a dangerous loophole that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has apparently done nothing to rectify. On Nov. 5, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick, hotly asking why the administration had not already banned chip sales to Megaspeed. Bessent told CNBC on Friday that the Treasury Department had been pushing for it for months. The president, according to The Times, was more sympathetic to Lutnick’s position.

Marco Rubio, a China hawk, began warning top Trump officials this spring about the dangerous liaison of the two Huangs. But Trump, no stranger to risky encounters, brushed it off. He likes rich, powerful, dominating men. And he surely liked hearing Jensen’s happy talk on A. I. because, as everything else around him faltered, the beleaguered president needed the rising stock market, disproportionately buoyed by Nvidia, more than ever.

Trump is a peerless con man, but he’s also an easy mark. He is so eager to have good relationships with Vladimir Putin and China’s President Xi Jinping that he sometimes seems like a patsy.

When A. I. models began blackmailing programmers, giving creepy advice to teens and hacking into other systems, many top tech executives and over 1,000 employees at A. I. companies signed a letter urging that we slow our roll and figure out some guardrails.

Seems like a no-brainer. But Huang wasn’t onboard.

As Witt wrote in The Times, the fallen Nvidia chief liked to present a facade of a humble family man. But in truth, Witt said, Huang was an arrogant narcissist with a penchant for dressing down members of his staff and was reportedly willing to have a widely known affair with a subordinate even though both of his children held senior roles at the company.

The chip king named his company after the Latin word for envy, invidia. But Huang is not someone to be envied; he is someone to hold in contempt. At a perilous moment, when we need to get control over A. I. before it gets control over us, Huang, Lutnick and Trump aren’t looking out for us.

Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies ever, has lost over a trillion in market cap since the spy story broke, causing some headline writers to call this the most expensive peccadillo in history.

Never mind artificial intelligence. What about a little intelligence?

Jensen Huang is part of the Trump era. An era epitomized by ego, corruption and flaunting of the rules. I don’t think any so-called tech “bro” has any great loyalty to this nation. It is all about what have you done for me lately and who can give me the power and recognition I deserve. The zeitgeist of our age. I don’t think there was ever a time when this nation’s national security was in such precarious hands. This nation is for a rough ride ahead, but a good start on a course correction was made on election day

Maureen Dowd exposes a danger far greater than Jensen Huang's personal misconduct: the surrender of the public interest to powerful technology billionaires and political leaders beholden to them. In Magnifica Humanitas, Pope Leo XIV warns that technological power does not confer the right to govern. He calls for independent oversight, accountability, and political leadership that does not abdicate its responsibility to the common good (§§105–110). Yet Dowd describes an administration willing to accommodate corporate profits even when national security is at stake. Artificial intelligence offers extraordinary possibilities, but technological brilliance is no substitute for moral judgment, and corporate profitability is no measure of human progress. If AI will profoundly shape humanity's future, why are we allowing a handful of billionaires and politically compromised leaders to determine its direction, rather than insisting on democratic accountability, enforceable safeguards, and the primacy of human dignity over private profit?

Maureen Dowd is an Opinion columnist for The Times. She won the 1999 Pulitzer Prize for distinguished commentary. She is the author, most recently, of “Notorious.” @MaureenDowd • Facebook

The Science One University Sacrificed to Avoid Trump’s Wrath

The New York Times November 14, 2026

Professors at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill worried how the Trump administration’s ire toward universities would affect them. But the school’s leaders thought they had a plan.

Supported by

The University of North Carolina’s chancellor tried to protect the school from the Trump administration. Work on cancer, suicide, AIDS and coronaviruses was hit anyway.

By Alan BlinderStephanie SaulIrena Hwang and Benjamin Mueller

Visuals by Mike Belleme

The reporters reviewed internal documents and recordings and interviewed dozens of people connected to U. N. C., some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation from the Trump administration.

The professor was crying.

She had joined the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to research race and environmental disasters. Now the Trump administration had cut off money that made much of her work possible, and university leaders had few ideas to keep it going.

Directly fighting back in the courts was not an option, administrators told a handful of professors during a video meeting in May 2025. Maybe, the officials suggested, researchers could rewrite their proposals to avoid mentioning topics that the Trump administration might find objectionable, like race.

That seemed like “whitewashing,” the anguished professor said in a recording of the meeting obtained by The New York Times.

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

One of the university’s top research officials, Andy Johns, fought tears himself.

“There’s no part of this that feels right,” he told the group. “But right now, we have to navigate it as best we can.”

As the Trump administration pursued the most consequential reshaping of American scientific research in generations, it sought to slash funding at private universities it depicted as hotbeds of intolerance and left-leaning ideology. But the campaign was so indiscriminate that it reached far beyond the Ivy League to include many of the nation’s large public research universities.

Leaders at most of those institutions, particularly the ones accustomed to navigating complicated politics in red and purple states, concluded that suing the federal government, like Harvard had done, was not realistic. Some hunkered down, minimizing the losses where they could while remaining largely out of the fray.

U. N. C. charted a different path — one of careful conciliation.

Quiet and often noncommittal in public, the university’s chancellor, Lee Roberts, maneuvered behind the scenes on two delicate fronts. On campus, he and his fellow administrators worked to calm an increasingly enraged faculty. With an eye on Washington, they also tried nudging Trump officials away from their most destructive impulses.

Major research projects — including on cancer, infectious diseases and heart failure — were canceled or disrupted. But the university also managed to keep the vast majority of its research funding intact.

Grant money from the National Institutes of Health, the university’s largest single source of research funding, dipped early in the administration. This year, it ticked back up, even rising slightly above its Biden-era levels. The university also found new sources of federal research dollars for Trump administration interests like artificial intelligence and quantum technology.

But there was another cost. While many professors sympathized with U. N. C.’s administration, mistrust deepened on campus as professors wondered whose side their leaders were on.

In an interview this summer, Mr. Roberts acknowledged the consequences of the cuts while avoiding direct criticism of the government that was causing them.

“It’s not an exaggeration to say that we have people here who have lost their life’s work,” he said. “It’s hard to overstate how devastating that is.”

Seventeen days after Donald J. Trump’s election, Mr. Roberts trooped to a meeting of U. N. C.’s faculty council.

The group’s leader, Beth Moracco, paced before professors in a video recording posted by the university. She quoted JD Vance, who had just been elected vice president, calling universities the enemy and said she had sometimes plunged into the “rabbit hole of speculation and catastrophizing.” But she pleaded with people not to engage in “anticipatory compliance.”

Then it was Mr. Roberts’s turn.

Urbane and taciturn, he was more seasoned in Washington’s ways — and less in higher education’s — than a typical university leader. His parents, Cokie and Steven Roberts, had been among the capital’s best-known journalists. Two grandparents had served in Congress. An uncle, a lobbyist, had been so powerful in Washington that Vanity Fair christened him “King of the Hill.”

In 1990, a newspaper profile noted that Lee Roberts, at the time a Duke University student, planned to become a lobbyist himself. He wound up as a finance executive, a budget director to a Republican governor and, beginning in 2024, U. N. C.’s chancellor.

When Mr. Trump was elected again, some looked at Mr. Roberts’s résumé and saw someone who could be effective in dealing with the new administration. Others worried that he might align himself with higher education’s Republican antagonists, who had already pushed the university system to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion programs.

As Mr. Roberts faced his faculty, he agreed the university should not jump to please the incoming Trump administration. But he also counseled patience.

“There is very little that is knowable,” he said, leaning against a lectern.

U. N. C. was positioned unusually well compared with its peer universities. Mr. Trump carried North Carolina three times, and the university already had Republican-aligned board members, lobbyists and administrators. As Mr. Trump prepared to return to Washington, he picked allies of the university for influential posts; an alumnus, for example, was named deputy director of the budget office.

In Chapel Hill, a liberal oasis in a perennially contested state, many academics viewed Mr. Trump as an aspiring autocrat. But U. N. C.’s leaders thought trying to guide Trump officials, rather than fighting with them, would better protect the university.

“We’d rather be in the room before policy is developed,” said former Senator Richard Burr, a North Carolina Republican and one of the university’s Washington lobbyists.

“We’re not paid to just sit and raise hell. We’re paid to have the conversations,” said Chris McClure, the university’s chief strategic officer. Talking to Trump officials, he added, “doesn’t mean you’re accommodating.”

U. N. C. slowly made inroads. The university forged “a direct relationship” with the all-important White House budget office, talking Trump aides through the arcane process of federal grant making, Penny Gordon-Larsen, U. N. C.’s top research official, said in an interview.

Still, the stop-work orders for projects had started soon after Mr. Trump’s inauguration on Jan. 20. By the end of February, according to an internal document, there were more than two dozen, unleashing havoc and anxiety across the campus.

Even when the government wasn’t sending explicit word of cuts, money was not flowing as anticipated.

In late February, Paul Maddox, a biologist who studies cancer, was still waiting for a routine extension of a grant to improve his invention, called the Mizar TILT — a light system that enhances cell images under a microscope.

“We thought, ‘They’re not going to attack our grants. Why would they attack our grants?’” he recalled. “We just kept working as normal.”

That was in line with the advice of U. N. C. leaders, who were telling professors that funding hiccups often happened during presidential transitions.

But as the government began targeting individual universities with hundreds of millions of dollars in cuts each, U. N. C. sought reinforcements. It hired a lobbying firm whose leader, Ches McDowell, was a brother of a Republican congressman and a hunting buddy of Donald Trump Jr. (Mr. McDowell, whose brother lost his re-election bid this month, did not respond to interview requests.)

It is not clear how much it helped. U. N. C., whose leaders were spending hours each day talking with one another and trying to talk to government officials, told faculty members in April that the disruptions were “fluid and change by the day, sometimes within a day,” according to an internal summary of an event for researchers.

By then, the document said, the university had counted 75 terminations or stop-work orders.

Universities around the country were experiencing similar cuts and confusion. The Trump administration had advertised its plans to target places like Harvard and Columbia, but they were also re-examining the entire federal research apparatus. U. N. C. leaders were not certain that the school could avoid the types of blanket cuts that the administration was pursuing against other top schools.

That month, Dr. Maddox learned formally that his funding program had been shut down.

“I’d never had to fire anyone,” he said. “I had to fire all these people.”

As federal funding disappeared, researchers looked elsewhere, even soliciting donations on social media.

“We invite you to give what you can to help keep this research alive,” Jaime Slaughter-Acey, an epidemiologist, posted on LinkedIn. “Every contribution — large or small — helps us continue gathering data, mentoring students, and producing science that matters.”

In May 2025, Dr. Gordon-Larsen and her deputy, Mr. Johns, held the video call with the researchers, who were considering tapping an outside funder to help cover grants the government had cut. Dr. Gordon-Larsen and Mr. Johns were not optimistic.

Instead, they warned that the university could face dire consequences if the government decided that projects defied Mr. Trump’s orders — even if the money for them didn’t come from the government.

During the private call, though, Dr. Gordon-Larsen told professors that she had a “burning anger in my heart.”

As Abbey Hatcher, a public health researcher, listened, the we’re-in-this-together messaging frustrated her. She knew other universities were more willing to test the administration.

“I liken it to the federal government pushing us off of a plank,” she said later, “and U. N. C. tying our hands behind our backs before we go in.”

In a statement, U. N. C. denied it had limited applications for outside funding. The government eventually rescinded the language that had unnerved university officials, and several of the researchers in the video call received grants from the private funder.

But around the same time, U. N. C. was grappling for other ways to stem the federal losses. A list that circulated inside the university in May 2025 advised people to “try to avoid” more than 50 words and terms, including “climate crisis,” “disability,” “diversity,” “sexuality” and “socioeconomic.”

Ganga S. Bey, an epidemiologist, expected about $250,000 to finish a project she had worked on for years. The study focused on a group of Black residents of Jackson, Miss., to understand factors that affect heart failure.

The work was just the sort of thing the Trump administration argued was exclusionary, because of its focus on one racial group. And its funding source, a pot of money meant to promote diversity, made it even more vulnerable.

The government cut the grant, forcing Dr. Bey to lay off assistants and eliminate the final leg of the project — personal interviews with the study participants.

“You have whole research portfolios that are obliterated,” she said.

The 16-campus university system capped new hiring on June 12. By late September, nearly 150 U. N. C. grants had been terminated or targeted with stop-work orders.

Like other universities, U. N. C. had been bracing for the end of N. I. H. grant money that surged during the coronavirus pandemic. But it was still a jarring shift for a university whose research projects were worth more than $1 billion. In recent years, U. N. C. has received more than $500 million each year in N. I. H. grants, its largest source of federal funding.

In the first fiscal year under Mr. Trump, that funding declined by about $27 million, compared with the average under the Biden administration.

U. N. C.’s renowned public health school, where much of the N. I. H. money has gone, was among the hardest hit.

Still, some observers thought Mr. Roberts’s Republican-friendly strategy was having some success.

Representative Valerie Foushee, a Democrat who represents Chapel Hill in Congress, said it had seemed that the administration was perhaps giving U. N. C. “a better shake” than other schools in her district, including Duke, as Mr. Roberts and his team pursued what she called “a calculated plan.”

In September, U. N. C.’s leadership faced the faculty again, and again promised it was lobbying on their behalf.

It did not feel that way to some professors.

Andrea Azcarate-Peril, a microbiologist, said in an interview that it had often seemed like faculty members, not administrators, were the ones screaming, “this is not right.”

The university sharply limited appeals to the federal agencies imposing cuts. Even a department leader’s support for an appeal could be overruled. U. N. C. said it backed appeals most likely to succeed.

It also pointed to litigation against the Trump administration led by outside groups that could benefit researchers. And behind the scenes, though the university did not publicize it, Mr. Roberts was helping indirectly.

According to two people in the higher education industry, Mr. Roberts consulted with the Association of American Universities, a group of the nation’s top research schools, as it considered whether to fight the government in court.

Some faculty members were sympathetic to the U. N. C. administration’s plight.

Abigail Knight, an associate professor of chemistry, said the university’s leaders were doing “the best they can.” But changes have been coming so quickly, she added, “I think a lot of times they don’t know what to do.”

In its statement, U. N. C. said its highest priority had always been “championing the importance of federal research funding to the university and to the state of North Carolina.”

It added, “Carolina’s results speak for themselves and have been achieved, to date, with minimal disruption compared to peer institutions.”

In the fall, Mr. Roberts found a line he would not cross. The Trump administration had floated a “compact” for universities to sign, dangling preferential treatment for research funding in exchange for ideological loyalty.

“There is really no way that we can sign the compact as written,” he told faculty members in November, “and we don’t plan to.”

No other major university in the country signed it either.

The public stance, arguably the university’s strongest pushback to the Trump agenda to that point, gave some professors hope that U. N. C. might be getting braver about standing up to the federal government. The hope did not last.

In July 2026, one of U. N. C.’s most prominent researchers made Fox News — the sort of publicity that many university leaders desperately wanted to avoid — when Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave an interview. Peering into the camera, he cast a new spotlight on a topic that had already unleashed turmoil in Chapel Hill.

Mr. Kennedy declared to Fox that Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, when he was director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, paid Ralph Baric, one of U. N. C.’s star researchers, to develop “techniques for weaponizing Covid-19,” which he then “taught” to a collaborator in Wuhan, China, where the pandemic began. No clear evidence has ever been offered that Dr. Baric’s work helped start the pandemic, and he has denied training Wuhan scientists on such techniques.

He had spent decades in Chapel Hill, sounding the alarm about coronaviruses in China and eventually helping to find treatments and test a vaccine for Covid.

But after Mr. Trump’s second term began, Mr. Kennedy’s health department clamped down on Dr. Baric, removing him from his federal grants. U. N. C. responded by placing Dr. Baric on administrative leave, barring him from his lab and opening its own review.

This January, U. N. C. reinstated him and sent the N. I. H. a four-page defense. Dr. Gordon-Larsen told the government that she hoped it would “conclude its inquiry,” adding: “U. N. C. deeply appreciates its partnership with N. I. H. and the federal government.”

Instead, the agency intensified its scrutiny.

In May, the health department suspended Dr. Baric from federal contracts and proposed that he be barred from receiving future grants. The university again placed him on administrative leave, though it has also provided him with significant financial support for his legal defense. Days later, it announced his retirement.

The case against Dr. Baric, who declined to comment, exacerbated fears on campus. If the university had seemingly abandoned someone so important, some professors worried, who would it protect?

“You go from a hero to an antihero for no obvious reason,” said Dr. Myron S. Cohen, an H. I. V. researcher at U. N. C.

In an interview in September, Mr. Roberts paused for 11 seconds when asked whether Dr. Baric had done anything wrong. “I don’t really know if I’m the best person to answer that,” he replied.

U. N. C. later said in a statement that Dr. Baric had “left behind a legacy of consequential research that reflected both his integrity and his extraordinary intellect.” The statement added that U. N. C. “supported him since allegations first surfaced in 2020, and that support continues today.”

During the university’s first faculty council meeting this semester, U. N. C. leaders acknowledged how stressful the year had been. But, Dr. Gordon-Larsen told professors, “the positives are plenty despite the overall challenges that we’re facing.”

“Research is thriving at Carolina,” she told the professors.

The Trump administration wanted American research to shift toward more artificial intelligence, robotics and nuclear energy, and U. N. C. had just won up to $35 million to harness A. I. to better understand rare diseases.

The funding came from a federal agency focused on high-risk and high-impact breakthroughs, rather than incremental research, and it has awarded U. N. C. tens of millions more for research on neurodegenerative diseases, drug development and cancer.

By the end of the fiscal year in September, U. N. C. had received about 900 N. I. H. grant awards, around 130 fewer than the average under the Biden administration.

But even as some individual researchers and departments saw their money shrivel, the university’s overall funding from the N. I. H. was even higher than before.

The university also built, or cemented, relationships with other parts of the federal government. In July, the Pentagon picked the university as a host for a program that the government had earlier yanked from schools that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called “woke breeding grounds of toxic indoctrination.”

And in October, U. N. C. and the Justice Department signed an agreement to close 19 federal inquiries and preserve the university’s access to research money.

Other universities had reached settlements more than a year earlier. The university did not pay any fines, but it pledged to comply with the Trump administration’s views on matters like D. E. I., admissions and the punishment of student groups for actions perceived as antisemitic.

Holden Thorp, a former U. N. C. chancellor who is now editor in chief of Science, said he thought some at the university had “lulled themselves into thinking that the university was somehow immune from political power.”

Now, he said, “I think Carolina is just trying to be the best U. N. C. it can in this environment.”

The midterm election results could scramble the plan after Democrats romped to big victories in North Carolina, diminishing Republican power in Washington and Raleigh. But whether Democrats will be able to reverse the president’s policies is unclear. The White House still controls the agencies overseeing federal research funding.

The toll so far has been steep. Paul Maddox, the biologist, took a leave of absence, temporarily abandoning his empty lab to run for office as a Democrat, although he returned this year. Some researchers gave up on Carolina: Abbey Hatcher, the public health professor, left U. N. C. and took her work elsewhere.

Dr. Bey, the epidemiologist, has remained. But she questions the rosy picture the university touts.

“What is success,” she asked, “when there are so many researchers who have lost their funding?”

My colleagues and I have spent months examining the Trump administration’s push to overhaul American science. We knew from the start, though, that we wanted to understand how a major university had responded to the sudden pressure from Washington.

We have looked at how Harvard, which sued the government, was affected. But we wanted to look beyond the Ivy League, too. U. N. C. stood out because of its longstanding record as a research powerhouse. As a public university in a purple state, it also has a long history of dealing with political pressure from all sides. We had also heard about misgivings on campus as administrators seemed much less willing to fight, or even criticize, the White House than leaders at other schools.

In the end, we found a university torn over whether its strategy to maintain most of its federal research funding was worth costs that are much harder to quantify. Its leaders told us they think it worked as well as it could.

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

Produced by Jeffrey Furticella and Umi Syam.

Alan Blinder is a national correspondent for The Times, covering education.

Stephanie Saul reports on colleges and universities, with a recent focus on the dramatic changes in college admissions and the debate around diversity, equity and inclusion in higher education.

Irena Hwang is a data reporter at The Times, using computational tools to uncover hidden stories and illuminate the news.

Benjamin Mueller reports on health and medicine. He was previously a U. K. correspondent in London and a police reporter in New York.

Olivia Wilde Hit Bottom. Here’s How She Bounced Back.

The New York Times November 14, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Devin Oktar Yalkin for The New York Times

Supported by

By David Marchese

When the actor-director Olivia Wilde was last in the public eye, around the time of her 2022 dystopian thriller, “Don’t Worry Darling,” things weren’t going very well. Wilde had to deal with the twin fallout of decidedly mixed critical reaction and a harsh wave of tabloid attention. The film was plagued by reports of feuding between Wilde and her star, Florence Pugh. Wilde was also hounded online for her relationship, which has since ended, with the pop star Harry Styles, who played a supporting role in the movie. If that wasn’t enough, the press cycle for “Don’t Worry Darling” brought with it continuing scrutiny over her 2020 breakup with her longtime partner, Jason Sudeikis, with whom she has two children. This year, though, it has all been very different.

“The Invite,” a painfully perceptive domestic sex comedy that Wilde, who is 42, directed and co-starred in, has been one of the year’s sleeper hits. She followed that up by playing, to delicious effect, a sexually domineering and manipulative art-world star in the director Gregg Araki’s “I Want Your Sex.” And she’s capping her year off with a small but scene-stealing role as an angrily spurned lover in the upcoming “Behemoth!” starring Pedro Pascal and directed by Tony Gilroy. I spoke to Wilde last month in London, where she was prepping her next directorial effort, a Christmas comedy called “Naughty,” about what it’s like to hit a low and how she so dramatically turned things around in her work and life.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

I was thinking about the three roles you played this year in “The Invite,” “I Want Your Sex” and “Behemoth!” All these characters are tightly wound, and I wondered if being a director has changed how you see yourself as an actor. Being a director freed me up to not feel pressure to be the ideal ingénue growing into the idealized female character in any film. I now choose roles from a much more curious place. But I hadn’t put together that these three characters are extremely high-strung in different ways. My character in “I Want Your Sex” felt like she was on the opposite end of the spectrum of femininity as my character in “The Invite.” They’re both movies dealing with the idea of sex and sexuality and desire and eroticism from two completely different perspectives.

Why are you interested in exploring questions of sex and identity at this point in your life? It’s funny. I turned 40 a couple of years ago, and I suddenly felt more present in my body and more connected to my sense of confidence and sexuality than ever. We were told for a long time that that’s when things start shutting down. Less is available to you in terms of your career, in terms of your exploration of your own identity, sexuality. Yet every woman I know from like 40 to 70 has told me: “Oh, no. That’s when you really understand yourself.” You’re so much more honest with yourself, and there’s an awesome blossoming that happens at that point. So I think I was curious about inspecting that in different ways and particularly in comedies, because it’s good to laugh at this stuff.

We don’t really think about it this way, but there is something inherently funny about sex. Oh, completely. It’s hilarious. There’s something funny about everything that we don’t talk about. There’s something funny about people white-knuckling things in life. I remember when we made “Booksmart,” I found it so funny to reconnect with the stress we felt in high school about what we had accomplished and where we were going to go to college. The intensity of that stress is very funny to me now. The idea of high emotional stakes in a low-stakes situation really makes me laugh.

“Booksmart” was the first film you directed. It’s about two high school friends who are wrestling with expectations about how girls are supposed to behave and what they’re supposed to want. What do you think those girls would make of your character, Angela, from “The Invite”? It seems to me that Angela is exactly who the girls from “Booksmart” don’t want to be. I love that. I think they’d be really disappointed in her for giving up her career for marriage and kids, even though she doesn’t really think that she did it for those reasons. It’s a slow erosion of self that happens through this sense of duty. She has subtly assigned responsibility for that erosion to her husband [Joe, played by Seth Rogen], but really it was a decision Angela made on her own to sacrifice her own dreams as an artist. Molly and Amy from “Booksmart” would be horrified by that. But of course, they’ll get older and confront what a lot of people do, which is this negotiation one goes through at a certain point in life where they feel they must make sacrifices. There’s this sense of what you’re supposed to do, and it happens so slowly. It’s a bit of the frog-in-boiling-water concept — a slow realization that you have given something up, and you’re not even sure when or how.

Have you gone through that? I didn’t go through a sudden realization of like, Oh, my god, what have I given up? But I certainly have pivoted. Specifically at 35, I started directing movies, and it did feel like I was suddenly turning the ship in a different direction. And the panic that I didn’t go to film school; I had a lot of insecurity about that lack of traditional education. But the anxiety that everyone confronts when they consider pivoting is about this sense of: Am I allowed to do this? Do I have permission? There’s that great Nora Ephron commencement speech where she says: “I’ve had four careers and three husbands. You can change your mind.” I remember being so liberated by that one comment.

The potential risks of trying something different can be very scary. Not everyone is comfortable making that leap. When did we decide that you have to figure out your whole identity by 24? Like, pick your partner, pick your career, pick your identity — and if you change, it’s a little bit suspicious, a little chaotic. What would people do with their lives if they felt like they were allowed to change careers and change versions of themselves past college?

I can find myself thinking skeptically about change. In the abstract, it can be easy to say, “I need a change” or “We need a change in our relationship,” but where is the line between selfishness and making changes that other people can actually adapt to? Do you know what I mean? We can’t deny we are changing. You are changing, so it’s not a decision to change. It’s a decision to acknowledge the change. Like in a relationship, you’re not saying, “Now I’m going to allow for my partner to change.” No, they’re changing. You’re changing. You can either embrace it or resist.

I’m thinking, what if I showed up at my house on Monday in a leather jacket and said, “Everyone get used to it!” [Laughs] “This is the new me! I’m leather-jacket Dave now.” You know, every year in school you’re like: “I’m going to be different this year. This is my new look. Different music, different vibe.” There’s this excitement of that creation and exploration of identity. I don’t know why we stop allowing it. It becomes something we don’t like. We don’t trust it.

Just to tie some of this into your work, “The Invite” does such a good job of acknowledging the ebb and flow within a relationship and how someone could have a desire for more or for something different. But what were the aspects of the film specifically to do with relationship dynamics that you felt most connected to? Oh, my god. The resistance to changing your life because of how it will affect others and the pain of that. Also just the difficulty of relationships. Because it’s [expletive] hard. It’s impossible. I’m going to try to link lives and cohabitate with somebody over a long period of time and co-pilot this life and this child? I think people are eager to release some of that shame and laugh. The movie’s obviously heavily influenced by Mike Nichols and “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” and one thing I love about that movie is that George and Martha fight and fight but they are so codependent. They follow each other around the house. They won’t be in separate rooms. It reminds me of my kids. My kids bicker and bicker, but they love each other. They hate when one of them goes away, even for a sleepover. I think that in a relationship, once people reach contempt, it’s not the aggressive rage, it’s the indifference that is truly terrifying. That is the sign that you may be beyond repair. These are all things that I’ve experienced at different points in my life.

You referred to shame a second ago. What have you felt shame about? It feels like a failure when you can’t make a relationship work, particularly if it’s with the person you have children with. We talk about a lot of different things in the film that are racy in different ways, but I think the most subversive part of the movie is a moment where Penélope Cruz’s character says, “You think you’re doing something noble by staying together for your children, as if they don’t notice, as if they don’t feel this anxiety that they’re marinating in.” That is by far the most difficult, painful decision I’ve ever made in my life, to understand that it was not better for my kids to live in a house where their parents were not aligned. My parents are still together and have an incredible relationship. They worked together for many years; they’re both journalists. And I always thought that would be me. And the shame also comes from that — when you feel like you haven’t nailed this thing that we’re supposed to nail. We’re told if you’re good at it, you’ll stay with someone forever. If you’re not so good, it’s a bit of a disappointment.

The idea of needing to stay together for the kids is obviously a hugely sympathetic and common one, but my parents divorced when I was very young and —— Really? How young?

I was 4 or 5. I cannot imagine a world in which my parents had stayed together. It was clearly the right decision, but I’m sure, particularly for my mother, incredibly fraught. Very, very brave. I really take pride in how good we are at co-parenting our kids in my family. We have reached this healthy equilibrium. It’s so hard. Anyone who pretends it’s easy — like, “Oh, you just consciously uncouple, and then you find a way” — that’s BS. I feel relieved that I’m able to give them a life with parents where there’s a real sense of authenticity in terms of how everyone’s feeling and doing. When you’re trying to hide it from your kids, they sense it. They’re the most intuitive people in the house. And then people start to feel, like, What is real? Because I can tell that something’s being performed for me. I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.

I want to ask a question about your character in “I Want Your Sex” — an art-world provocateur. I read that you drew on Madonna from her “Truth or Dare” documentary for your performance. Can you tell me what you took from her? The most incredible documentary. I think it’s my favorite music doc. There’s the famous scene where I think she was in Toronto performing, and they were told right before the show that if she performed one lewd act, which was just a part of her performance, they would arrest her. And she’s like, Great, put me in jail. There’s this complete fearlessness. She knows her power. And I think that was exactly how it related to Erika Tracy, the character from the film. It’s this awareness of one’s ability to provoke and a fearlessness to do so. I also appreciated being able to be very comfortable in my body in that film. You don’t think that you’re going to turn 40 and play a dominatrix.

That’s the second time you’ve referred to getting older and feeling comfort in your body. Were there times earlier in your life when you felt a lot of discomfort in your body? Yeah, and it’s been a pretty smooth, exponential evolution toward being comfortable. I think having kids made me feel more comfortable in my body. Again, there’s a lie we’re told that you have kids and you’re done, just put you out to pasture and shoot you in the head because your body means nothing. But it’s the opposite. Once you’re aware of what you’re capable of in having kids, I think suddenly you’re like: Wait a minute. Am I a superhero? What else can I do? And then watching your body repair itself from this insane endeavor of making a human — wow, respect. I had my first kid at 30 and then 32. So it’s been 10 years, and I feel like I’ve just become more and more comfortable.

You know, the last time you were making the big press rounds was for “Don’t Worry Darling,” and that whole thing got, I don’t want to say derailed, but —— “Derailed” is a fair word.

It got wrapped up in a lot of extracurricular stuff about your personal life and rumors of tension on set and things like that, in a way that seemed wildly —— Disproportionate.

How much of that do you think had to do with sexism? I don’t know. I think a lot has to do with the way we receive information. I don’t begrudge a populace who is inherently distrustful of public figures because of the way that our country has run itself into this very dangerous rut of fascism, or nearing fascism. And it’s happened because we have lost track of certain skills of critical thinking. But it’s been fed to us with this onslaught of information that’s impossible to unwind and organize. I know it seems crazy to take your question about a tabloid storm and relate it to something like fascism, but I come from a family of journalists. Beyond my parents, my grandfather was a wonderful journalist who’s famous for this saying: “Believe nothing until it is officially denied.” I think that’s healthy. So I didn’t blame people for feeling curious about what became this media storm around that movie. When there’s a lack of information, people fill the void with assumptions. Some of it has to do with the way the media talks about women, but I think it’s broader than that.

I want to make sure I understand you. Your hypothesis is that there would be dribs and drabs of maybe-inaccurate information coming out about the film, and in the absence of factual information, people became attracted to the story because they were filling in the blanks themselves. Yeah, they become storytellers. I think we all do that. So, yes, my hypothesis is that because there was something kind of titillating and mysterious about what people felt they knew about that movie and everything around it, they created a narrative that was so far from the truth. And every story needs a villain. I was cast as said villain. It’s something I don’t have any rage about. I think it took me a few years of zooming out and thinking about lots of other things to realize, Oh, that really had very little to do with me. I also grew a lot from it. I’m a very different person now. Anything that forces you to do a bunch of therapy and think deeply and read a bunch of books and travel — anything that throws you off is actually potentially very, very good for you.

How are you a different person now? I’m way less concerned with how I am perceived. It’s sort of like the saturation point. You’re outside with an umbrella, but you’re already wet, and you’re like: I don’t need this umbrella. I am already soaked. So I think that I approach things without a real fear of whether or not I’ll be adored. I didn’t even realize I had that before, but I did feel this kind of heartbreak of like, Oh, no, I’ve been misunderstood. It’s so destabilizing, and I’ve lost that. There’s a certain amount of vulnerability that I’m now able to express in my work that before was locked away. So it broke me, but in a way that was necessary in the end.

I don’t want to put you in a position where I’m asking you to unpack the worst moments of your life. And yet —— [Laughs] That’s what I do!

But when you say something like “It broke me” —— It’s a very dramatic thing to say.

It sounds dramatic, but it could also be true. Earlier this year, you were on Alex Cooper’s podcast, and you talked about that moment around “Don’t Worry Darling” as when you hit rock bottom. Very few other people have had the experience that you’re talking about. So can you help us understand what that was like and why it made you feel broken? You say very few people have had the experience. Maybe at that scale, but people are going through ruptures in their lives all the time. For me, the real heartbreak has nothing to do with public scrutiny or anything in the media. I went through a rupture in my own life. I went through a separation that was incredibly heartbreaking. So to go through that and then to avoid dealing with the real pain of what was happening to then launch into a movie in Covid, that’s an insane thing to do. All of that personal stuff being warped and twisted and used in this public way, that’s the part that’s specific to this industry. The crazy thing is, that was four years ago, and it is the least interesting thing about me. And yet I find myself having to talk about it over and over again. The annoying thing is that we could have a conversation about so many things, and the pull quotes and headlines will be about the past. That’s the part that bums me out. Because I don’t live in the past. It’s not the experience itself. It’s having to rehash it.

Which I’m asking you to do. But I get it. I understand. I also think if you’re going to make a movie about relationships and pain and identity, you have to be willing to say, I’m not coming from a place of complete ignorance. I have been through some [expletive] that gives me a little bit of authority on some of these topics.

You know, I’m thinking about your hypothesis from a second ago. I’m sure it’s correct, but on a more base level, you were dating a pop star, and people since the 1920s have been hungry for stories about backstage drama in Hollywood. Your story had the elements tabloid readers and tabloid makers are into. So maybe there was also a more straightforward reason for the attention. Or maybe it all worked together. It all worked together. A perfect storm. It’s funny, sometimes this business reminds me of the scene in “Galaxy Quest” when Sigourney Weaver and Tim Allen are running down that tunnel on the spaceship with all the big slicers. And Sigourney Weaver’s character just goes, “This is a terribly written episode.” Sometimes this business feels like a terribly written episode. But then, you know, that episode ends. It was just for sweeps week.

Something that I was curious about was how earlier in your career you were on the cover of GQ posing in a swimsuit, and you were No. 1 on Maxim’s Hot 100 list. But as someone who is clearly an intellectual person, did you have ambivalence about primarily being appreciated publicly for your appearance? I would think that would be weird. I feel so relieved to no longer feel pressure to be that. It’s so clear to me that I’m only still working because of my brain. It’s so fun when you get past the point where your physical self is the valuable thing, or could even be misinterpreted to be the valuable thing. I mean, the Maxim thing is so insane. Can you imagine if they did that today? Ranking women based on looks?

I mean, I hate to tell you —— [Laughs] You’re like, Have you seen the internet? This is why I love directing, because my only purpose as a director are the decisions that come from my mind. I don’t have the physical ability to move the lights, to run the cables, to shoot the cameras. My brain is the valuable thing on set, and my heart. I feel so happy to be in this place where I get to enjoy aging in a way that some actresses don’t. There aren’t many professions where the more experience you have, the less valuable you are. But acting is one of them.

I read that Esther Perel was your therapist in your 20s. Is that true? I revealed that, and then realized that I wasn’t supposed to.

I was just curious if there is a piece of guidance that she gave you back then that you still carry with you. I should note, Perel was a consultant on “The Invite.” I think she’s given me advice more recently as a friend and as a colleague — the idea of taking responsibility for your own happiness and understanding the value of your choices. It seems so simple, but it’s very easy to accidentally blame your unhappiness on your profession, on your partner, on your parents. Taking responsibility for your own happiness is a worthwhile endeavor.

It’s also hard because that requires you to look critically at yourself, and people don’t always like to do that. They don’t. I used to go around being like, I don’t have any regrets, and you get to a point where you’re like, Yeah, I regret things. The idea that it somehow makes you stronger and better to be like, I have done nothing wrong and I feel no shame, why is that strength? I am very happy to be open about having felt that sense of failure. I have confronted that darkness, and it’s OK. I think we have to start framing life as an inevitable series of failures, acknowledging that the definition of success is not avoiding regrets. It’s learning from everything.

So to wrap up: When you were promoting “Don’t Worry Darling,” it turned into a weird hot mess but now feels like a celebratory moment of accomplishment for you. I wonder if that change feels like it reflects something about who you are right now? Or maybe it reflects the fact that the public reception to you or your work actually has very little to do with how you feel about yourself? That’s so interesting. You would think I’d have given that some thought. If I had tried to make “The Invite” right away, I don’t think that there would have been this kind of reception. I don’t think people would have accepted it from me. I think that I needed to go and do the work and take space and get smarter and better. And, I don’t know, maybe the world moved on to someone else. In high school, the bullies end up getting sick of picking on the same kid, and they’re like, Well, he didn’t die, and move on to the next. I made myself a man in that metaphor. Unpack it.

Paging Dr. Freud! Hmm. But to come full circle on this conversation, the concept of change and pivoting — it’s not like, Now I’m whole and evolved and this is me. What this experience has shown me is the capacity for change, and I can’t wait to figure out who I get to grow into. I’m very curious about what’s next, what else I have to learn, and say, and be.

This interview has been edited and condensed. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Aaron Katter

David Marchese is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a regular series featuring influential people across culture, politics, business, sports and beyond.

Top Democrat Eyes Filibuster-Proof Bill to Unlock Affordability Agenda

The New York Times November 14, 2026

120th U. S. Congress

Advertisement

Supported by

The lawmaker set to lead the House Budget Committee outlined Democrats’ options for forcing a negotiation with President Trump on an economic package to bring down living costs.

By Catie Edmondson

Reporting from the Capitol

A top House Democrat mapping out how to leverage his party’s vast majorities in Congress next year to push through a sweeping economic agenda is considering using a filibuster-proof bill to muscle it through both chambers and to President Trump’s desk.

The approach, outlined by Representative Brendan Boyle, the Pennsylvania Democrat in line to be chairman of the House Budget Committee in January, would be one way of forcing Mr. Trump to either embrace or veto broadly popular measures to lower living costs.

Triumphant after electoral victories delivered them more than 255 seats in the House and at least 55 seats in the Senate, Democrats are weighing the best strategy for quickly delivering the affordability agenda they promised voters, including tackling the soaring costs of health care, child care and housing.

Mr. Boyle, the 49-year-old son of a janitor for Pennsylvania’s transportation authority and a school crossing guard, is now positioned to lead the way from his perch at the helm of the House panel that handles budget matters and sets spending priorities.

In an interview, Mr. Boyle said it was “worth exploring” using budget reconciliation — a tool that allows the party in power to bypass opposition from the minority and push through fiscal legislation on majority votes — to unlock the affordability agenda Democrats ran on, including reversing Medicaid cuts Republicans enacted unilaterally in 2025.

“I think any time we can pass good, popular, meaningful legislation, that only strengthens our hand in any ultimate negotiation with the White House,” Mr. Boyle said.

He also said he would like Democrats to forge a deal with Mr. Trump on the statutory limit on the national debt, ending what has become a perennial cycle of high-stakes fiscal clashes between the president and Congress that have repeatedly brought the country dangerously close to a federal default. Mr. Boyle has long pushed for legislation that would allow the Treasury Department to suspend the debt limit, subject to congressional override, rather than requiring an affirmative vote by Congress to increase it.

“He wants it raised,” he said of Mr. Trump. “We never again want to see a Democratic president have to have this held like a gun against their head, the same way it happened to Joe Biden and to Barack Obama.”

A sharp but sociable communicator, Mr. Boyle is part of a younger vanguard of House Democrats rising to the top echelons of the party. He said that no final decisions had been made, but outlined a scenario in which Democrats early next year would first try to pass their economic agenda with some Republican backing, which they would need to steer around a filibuster in the Senate. He suggested Democrats could then move to a partisan reconciliation package if they failed to win over G. O. P. supporters.

“It’s worth exploring reconciliation now that we have both the House and the Senate; however, I think it’s also worth exploring the fact that we’re 56,” Mr. Boyle said, referring to the number of Senate seats Democrats would control if they won a seat in Alaska, where their candidate was leading. “Are there four Senate Republicans who we could work with on issue X, on issue Y, to get things passed in a more expeditious manner?”

That strategy would be in step with what Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, has privately outlined to his caucus. He has said he is prepared to move to a filibuster-proof effort if Republicans will not back Democratic legislation meant to address cost-of-living issues.

Mr. Boyle said he would defer to Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader who is expected to become speaker, on whether the costs of an economic package would need to be offset by new taxes.

Democrats could try to pay for the cost of such a plan by rolling back tax cuts for the “megawealthy” that Republicans enacted during the first and second Trump administrations, he said.

Or they could not pay for them at all. Mr. Boyle said Democrats could argue: “Look, those folks passed a massive, $5 trillion bill and only paid for a fraction of it; we certainly shouldn’t be held to a different standard.”

In 2021, when Democrats used their governing trifecta in Congress under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. to advance a legislative package through reconciliation, feuding broke out between the moderate and progressive flanks of the party over the scope and cost of the bill.

The House eventually passed a $2.2 trillion measure known as “Build Back Better.” But in the months of debate, centrists in the Senate pushed to narrow the measure substantially, outraging progressives, who then threatened to withhold their support for a separate $1 trillion bipartisan infrastructure bill.

Not yet at the helm of the budget panel, Mr. Boyle still vividly remembers the internal party churn that threatened to tank both bills and the multiday slogs he endured to pass them out of committee.

“When it got to the Senate, because of the math of 50-50, where every Senate Democrat could be king or queen, the bill got slimmed down considerably, about half of the size,” he said. “The name changed, and a lot of the things that I felt the best about in that bill were stripped out.”

“The biggest difference now,” Mr. Boyle said, “is 56 is a lot easier than 50.”

Michael Gold contributed reporting.

Catie Edmondson covers Congress for The Times.
